en: Śrīḥ.

May that divine horse-headed one (Hayamukha) constantly bestow upon the subjects and the king the four aims of human existence—which are determined by dharma through the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and established custom, as well as by their own extensive conventions—and grant them wisdom, power, enthusiasm, and unwavering fortitude. Salutations to the Sacrifice, the Supreme Self! "The Vedas are our supreme wealth"—this is the proclamation of those who have realized Brahman, beginning with Āyodhyaka.

Study is unavoidable and beneficial according to one's capacity; it is not impossible. This is the designation of "wealth. The Śruti states: "The Veda with its six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) must be studied and known by a Brāhmaṇa as a duty without motive. [The sages] consider that for a Brāhmaṇa, the very attainment of his true nature is impossible without the study of the Veda, and that through such study, the highest spiritual good (śreyaḥ) in the hereafter is easily accomplished. Therefore, having studied the Veda along with its limbs, one is glorified in the world of Brahman.

Thus, while instructing the Vedic community in steadfastness, the supreme seer Pāṇini also taught that the Vedas are the means for attaining the highest good (*śreyas*), and that their auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*)—namely Śikṣā, Vyākaraṇa, Chandas, Nirukta, Jyotiṣa, and Kalpa—are the necessary equipment for understanding how they serve as such means. Regarding this, both Śaunaka and Pāṇini teach that the *Kalpas* constitute the primary instruments for the undertaking and avoidance [of ritual acts], stating: "Among them, the Kalpa is recited as the hands."

Regarding the commencement of the *Kalpasūtras*, the word "kalpa" refers here to ritual application (*prayoga*). And such ritual application was easily to be mastered without effort during a period when there were many great sages who were deeply learned and skilled in performance, who were preoccupied primarily with wealth, who were far removed from even a trace of the defects of the Kali age, and who, as students of various recensions (*śākhās*) along with their auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*) and secret doctrines (*rahasyas*), propagated the continuous flow of the tradition by synthesizing the various specific details contained in those different recensions.

Subsequently, as the [Vedic texts] were circulating among those who were neither seers nor even those who had heard them from seers, the great seers possessing authoritative status—anticipating defects such as deficiencies in performance and desiring to favor the faithful practitioners—composed Sūtra compositions that were easy to understand by means of a method of both concise and detailed treatment, through a compendium of various specific details found in the various Śākhās.

It is said that those who are renowned for the sake of awakening [do so] precisely through the words of the *sūtras* adorned by the well-chosen names of Aśvalāyana, Āpastamba, Hiraṇyakeśin, Khādira, Āhryāyaṇa, Lāṭyāyana, Śāṅkhāyana, Mānava, Vārāha, Kauśika, Vaikhānasa, Bhāradvāja, and others. Regarding them, the *Juhūkalpa* (Su. 633; 18-1-3 Su. is so called because Dhūrtasvāmin and Par̤isvāmin explain it as "the ritual manual (*kalpa*) is the injunction (*vidhi*). And the *Rāmāgnicitā* completes the sense with the phrase "by way of practical application (*prayogatayā*)."

Furthermore, because the two commentators explain the word *kalpa* as being synonymous with the word *vidhi* (injunction) elsewhere, its status as such is determined. The commentators and others consider the very reason stated for the commencement of the *Kalpasūtras* to be the one intended here: regarding the statement "We shall explain the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices," in order to establish the necessity of this explanation, someone might object that "there is no need for the effort of a Sūtra-author since the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices have already been explained in the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas"; and to that, [the reply is] "that is not so."

"Because the meaning [of the Veda] is difficult to perceive through the individual *āyatanas* (branches/sections), and because there is a compendium of manifold varieties, it is not purposeless"—so says Bhavasvāmin (in his commentary on *Tattvabodhinī*, p. 10). Likewise, at the beginning of his commentary on the *Bodhāyanakalpa*, Bhavasvāmin states: "Because of the great number of Brāhmaṇas, because the meaning is not fully completed within each single *śākhā*, and because the meaning is difficult to comprehend, the Teacher has commenced this *Kalpa* for the sake of providing a comprehensive exposition so that, having easily understood [it], they may perform the rituals and attain all the fruits."

Likewise, in the *Āśvalāyana-śrauta-devatrāta-bhāṣya* it is stated: "In that regard, having observed the limitations of human capacity, ritual manuals (*kalpas*) were composed by Śaunaka and other teachers according to established practices. Furthermore, the venerable Āpastamba recorded in his *Dharma-sūtras*: "The term 'austerity' (*tapas*) refers to observances (*niyamas*). If these are transgressed, knowledge and action flow away from this person along with their offspring; [such conduct] is ruinous to one's family and detrimental to longevity."

"Therefore, Ṛṣis are not born among later generations due to the transgression of observances; yet some 'Śruta-ṛṣis' (Ṛṣis by learning) come into being through the remainder of the fruits of their actions upon rebirth, such as Śvetaketu" (Sūtras 1.5.5–1.6). Regarding this, Haradatta states that "the status of a *kartapatya* is a cause for falling into hell. We understand from the words of the venerable Pāṇini that the Kalpas existed prior to him, for he says: "The Kalpasūtras composed by the Great Ṛṣis have been brought into circulation by the Ṛṣis themselves."

For, having commenced with the word *pravacana* (proclamation) in the sense of "taught by him" (*tena proktam*), [Pāṇini] likewise records in his *Smṛti* that the authors of the *Kalpas* are like the authors of the Vedas, such as Tittiri and others, in the rule: *purāṇaprokteṣu brāhmaṇakalpeṣu*.

Although it may be argued that the word *kalpa* in the expression “the Purāṇas and the Kalpas” refers to a portion of the Veda—as seen in its usage there—and that its recitation is as natural for it as it is for the *Maheśyāmnāya*, nevertheless, in the rule “from *pārāśarya* and *śilālin* [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] to denote the *bhikṣusūtra* and the *naṭasūtra*,” the author of the *Kalpasūtras* is mentioned; and since Jaimini, the founder of the Mīmāṃsā system, while citing the composition of the *Kalpasūtras*, refers to the teacher Bādarāyaṇa...

Pāṇini himself firmly acknowledges the great antiquity of the oral tradition of the sacred teachings (*pravacanaparamparā*). And Kātyāyana, the author of the Vārttikas, explicitly states its antiquity when he says, "The mention of Kāśyapa and Kauśika in the Kalpa-sūtra is for the sake of restriction. Furthermore, among the authors of the Kalpa-sūtra compositions, Āpastamba is renowned as one of the foremost. Since it is certain that this work [the Aṣṭādhyāyī] predates Pāṇini by a very long time, we shall now demonstrate the agreement of the Commentator (Patañjali).

Regarding the rule *tadasyāstyasminniti matup*, there is the Vārttika: *sanmātre ca ṛṣidarśanāt*. And regarding that, the Bhāṣya states: "And with respect to mere existence (*sanmātra*), the Seer (the Vedic sage) shows the use of the suffix *matup*: 'He sprinkles the sacrificial post with barley-grains (*yavamatībhiḥ*)."

And this statement is seen in the seventh book, ninth section, ninth sūtra of the Āpastamba-kalpa, beginning with "Having placed the sacrificial post (yūpa) in front of the banyan tree," and continuing with "Having washed the sacrificial post, he then sprinkles it with water containing barley. In this context, the word *yūpa* is employed by Patañjali as an explanatory gloss for the pronoun *enam*. This will become clear later in the discussion following Jaimini’s rules for ritual construction.

Who was this Āpastamba, and when did he live? Since Patañjali stated that the sentences of the *Kalpasūtras* are the words of sages (*ṛṣi*), and since Pāṇini also referred to the *Kalpasūtras* as having been proclaimed in antiquity, it is established that the lineage of sages dates back to the end of 450 years from the beginning of the Kali Yuga. Thus, Bhagavaddatta firmly concludes that the antiquity of the *Kalpasūtras* composed by sages extends back to within 450 years of the start of the Kali Yuga. And Yājñavalkya says: "Yama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Kātyāyana, and Bṛhaspati..."

"Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śaṅkha, and Likhita, Dakṣa and Gautama, Śātātapa, and Vasiṣṭha are the authors of the Dharmaśāstras. Thus, while composing his own compendium on Dharma, he recalls the authors of ancient Dharma-nibandhas and considers Āpastamba to be one among them.

Regarding this, Yajñeśvara, the commentator on the Bodhāyana-kalpa, says: "May Bodhāyana grant you wisdom—he who, together with sixty thousand disciples, had Āpastamba as his preeminent disciple, the master of one hundred and one *yajus* formulas; he who composed a Sūtra containing a clear, soft, yet profound and mature composition, suitable for the comprehension of various practical applications by Adhvaryu priests skilled in many methods. He, by his own power, churned the ocean of the Vedas and bestowed the nectar of the Kalpa upon the multitude of Brahmins."

"Salutations to that Bodhāyana, whose pair of lotus-feet are worshipped by sages, and who is the son of Kaṇva. Furthermore, in the compendium titled *Prāyaścittavicintana*, it says: "I bow to Bodhāyana, Jaimini, Kauṣītaki, Āśvalāyana, Vādhūla, Kātyāyana, and others—the originators of the Śākhās. Thus, this demonstrates that Āpastamba is included among the originators of the Śākhās.

By citing the *Bahuca-Śāṭyāyani*, *Paiṅgi-Chandoga*, and others by their specific school names (*pada*) as authoritative Brāhmaṇas, the venerable Āpastamba provides sufficient ground for the conclusion that he lived in a period subsequent to the venerable Vedavyāsa, the classifier of the Vedic branches. Furthermore, his inclusion among the promulgators of the *Dharmaśāstra* alongside Parāśara makes it highly probable that he belonged to an even earlier era.

Even his manifestation—which is based on the grace of the Supreme Person, which in turn depends upon the meritorious deeds of various ascetics—is known through the very tradition of the Śrutis in such passages as, "By this indeed does the hymn (sūkta) of Viśvāmitra come into being," and "The Veda breathed forth from the Self-existent; that constitutes the seerhood of the seers. This same principle applies to the Brāhmaṇas as well; such is their provenance.

Since even the examples for that [classification] must conform to it, there is no certainty that it necessarily arose only after the division of the Vedic branches (*śākhā*). However, even so, because the four portions contained within the ten *daśas* were not compiled as one, following the Lord Vyāsa—who was the instructor of each individual branch—there arose, among the various branches of the oral tradition passed down through the lineage of Vaiśampāyana’s disciples, the Taittirīyas, which consist of two divisions: the Āukheyas and the Khāṇḍikēyas.

In this regard, since the second section of the *Caraṇavyūha* states, "Therein, there are five divisions known as the Khāṇḍikēyas: the Kāletā, the Hairaṇyakeśī, the Bhāradvājī, and the Āpastambī," it is established that the branch (śākhā) initiated by the venerable Āpastamba is conventionally designated by his name; thus, the venerable Āpastamba can be understood as being the very form of the teacher of that branch.

The venerable Āpastamba, who belongs to the lineage of disciples of Bādarāyaṇa, was also the author of a Kalpasūtra; this is also evident from his own Kalpasūtras, where [the following] is recited: "The Vājasaneyins, some [recite]: the Kaṭhas, the Kapiṣṭhalakaṭhas, the Kālāpaka-Brāhmaṇas, the Kauṣītakins, the Chandoga-Brāhmaṇa, the Tāṇḍaka, the Tāṇḍins, the Bahvṛca-Brāhmaṇa, the Bhāllavika, the Vājasaneyaka, the Śāṭyāyanaka, the Śailāli-Brāhmaṇa, and the Śāṭyāyanins."

If it is argued that this was revealed by the venerable Āpastamba himself—who, in establishing the authority of the various Vedic portions propagated by Bahu and others following the division of the branches—then we say no; for the acceptance of those [texts] as authoritative can be explained as referring to those specific corrupted portions, and their antiquity is established through the sequence of reliance on what will be stated hereafter. Furthermore, it should be noted that the venerable Āpastamba enumerated in the lineage of transmitters is indeed another person.

1. Regarding the *Śulbapraśna*, [the author] cites a verse concerning the measurement of chariots as stated by Gārgya, Agastya, and others in Takṣaśilā in a number of verses (sixteen). From the introduction to this sūtra, it is also understood that this Āpastamba is posterior in time to Gārgya, Agastya, and others; for he says, "as it occurs in the Kalpasūtras and Bhāṣyas."

Even the refined Kalpasūtras, though originally of excellent form, have over time become difficult to understand; yet, considering that familiarity with them arises through those who—having long served their gurus and attained the secret meaning of the Vedas—are experts in performing and teaching rituals without doubt, these texts are being revitalized by the composition of commentaries and other works so that they may once again be capable of conveying their own intended meanings.

In that regard, Dhūrtasvāmin and Kapardisvāmin are the authors of commentaries (*bhāṣya*) on the collection of Āpastamba’s *Kalpasūtras*, and Rāmāṇīci is the author of the sub-commentary (*vṛtti*); these three are agreed upon as its protectors. Regarding the fact that the *Kalpas* are based upon the *Mīmāṃsā-darśana* and preceded by it: the certainty is that the *Kalpasūtras* are even more ancient than Jaimini’s *Mīmāṃsā-darśana* and are therefore the very source upon which it is founded.

For this reason, the *Kalpasūtra* of Āpastamba states, "On this night, neither the boys nor the horses obtain milk" (1.4.2), and it reiterates this same point in substance through the sūtra, "Likewise, there is a prohibition of milk for the boys" (11.1.51).

According to Āpastamba’s Sūtra, "The season and the lunar mansion [are not prescribed] for the *natu* sacrifice" (5.4.6)—this being the statement regarding the omission of the season and the lunar mansion—and because of the rule that "one mutters the *manthān* [verses]" (4.1.3), and because "the *mantras* are not instruments of action; they are like that" (3.8.15; 12.3.25), meaning that *mantras* serve as the means of performance, and because "the *pitṛyajña* is prescribed for its own specific time" (Pariśiṣṭa 2.35), it would follow that [the *natu* sacrifice] is not a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of that [main rite], as it occurs according to its own sequence.

(4-4-19) "And because it is enumerated as equal" (2.1.6); (4-4-20) "And because it is seen [to be so] even when prohibited" (2.3.7); (4-4-21) "Of the fire that does not carry away," etc.; and "not [the word] *devatā*, *agni*, *śabda*, or *kriyā*" (6.3.18).

1.1. In a conflict between purpose (*artha*) and substance (*dravya*), purpose is stronger—[this is the principle]. By that very sequence [of rules], [the rule] "in a conflict between substance and refinement" (ĀpDhS 6.3.38), and "now, the ritual acts according to custom" (ĀpGṛS)—when customs are being observed—"according to custom" (ĀpDhS 6.2.30), and so forth; as well as the *Vāsiṣṭha* [text] stating "that which is enjoined by rule, that which is praised as a debt"—[namely] the statement regarding the debts of Soma, Vedic study, and progeny (ĀpDhS 6.2.31)—and so on, by restating the *Āpastamba-kalpa* and the domestic rites (*gṛhya*) of others, it is understood that [the latter] is not inferior to the former.

In the sixth chapter [of the *Jaiminīya-sūtra*], [the following topics are treated]: 51–28; 6-3-1–7; 6-3-8–10, and likewise: in the first chapter, the qualified person (*adhikārin*) [is discussed]; 1-25, the distinction between sacrifice (*yāga*) and oblation (*homa*); 26–30, the obligatory rites (*nitya*) to be performed; 27–41, the performance of optional rites with their constituent parts (*sāṅga-kāmya-anuṣṭhāna*); 42, the efficacy of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*); 43, the meaning of the word "mantra"; 45, the definition of the *yajus*; 46, the reason for ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*); 47; the determination of the number of mantras; 48; the connection between mantra and ritual action (*mantra-karma-sambandha*); 49–53; 6-3-9; 11; 2-1-37).

2-1-48; 2-1-47; 12-3-25; 2-1-41: *upacaraṇa* (approach/application); the semantic power of the word *barhis*; the status of being both original and modified (*prakṛti-vikṛti-arthatā*); 54–55; 56; 1-4-11; 73; 11; 6-8-9: discussion on substitutes (*pratinidhi*); 86–100; by the force of purpose, substance, and so forth; 101–104; 6-3-13–41; 6-3-39; 1; 5-1-14: the sequence of subsidiary acts (*aṅga-karma*); 105–113; by the force of determinants of sequence; 9; 114–121; 5-1-1–5: the agent when the portion cut off (*avatta*) is lost; 122–126; 6-4-1–2: determination of eligibility for the *sattra* sacrifice; 134–148.

(10-6-45-50) An investigation into the Tantras; (149–165) Oṃ; (11th Adhyāya) the cause of the beginning and end, 175; Alternatives and Combinations: 176–190; (12th Adhyāya) [Continued]; (11) 195; (12-3-20-22) The stability of vowels within mantras; 196–199; (12th Adhyāya) Thus, Kātyāyana, the author of the Kalpasūtra, has conducted this deliberation on matters useful for the determination of the meaning of the Vedas.

It demonstrates the connection of each preceding [work] with its predecessor, such as the *Pravacana* (the Veda), and Jaimini treats that very subject in detail. Jaimini’s definition of injunction (*vidhi*) is found at *Pūrva-mīmāṃsā-sūtra* 1.1.1; Satyāṣāḍha’s definition of the Brāhmaṇa is at *Śrauta-sūtra* 1.1.32.11.1) 9.

Jaimini, as well as Satyāṣāḍha, delineates the framework for determining the meaning of the Vedas within his own ritual system (*kalpa*) as follows: the determination of the scope of application (*viṣayavyavasthā*); the section on the *darvihoma* (8.4.1.28); the investigation of extended application (*atideśavicāra*) in the eighth book; the investigation of modification (*ūhavicāra*); the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*), and the transformation of the body (*pratardehavikāratām*). It is in this manner that Jaimini establishes the apparatus for the ascertainment of Vedic meaning, and Satyāṣāḍha likewise does so.

Thus, throughout beginningless time, the investigation into the performance [of rituals], their authoritative sources, and the various methods of their practice has been described by various authors of Kalpasūtras, both concisely and in detail, as appropriate. Consequently, what among the logical determinations required for sacrificial acts remains unestablished in the many compendia of ritual? Therefore, following the very path already trodden by the highly wise sages of the past, the teacher Jaimini also, while proceeding, composed this vast and comprehensive system of philosophy (*darśana*).

The trustworthy [authorities] state that he caused [the Veda] to be recited. This is also established by the mention of the name Jaimini in the *Jaimini-sūtra*. Likewise, Bādarāyaṇa also [states this] in the sūtra: "If it is argued that it is for the purpose of the *pāriplava*, no, because of its being specified" (*Pūrva-mīmāṃsā-sūtra* 4.3.10). In this sūtra, by the word *pāriplava*, those [stories] which were referred to by Āpastamba with the words, "To the south of the Āhavanīya fire, the Hotṛ sits upon a golden cushion, desiring to recite the *pāriplava*, the *bhauvana*, and the *ānuvāka*," and which were also [referred to] by Āśvalāyana as "to the south... [are intended].

By stating, "Seated on a golden cushion at the Āhavanīya fire, he should recount the Pariplava [narratives] to the consecrated king who is surrounded by his attendants," and so forth, [the text] merely reiterates those very narrations and recitations prescribed for the nine-day session; therefore, even the view of Bādarāyaṇa is certainly posterior to that.

In the *Gṛhyatātparyadarśana* it is also stated: "The sacrifices (*yajña*)—which require various means, which have constituent parts located in various Vedic branches (*śākhā*), whose verbal expressions are determined by thousands of principles of Mīmāṃsā, which are difficult for those of dull intellect in the present day to perceive, and which cannot possibly be performed if they remain unknown—might lead one to incur sin [through non-performance]. Therefore, with a mind filled with compassion, the Author of the Sūtras, having briefly explained twenty-one sacrifices in the introductory definition (*paribhāṣā*) with the words 'We shall explain the sacrifice,' and finding that much alone to be insufficient, [proceeds with] 'Now, therefore, the Darśapūrṇamāsa...'"

Beginning with these words, Sudarśanā states that the *haviryajña-saṃsthās*—such as the *kṣāmavatī* and others—along with the *naimittika* and especially the *kāmya* rites, have been explained in detail for the sake of the listener. Furthermore, the intention here is that the entire collection of *mīmāṃsā* principles is currently in practice, being transmitted both concisely and in detail through the lineage of sages who initiated the successive *kalpa-sūtras*.

This being the case, just as the commentaries on the *Yajñaparibhāṣāsūtra* and the treatises composed as commentaries on the Vedas accepted therein, the Mīmāṃsā system also becomes established as being essentially a commentary on the science of sacrifice (*yajñaśāstra*). Thus, it is proven that the purpose of the Veda must be fulfilled through all these scriptural commentaries in perfect harmony.

The exposition of the *Yajña-śāstra* and the exposition of the Vedas as embraced by it—only those who know the secrets of such a system of Mīmāṃsā philosophy are capable of commenting upon the *Kalpasūtras*, which constitute the *Yajña-śāstra*. Indeed, Dhūrtasvāmin, Kapardisvāmin, and Rāmāṇḍāra, being precisely such individuals, are renowned as the authors of commentaries (*bhāṣya*) and sub-commentaries (*vṛtti*) on their respective *Kalpasūtra* treatises, and as the authors of extensive works that preserve the path of sacrificial performance.

XIV.11.11. According to the opinion of the authors of the Sūtras, the Agnihotra begins in the evening and concludes in the morning; there is a desire for the commencement in the evening and a restriction regarding the materials. For the Mīmāṃsakas, however, "Agnihotra" is merely the name of the ritual act and does not refer to the entire complex [of rites]; thus, for them, the commencement may take place at whichever homa one chooses. (Bhāṣya) According to the view of the Mīmāṃsakas, the initial resolve (*saṅkalpa*) is: "I shall sacrifice with the Āgrayaṇa so that I may attain the heavenly world. Where a specific desire (*kāma*) is not mentioned in the scripture, there is the instruction that no desire should be entertained. (Bhāṣya)

Because the *Āgrayaṇa* is adventitious (*āgantuka*), the *ajyānya* verses are performed without contradiction. For the Mīmāṃsakas, the *Āgrayaṇa* is primary; thus it is an application of that which is non-permanent. Since the archetype (*prakṛti*) is to be accomplished with or without qualities, its procedure (*tantra*) applies there in every respect. (Bhāṣya) 11. Although the Mīmāṃsakas have stated that the term *vaiśvadeva* applies by way of the "staff-bearer" logic (*daṇḍinyāya*) due to its association with the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) in the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, here the etymological explanation given in the Brāhmaṇa is relied upon. (Bhāṣya)

11. Eleven officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) perform the ritual of the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*). Even though there is a slaughterer (*śamitṛ*), he does not [thereby] become an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). Although the Mīmāṃsakas have stated that the slaughterer is indeed the *adhvaryu* priest, because we see in the *Viśvasṛjām Ayana* that "the lord of the people is the slaughterer," the slaughterer is someone else; there is no authority to designate him as an officiating priest. (Vṛtti) Therefore, since the ritual procedure (*tantra*) was commenced when the primary time had arrived, this is the occasion for the [ritual] performance.

"The distinction of its state is grasped through etymological interpretation (*nirukti*). For the Mīmāṃsakas, however, there is no intention to express [the meaning] in *nirukti* and so forth; rather, the sole cause is the mere commencement of the ritual procedure at the improper time. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya 1.1.13) "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni and Varuṇa as the Sviṣṭakṛt; recite the offering verse for Agni and Varuṇa as the Sviṣṭakṛt," say the Mīmāṃsakas (Bhāṣya 19). "The *aupayaja* offerings and the *pāśuka* rites beginning with the carrying of the fire to the shed are performed even though they are not explicitly prescribed by a specific injunction."

The Mīmāṃsakas [claim] that because of the statement ending with the sprinkling of the *praṇītā* water and the purification (*mārjana*), the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) returns to the house; they say, "And she, being the fee, should go to the virtuous ones," because it occurs at the conclusion of the principal fee. This is not tenable; therefore, the fee there is a single subordinate part (*aṅga*). There are many such examples. Mahādeva himself clearly stated this, having understood the opinion of the ritualists and the authors of the Sūtras.

"Those who are fearless strengthen [their position] by means of the very arguments indicated therein; favoring established tradition, they are worthy of honor in the performance of Vedic rites. Thus, "this [position] is not a refutation of mine that deviates from the doctrine of Jaimini. However, the followers of Jaimini (the Mīmāṃsakas), having raised the doubt regarding the animal being the archetype (*prakṛti*), have refuted it through logic. In our own school, however, the intended meaning of the Sūtra has been demonstrated in the exposition of the logic indicated by the direct instruction (*svopadeśa*). Therefore, this very method is to be understood in our Sūtra.

Thus—some assert an alternative between *nyāya* (reasoning) and *upadeśa* (instruction), but that is not correct; for how could *nyāya*, which is inference (*anumāna*), ever be equal to *śruti* (revealed scripture)? So it is said. Therefore, among the views expressed by the Mīmāṃsakas, only that which does not contradict one’s own respective tradition should be accepted; this is the position of the ritualists (*yājñika*). That which is accepted by the commentators on the sacrificial scriptures (*yajña-śāstra*) regarding the form and other attributes of the deities (*devatā-vigrahādi*) alone is to be adopted. As for the effort of the commentators on Jaimini’s work: they do not accept the form and other attributes of the deity in any way whatsoever; the deity is merely sound (*śabda-mātra*).

However, some object—whether conscious or unconscious—is accepted [as the deity], but not one possessing a physical body and the like. "In the case of worship and so forth, meditation upon it is merely superimposed" (Bhāṭṭadīpikā 914). And: "The deity possesses a physical body and the like, but not the capacity to bestow fruits, because that would involve a logical contradiction" (Śāstradīpikā).

This doctrine, originating with Śabarasvāmin, has been propagated by Mīmāṃsakas—who follow the conventions of Jaimini—through the presentation of logic and other arguments according to the strength of their own intellect.

Among those disputants, Khaṇḍadeva was the preeminent one; although he himself was capable of independently reflecting upon the intended meaning of the appropriate sūtras, he described this debate with the thought that his purpose was merely to propagate the confidence derived from the words of the successive tradition of Mīmāṃsaka scholars such as Śabara. Thus, he cried out aloud: "For me, speaking in this manner, my speech may be flawed; therefore, the remembrance of Hari alone is my refuge. This choice of refuge was made by him, who stood in the position of a representative for the entire class of earlier Mīmāṃsakas.

Indeed, merely by describing Jaimini’s intention [that there is no deity], one cannot claim that taking refuge out of fear of sin would—contrary to reality—become an object of practice for one whose mind is destroyed by atheism due to the deity, its grace, and so forth.

For even Khaṇḍadeva certainly knows the hidden intention of the Lord, the Veda-Purusha, which pertains to the reality of the deity, its grace, and so on; an intention he has received through the lineage of instruction from his own ancestors, and which is established by the words of the authors of the Kalpasūtras and the Vedabhāṣyas, who were masters of the entire essence of Mīmāṃsā and a multitude of most virtuous scholars.

Since the natural excellence of proficiency—rooted in the initial faith born from familiarity with the practice of that which is being protected—is difficult to suppress, such a censure of the doctrine is merely excessive. Furthermore, no one would be inclined to impute any fault to Jaimini, who stands at the forefront of those who proclaim Brahman.

The ultimate purpose [of the Mīmāṃsā] is the cultivation of faith in the system by refuting those who maintain that there is no desirable or undesirable fruit for what is eternally prescribed or prohibited, and so forth; for where else in the world is such unanimity observed, since some even hold exceptions regarding both liberation and heaven?

Thus, by demonstrating the absolute certainty of the purpose of the scripture—which consists of the human goals of heaven and liberation as distinguished by the differences among qualified aspirants—and by revealing the reprehensibility of those who do not accept it, [the author] states: "When students and teachers, or even those at the level of cattle, contemplate the Vedic sentences and their meanings, they then ascertain its non-human origin (apauruṣeyatva) through their own self-awareness. However, the conviction or mental impression of external logicians does not arise from that alone; therefore, [the scripture’s authority] is established by the Veda itself, which is capable of producing such a realization."

The authors of the *Vārttika*, stating that "the Mīmāṃsakas have drunk nothing but fame because of their composition of logic" (*Nyāyopanibandhanāt*), consider that Mīmāṃsā consists in the formulation of logic (*nyāya*) as accepted by those who know the meaning of the Vedas and are in agreement with them; they further hold that a great responsibility has been placed upon the heads of the Mīmāṃsakas to awaken outsiders (*bāhya*) and those who have entered the paths of logicians (*tārkika*), but not to disparage the path embraced by the supreme Vaidikas.

Those who are devoted to the path of practicing the eternal Dharma (*sanātanadharma*) and who, through the harmony of the multitude of words of the practitioners, possess hearts adorned by others—namely, the commentators on the *Kalpasūtras*—maintain this very position. For instance, regarding the offering of flour-leavings and husks in the third *praśna*, the commentator Rāmāṇḍāra states: "The deity of this oblation is either the Sun or the Person within the heart. Furthermore, regarding the fourth *praśna*, the author of the *Bhāṣya* states: "I shall perform the propitiation with the worship of the *vanaspati* (tree/plant)," and [he adds] "because [the deity] has been propitiated by the oblations."

Dhūrta Svāmī [on the] Fourth Question: Regarding the "Jyotiṣmatī" section—when the fire that was taken out for the sake of the Agnihotra goes out during the Agnihotra, its origin is as follows: that very Āhavanīya fire which previously went out is this same fire here that has become the deity. Of the previously extinguished fire residing in the embers, only the light (*jyotirmātra*) was destroyed; however, because the light of the Āhavanīya fire, though destroyed, continues to exist as the deity.

"In that very light of his which has flown away, he obtains it"—thus, according to the fourth view, this sacrifice is for the purpose of restoring the lost light, which is of the nature of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*). Regarding the mantra used during the descent (*upāvaroha*), the *Bhāṣya* states: "The Gārhapatya and other fires, having become deities, descend to the worldly realm. According to the author of the *Vṛtti*, in the sixth question, one propitiates [the fire] with oblations and then makes a request through benedictory prayers (*āśis*), because there is the possibility of provoking the deity's anger.

In the sixth book: "The first attainment belongs to the gods; that is the *āgrayaṇa* ritual"—this is the commentary of Svāmī. In the seventh book, regarding the etymological explanation of the word *vaiśvadeva*, the purpose here is the knowledge that the Supreme Self, named Agni, is to be worshipped by means of this collection of eight rituals; such is the Śruti. (Srauta-sūtra, Vol. I).

xvi. In the eighth question: "Prajāpati [is the deity] through the mind, for the blind one," because in the oblations the sacrificial deities take on the form of Soma according to their respective states, Soma possesses the nature of a deity. Thus says the Vṛtti. In the twelfth section: Indra alone is the deity, being the form of the Supreme Self, according to the Śruti: "To Indra from the self. Thus says the Vṛtti.

In the *Iṣṭihautrakalpa*: "Having taken up the mantra 'Bring forth your own majesty,' in our own view, the supplementary portion of the sentence is 'Bring forth the majesty of all the deities,' as it serves as an ancillary for the invocation of all deities. The commentary (*vṛtti*) states: "'This indeed is the majesty of the gods, which is Viṣṇu Parameṣṭhin'; [thus it refers] to Viṣṇu, the inner controller of all deities. In the fourth *praśna*: "When desire is absent, the word 'desire' is dropped; or even when it exists, its renunciation is better."

For this is the established principle of all scriptures: that the supreme propitiation of the Supreme Deity leads to the highest beatitude (*niḥśreyasa*). As it is said in the *Gītā*: "Whatever action is performed as a duty alone is considered to be of the nature of *sattva*. And the author of the *Sūtras* says: "These bodies are not produced by performing dharma while placing worldly ends before oneself. And Śruti teaches the bliss of one who is untouched by desire; thus says Vṛttikāra Kuṭuḍradatta. Likewise: "To Agni, whose form is the Supreme Self."

"Thus it should be understood everywhere that words denoting deities, such as 'the Axe' and so forth, ultimately terminate in the Supreme Self. Various reciters should perform discourses on Brahman, beginning with 'In the beginning, O Agni, this was indeed nothing at all,' and so on—this refers to the inquiry into Brahman. Furthermore, the author of the Kalpasūtras shows that the propitiation of Prajāpati is a great matter, and thus demonstrates his worship: even the authors of the Kalpasūtras compose hymns to the deities which bring about the excellence of ritual action."

As Drāhyāyaṇa says: "They call it the Brahman-space; they should chant the Gāyatra three times," and so on; Dhānañjayya says this refers to the fourfold hymn, while Gautama holds [a different view]. In his commentary on that, Dhanvin states that each of these [passages] establishes the Supreme Brahman.

By thus reflecting upon the statements of the author of the Bhāṣya, it is understood that the following points—His omnipresence as something beyond mere sound, His propitiation through worship, His pleasure and displeasure, His consumption of the oblation, His bestowal of fruits, and His possession of a form consistent with all these attributes—are established as the intended meaning of the Śruti. Furthermore, the sage Jaimini, who is counted among those who teach the entire collection of such virtuous rites, would not instruct that a deity devoid of essential nature (niḥsvarūpā) constitutes the meaning of the Veda.

The teacher Madhava, author of the *Āśvalāyanaprayogadīpikā*, also states in the twelfth book that although it was established in the determination of the archetypal performance (*prakṛtibhāva*) that the commonality of deity is weak, nevertheless, due to the commonality of the material substance mentioned in the context (*aupagranika*), the direct commonality of deity is indeed stronger. Furthermore, the commentator on the *Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana* supports the view that the ninth-book [discussion] refuting the corporeal form of the deity and so forth is not based on a sūtra (*utsūtra*).

Mahādeva, the commentator on the *Satyāṣāḍha-kalpa*, also states in his *Vaijayantī*: "The referents such as Indra and others are not worldly—that is, they are not objects of common experience—such that the denotative power (*śakti*) of words like 'Indra' could be grasped from the world. Rather, even they are to be known solely from the scripture (*śāstra*). And the scripture [speaks] of them as possessing a physical form (*vigraha*). The grasp of their denotative power pertains precisely to those [beings] with form; there is no linguistic usage regarding that which is devoid of form. Nor is the word itself the very nature of the deity, for there is a lack of evidence for such a thing being the meaning of a term, and because no such cognition occurs."

Therefore, whatever kind of entity is grasped through the apprehension of a word's power (*śaktigraha*), that alone is to be expressed by the respective deity-word; it is precisely therein that the injunction regarding [the entity] as a deity occurs. Bādarāyaṇa also established this point, as [the author] states. Furthermore, Sāyaṇācārya and others also support the corporeal form of the deities and so forth in their Vedabhāṣya.

If it is asked: "How can this objection by the great author [Vedānta Deśika], which takes the form of a critique that the refutation of the deity’s body and so forth is contrary to the Sūtras, be consistent with the fact that Jaimini himself accepts the deity’s body and so forth? And what is the manner of its resolution?"—let this be considered here. By revealing the heart of Jaimini, the venerable Nigamānta Guru [Vedānta Deśika] provides an awakening for those who propound the non-existence of deities (*nirdevatavādin*). Furthermore, in the first pāda of the ninth chapter [of the *Tantravārttika*], he states: "And regarding the fruit and the deity... (*phaladevatayośca*). Thus, through his commentary on the *Tattvaṭīkā*, he demonstrates how Jaimini’s own intention is to establish the existence of deities.

Since it follows from the injunction that both the fruit and the deity are [objects of the sacrifice], we shall explain those sūtras concerning the deity—beginning with "Or the deity might prompt [the action]"—among which the substance to be given is intended for the deity: why would the deity not prompt [the action]? Because, as in the case of agriculture and the like, it is logical that the action itself, which serves as the means to the fruit, is the prompter. To this, the sūtra says:

"Or rather, the deity should be the motivator for the feeding of the guest, because that [feeding] is for its sake. (9.1.6) The word "or" (*vā*) serves to set aside the doubt. The deity intended as the recipient of the oblation (*havis*) should be the motivator for the act of worship by one seeking a fruit. Why? Because the feeding—the offering of the oblation and the presentation of it—is for the sake of that [deity]; that is, it is subordinate to it.

For the deity, being the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), is primarily engaged in its own interest—the surrender of the substance—in sentences where the action is predominant; yet, although the deity is subordinate in such action-predominant sentences, it possesses primacy of purpose through the power of the respective mantras and other factors. Nor should it be argued that the deity is not an agent because of the impossibility of the fivefold attributes such as having a physical body (*vigraha*); for that [agency] is established by means of traditional authority (*smṛti*), metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), and scriptural indications (*anyārthadarśana*) which refute such objections.

Therefore, just as a guest is to be honored according to his specific form and so forth, and one employs ritual service for one's own sake and desired goal, so too is the deity. Because [the deity] possesses purpose (*arthavattvāt*), according to [Sūtra 1.1.7]: "Now, these are called *vibhūti* because they are attained (*prāpyante*) or because they are sought after (*aryante*). Consequently, one should not suspect that [the deity] is unworthy of worship due to the absence of such [purpose], or that it is ineffective because it does not grant what is desired. Indeed, the Supreme Deity is the goal of all; and the subordinate [deities] appointed by Her grant their respective powers (*vibhūtis*) according to the qualification [of the worshipper].

Nevertheless, since a deity who is independent would neither be pleased by anyone nor cause anyone to be pleased, how could she be the motivator? To this, he says: "And therefore, there is a connection with that" (9.1.8). "Therefore"—even though [the deity] is independent—just according to the worldly principle of kings and gods, when a deity who is gracious and endowed with compassion is served, it is solely for the sake of that very deity that those who serve her become connected with their desired fruit; this is established through such means as recollection (*smṛti*) and ritual practice (*upacāra*). This is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is stated in the sūtra: "Or rather, because it is preceded by the word [of the Veda], the ritual action must be primary" (9.1.9). Here, the phrase "or rather" (*api vā*) indicates the presentation of the opposing view with its own conviction. Although the pentad beginning with the embodied form of the deity is difficult to refute, the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is primary in comparison to the substance and other factors.

Since the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) signifies the propitiation of a deity, it follows that the sacrifice is for the sake of that deity; furthermore, in established scriptural passages (*siddha-vākya*), we learn from authoritative sources that the nature of both the higher and lower deities is not for the sake of anything else. Nevertheless, in the injunctions regarding what is to be performed (*kartavyopadeśa*), the ritual action consisting of the sacrifice and so forth—being enjoined as a means to a result—is primary; thus, by appearing as something to be accomplished, it impels the person toward action. And the deity and other factors are merely subordinate to the action.

Is it not the case that we maintain the primacy of the deity who bestows the fruit, on the grounds of being the object of worship? To this, he replies: "The scripture [regarding] the deity [indicates its status as] subordinate" (9.1.10). For we hear of the deity as being subordinate with respect to the offering of the oblation (*havis*). The *apūrva*—consisting of the gratification of the deity, which is presented through the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) for the sake of connection—belongs to the enjoined action, which, though momentary, [produces this result]. (1.4.4)

It is adopted as a means to a result that arises at a later time. Therefore, even though the deity possesses actual primacy, because it is subordinate to the action which is the primary factor in bringing about the desired fruit, the deity is not the motivator by way of its own primacy. If so, how then does the guest function as a motivator? To this he says: "In the case of a guest, there is primacy; in the case of the ritual act, there would be non-existence" (9.1.19). Regarding hospitality, the guest attains primacy.

Otherwise, since there would be no instigator for the action directed toward that end, it would not exist. If it is argued that the very injunction for its worship is the instigator, he replies to that: "Because it is a counter-injunction" (9.2.12). For the injunction regarding the act of honoring a guest is indeed a counter-injunction to the arrival of the guest. Since the deity is dependent on the person performing the ritual action, the deity does not come into proximity [of the sacrifice] by his own will; rather, he is brought there by the desire of the performer. However, the guest is independent and may pursue his own desired ends. Therefore, the injunction for the worship of the guest is made solely for the sake of fulfilling the guest's own desires.

Therefore, because of the distinction between what is already established and what is newly attained, there is the statement regarding the preeminence of the guest and the *śrāddha*. Just as when a guest possesses the qualities of being a planet (*graha*) and so forth, there is never any loss to the place intended for his reception; rather, on the contrary, it attains its own true nature—so too it is with the deity, even though it exists within that [guest]. Nor do we perceive any futility in the negation of that [deity's status]. If it is asked, "What is the purpose even in establishing [the deity] as subordinate? [the answer is: it serves to destroy the lack of faith in ritual action among those whose primary importance of the ultimate reality remains undetermined.

In these very examples, because of the absence of a deity and so forth, the status of being a *smṛti* (tradition) is denied for both sides. [1] In cases such as the absence of a deity mentioned in the examples cited by both sides, there is no rejection [of the authority of the Veda] for those who know its inherent validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*). [2] [This is] because it is spoken of as a *smṛti*, because of figurative usage (*upacāra*), and because of its being seen otherwise. [3]

Nor can [the existence of] other things be denied by mere words. (2) In the case of the *adana* (eating), *katakra* (sour gruel), and so forth, when there is a sprout of rice and the like, the production of all the auxiliary conditions (*upasarjana*) occurs through the ripening of the *cāvīka* and other factors. (4) Furthermore, the statement that the *vibhraṣṭa* (fallen) and others are "imagined" (*kalpya*) is born of delusion; for there is indeed a logical complexity (*gaurava*) in imagining the absence of the *śruta* (revealed scripture), *śakti* (potency), and so forth. (5) When considering what the gateway to the fruit might be for that which is momentary (*kṣaṇika*), it is better to accept the gateway already established there than to invent a new one. (6)

The purpose of the deities is for the sake of ritual action, and the purpose of rituals is for the sake of those deities; since this is established through different perspectives, they do not deserve to contradict one another. (7) Bādarāyaṇa, by establishing the meditations on the Sun and other deities as being upon the limbs [of the sacrifice], indicated that the primacy of the deities is established as a matter of fact. (8) Furthermore, a meditation consisting of viewing something else as having the form of a deity whose nature is unestablished is not appropriate; nor should the method of enjoining such a meditation be postulated everywhere where it is already uncontradicted. (9) And the scriptural accounts of the performance of austerities and other practices by the deities are not contradictory.

The engagement [of the Lord] in various actions follows from the logical necessity of pleasing His own superior Lord (Śiva), and from the desire of the Ruler to establish dharma out of compassion for those who are subject to karma. These deities—whether they be rivers, stationary objects, or lifeless things—are regarded as divine through the continuous mental identification with their specific qualities and functions; this is indeed heard in the Śruti. Furthermore, according to the principle of kings and others, these deities bestow different fruits in accordance with the specific offerings made to them, and they become provoked by prohibited acts.

If the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) [of deities] in relation to the oblation and other elements is established according to scripture, then it is appropriate for that very [nature] to be accepted as the object of worship for each respective [deity]. (14) Even where the meaning of mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) is established, if no contradiction is observed, then the Smṛti rooted therein is likewise not subject to contradiction, just like its own source. (15) The conceptualization of different deities occurs both in cases of synonyms and in cases of specific distinctions, by means of the application of various words, in order to establish their status as the intended objects of worship. (16) Without recognizing their own intellectual feebleness, the atheists here among the believers—

Those who asserted that [the deity] is insentient are objects of pity for those of subtle vision (17). Furthermore, when substance (*dravya*) and deity (*daivata*) are common [to a rite], substance is more powerful; this is because it is established as a means of proof both perceptibly and imperceptibly (18). There is a distinction: the status of being an oblation (*haviṣṭva*) belongs to the substance, which is established through direct perception, and falls within the scope of the scriptures; whereas the nature of the deity and its status as a religious duty (*dharmatva*) are distinct [from that] (19). Because it depends upon perception and other [means of knowledge], cognition derived from scripture is delayed. (XXIII)

For that very reason, there is a progressive weakening of authority even among the means of proof such as direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth. (20) The difference between the sacrificial material (*dravya*) and the deity (*devatā*) does not arise from a distinction between reality and unreality. If the deity were unreal, how could it possess attributes such as differentiation? (21) Whether its nature consists of words connected with an object, or whether it consists of words alone, or whether it is grasped exactly as it is heard in scripture—the deity is indeed real. (22) Furthermore, the attainment of supernatural powers (*siddhi*) through gems, mantras, medicinal herbs, and the like, which is taught [in the scriptures], is accepted [as valid].

Even though [the capacity for action] is established by birth, why is it not accepted among the gods? (23) A real entity cannot be postulated here as existing in another place, like the injunction regarding divine vision, because the injunction concerning its own nature is well-established. (24) Furthermore, according to the principle of the *rātrisatra* sacrifice and in accordance with the requirement of an injunction, the deities are proven to be bestowers of fruits, since they themselves constitute the fruit. (25) Thus, by this traditional method, the view that there are no deities has been refuted; the remainder will be addressed in the commentary on the sūtra beginning with "tadupari" (above that). (26)

The commentator Drāmiḍa has also stated: beginning with "The very form of the Creator of the universe," he concludes, "For no form is taught for a deity that is formless; indeed, the scripture speaks of things as they truly are. Regarding the acquaintance with Dhūrtasvāmin: when considering when and which region of the earth the author of the *Āpastamba-Śrautasūtra-bhāṣya*, Dhūrtasvāmin, adorned, neither his *bhāṣya* nor his *vṛtti* provides us any assistance.

Furthermore, in the *Vedārthasaṃgraha*, the author of the *Śrībhāṣya*—when demonstrating that the Upaniṣads possess the intended meaning he has established himself, in accordance with the consensus of ancient Vedic commentators—states: "This [meaning] is determined by the labor of explaining those [Upaniṣads], which is swiftly embraced by a multitude of various Śrutis."

And regarding the statement, "This path has been shown by a multitude of Śrutis whose meanings are clearly manifest, as explained in ancient commentaries on the Veda and Vedānta, which have been accepted by authoritative persons (śiṣṭas) such as Bodhāyana, Taṅka, Dramiḍa, Guha, Devaka, Kapardin, Bhārucī, and others," we determine that Dhūrta-svāmin—who commented on the earlier portion of the text that is to be explained by Kapardin—must be later than Kapardin, based on the inclusion of Kapardin among those who accepted and explained the Veda and Vedānta as handed down from his own predecessors.

Regarding the statement, "It indeed becomes inexhaustible," Kapardisvāmin explains it as a restatement of the fruit of heaven (*svarga-phala*) in the context of the *haviryajña* sacrifices; by thus citing Dhūrtasvāmibhāṣya while omitting its specific name, his own posteriority to that work is determined. Furthermore, Dhūrtasvāmibhāṣya states: (2-2-28) "The two groups [of offerings] in the *upabhṛt* ladle, intended for the *prayāja*s and *anūyāja*s, have been established by the Mīmāṃsakas."

(4-1-7) Furthermore, in the *adhikaraṇa*, Śabarasvāmin establishes that the *caturgṛhīta* (four-fold portion) consists of two parts in the *upabhṛt* ladle. Likewise, in section 4-11 (*khaṇḍa*), regarding the statement "But the *subrahmaṇyā* should be common (*tantra*)," the *bhāṣya* says: "'But the *subrahmaṇyā*'—according to the view of the Mīmāṃsakas. Śabarasvāmin’s own words are seen exactly like this in the Sūtra. By examining such passages as these, it can be determined that he is indeed the Svāmin (the Master).

Furthermore, one should not suspect that Śabarasvāmin’s Bhāṣya is based on another Bhāṣya merely because his name ends in the title "Svāmin" and thus he cannot be later than that [other author]; for titles ending in "Svāmin" are accepted even among those who are later than him, such as Bhavasvāmin and Keśavasvāmin. Vināyakarāya maintains that Śabarasvāmin, the younger contemporary of [the elder] Śabarasvāmin, lived two hundred years prior to the commencement of the Śālivāhana Śaka era.

We understand from the statement of Dhūrtasvāmin, "Not by many branches," namely: "But this cannot be a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*), because [the procedure] is not seen even when the [relevant] branches (*śākhā*) are being recited. In the tenth *praśna*, there is the sūtra: "With the words 'Thou art the fringe' (*nīvir asi*), he fashions the fringe. Regarding this, Dhūrtasvāmin’s commentary states: "There, he wraps [the garment] up to the end with the words 'Thou art the fringe of Soma' (*somasya nīvir asi*). And on this point, Rāmāṇḍāra says: "So that they do not remain above, and so that the ends of the cloth are not visible."

By this textual sequence, the manner of dress for a householder is taught as a common practice; and that mode of wearing clothing, pertaining to the *agha-rīya*, remains observed even today by the Vaidika Śrīvaiṣṇavas. XXV. The term "Śrautasūtra" is also used as a designation for that portion of the Kalpasūtras which deals with the exposition of rituals such as the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*. This usage is well-established.

Relying on that very usage, we too have designated it by the name *Śrautasūtra*. And the basis for this is precisely the usage of the authors of the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vṛtti*; for instance, at the beginning of the second section of the fifth *praśna*, after describing the procedure for the *Nāndīśrāddha*, Dhūrtasvāmī states: "This is the rule everywhere at the beginning of both *Śrauta* and *Smārta* [rites]; it is not obligatory, because Āpastamba did not prescribe it. Regarding this, Rāmāṇḍāra says: "[It is] because it was not prescribed in the *Śrauta* and the *Smārta*."

Furthermore, the designation "Kalpa" as being common to the Gṛhya-sūtras and others is established by its very own natural implication (*svarasataḥ*). Commentators such as Ratnamālākāra and others record the enumeration of the Kalpa-sūtras as consisting precisely of those dealing with Gṛhya-dharma and Pitṛmedha. What is the commencement of the Kalpa-sūtras? We shall consider what the commencement of the Āpastambīya Kalpa-sūtra is: therein, first of all, in the section on the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the initial sūtra is: "Now, therefore, we shall explain the New and Full Moon sacrifices. (*athāto darśapūrṇamāsau vyākhyāsyāmaḥ*)

Explaining this, Rudradatta says: "Now, this word *atha* is generally employed by the elders at the commencement of a section; occasionally it is used for immediate succession (*ānantarya*), as in such passages as, 'These Bhṛgus have been explained; now [follow] the Aṅgirases,' and so forth. But here it does not mean immediate succession, because no preceding subject is perceived that could follow immediately. By this passage, it is understood that the Kalpasūtra proceeded starting from the words, "Now, therefore, the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*athāto darśapūrṇamāsau*).

And he says quite explicitly: "Because the mantras for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices come first in the Samhitā, [the author], intending to explain those two first, demonstrates the scope [of the work] as follows. Furthermore, the teacher Cauṇḍapācārya, who lived later than Sāyaṇa, states in his *Prayogaratnamālā*: "The Sūtra proclaimed by the sage Āpastamba consists of thirty chapters (*praśna*); therein, five [chapters] teach the Śrauta, Gṛhya, and Smārta rites. (XXVI) Having begun thus, he continues: "Then, in the twenty-third chapter, is the sequence of rules for the Sattra-sacrifices."

In the twenty-fourth book, the duties of the *hotṛ* priest according to the *Nyāya* school are set forth. In the twenty-fifth and twenty-sixth books, the domestic (*gārhya*) mantras are explained in detail. Then, in the twenty-seventh book, there shall be the sequence of rules for the domestic ritual system (*gārhya-tantra*). In the twenty-eighth and twenty-ninth books, the sacred rites prescribed by the *Smṛti* are treated both generally and specifically. In the thirtieth book, the determination of the *Śulba* (sacrificial geometry) is presented. Thus, the determination of the meaning of all the books has been given in general.

Thus, while describing how the section on technical rules (*paribhāṣā*) forms part of the twenty-fourth book within the *Āpastambīyakalpasūtra-praśnārthasaṃgraha*, he also indicates that the position regarding the primacy of the *paribhāṣās* is not accepted. This very work is known by the name *Nyāya*, and it is celebrated for having two commentaries—the one by Kapardisvāmin and the other by Haradatta—published long ago from the Oriental Manuscripts Library.

In the commentary on those two [texts] by Kapardin, the introduction of the *paribhāṣā* is seen beginning with the words "The name 'Exposition' (*vyākhyāna*) [is applied] to this work," and concluding with: "This exposition, although it logically belongs at the beginning because it is subsidiary to all ritual acts (*karma*), has been placed at the end for the purpose that the definition of the subject matter (*adhikāra*) and so forth might apply as far as possible even to the customary and domestic rites (*ācāra-gṛhyakarma*). By this, it is understood that the Sage (Kapardin), although the placement of the *paribhāṣā* at the beginning was the logical order, intentionally disregarded it for a specific underlying purpose.

At the beginning of his commentary on the *Iṣṭihautrakalpa*, the commentator Rāmāṇḍāra introduces the Bhāṣya with the words: "Although [the procedure] has been stated by the author of the Kalpa in the section on technical rules (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the *Iṣṭihautra*, it is stated here by the author of the Bhāṣya for the purpose of providing the ritual application (*prayoga*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). By the phrase "although... has been stated," it is clearly indicated that the recitation of the technical rules (*paribhāṣāpāṭha*) occurs prior to this point.

Furthermore, in the context of explaining the meaning of the sūtra *athāto darśapūrṇamāsau*, Dhūrtasvāmin says: "The sacrifice has been explained in brief in the Paribhāṣā; it is now being explained in detail immediately after the Darśapūrṇamāsa [section]. The word *ataḥ* signifies a reason (*hetu*). By stating both "immediately after" (*anantaram*) and that the word *ataḥ* signifies a reason, the commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) clearly intends the Paribhāṣā to come first.

Furthermore, in the *Daśamapraśna*, the commentator Rāmāṇḍāra states in the *Paribhāṣā-sūtra*: "First, in the *Paribhāṣā*, twenty-one sacrifices were promised as subjects for exposition. Among them, the seven *pākayajñas* have been explained in the *Gṛhyasūtras*. Regarding the remaining ones, the seven rites consisting of *haviryajñas* have been stated starting from 'Now, therefore, the New and Full Moon sacrifices' (*athāto darśapūrṇamāsau*) up to 'Now, the *Anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice' (*athānvārambhaṇīyā*). Since they have already been explained in the *Paribhāṣā*, I shall not explain them here."

The purpose of this [statement] is as follows: "Whatever has been stated here, from the Paribhāṣās up to the Prāyaścittas, and whatever is required therein, that should be understood here exactly as it was explained there. By this passage, it is clearly understood that the *paribhāṣā-praśna* (the section on technical rules) holds primacy. And between these two views, according to the first, the *paribhāṣā-sūtras* constitute the twenty-fourth *praśna*, but not the beginning; whereas according to the second, they do indeed constitute the beginning.

And in the *Tātparyadarśana*, Sudarśanācārya has stated: "The author of the Sūtras, having briefly explained that 'we shall explain the sacrifice,' [noted] that since it would be of no use with only that much, he began the explanation starting from the words 'Now, therefore, the New- and Full-Moon sacrifices'."

Furthermore, in the *Śulbapraśnavivaraṇa*, the venerable Āpastamba—who, by making the formal declaration "We shall explain the sacrifice," indicated that the *haviryajñas*, *somayajñas*, and *pākayajñas* were to be explained—was stated by Karavindādhipa to have adopted the position that the *paribhāṣās* (general rules) come first, as he both declared them to be what was to be explained and actually explained them at the outset.

Thus, by Ahovalasūri, the son of Nṛsiṃhayajvan: "O best of sages Āpastamba, I always bow in my heart to the authors of the Bhāṣya and Vṛtti, as well as to the authors of the *Prayogavṛtti* and others. For the sake of the understanding of children, a commentary (*vṛtti*) on the meaning of the *Āpastambīya Sūtra*, following the *Bhāṣya*, is now composed. Having thus made his promise, he takes up the sūtra beginning with "atha ataḥ" and explains: "The word *atha* signifies immediate succession (*ānantarya*). In the general exposition of sacrifice as a whole, the succession of the technical rules (*paribhāṣā*) is stated by implication (*sāmarthyāt*)."

Because it would be impossible to compose the subsequent treatise in the form of an exposition in the midst of the *paribhāṣā*s. [Objection: Since the *paribhāṣā* stating "Now we shall expound the sacrifice" (*yajñaṃ vyākhyāsyāmaḥ*) is studied now after [the *paribhāṣā*s], is it not inconsistent for the exposition of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* to follow immediately after that? [Reply: It is said: For the sake of ease of exposition, it is studied at the end by the students, as it has been explained in various places by the authors of the *bhāṣya*s and others.

It should be understood, however, that their application occurs at the very beginning, because it has been stated that the *liṅga* (indicative power) in the form of functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) overrides the order of recitation (*pāṭha*). By this discussion, it is clearly stated that the treatises on ritual procedure (*kalpa*) begin with the *paribhāṣās* (general rules). This beginning with the *paribhāṣās* is observed in the *kalpas* of Hiraṇyakeśin, Lāṭyāyana, Drāhyāyaṇa, Śāṅkhāyana, Kātyāyana, Āśvalāyana, and others, and it has also been explicitly stated by their respective commentators.

In this regard as well, Dhūrtasvāmin, while stating in the second chapter of the fourteenth *praśna* that "since it is established that modification (*ūha*) occurs according to the actual meaning, [the rule] is stated again," has thereby demonstrated [this point]. For the statement regarding a "re-statement" (*punarvidhāna*) is not tenable without the prior application of the *paribhāṣā*.

Although in the *Sūtrakośa* the text is seen as consisting of twenty-four questions (*praśna*) alone, with no separate section for general questions (*sāmānyapraśna*), yet the technical usage of the term "paribhāṣā" applies only to the *Nyāya* portion; this is observed in the introduction to the *Paribhāṣā* published and circulated from here. Furthermore, the use of the word "nyāya" for the *Paribhāṣā* alone is also accepted by the author of the *Prayogaralamālā*.

Nevertheless, it must be stated that the usage of the term *paribhāṣā* for this general portion of the Sūtra is accepted by the commentators on this Kalpasūtra, as Rāmāṇḍāra states in the introduction to his *Iṣṭihautrakalpabhāṣya*: "Even though the author of the Kalpa has stated the *paribhāṣā* regarding the *iṣṭihautra*..."

In the *Bhāṣyavivaraṇa* on the statement, "The status of the Brahman priest (*brahmatva*) belongs to the context (*prakaraṇa*): this is the instruction," and in the remark, "Because of the scriptural injunction that 'the one most proficient in the Veda (*brahmiṣṭha*) is the Brahman priest at the New and Full Moon sacrifices,' the section on the duties of the Brahman priest is recited within the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, just like the *hautra* [section], the *pravara*, and so forth," the author undoubtedly demonstrates that even the portion concerning the *hautra* is designated as a *paribhāṣā*. Thus, although the two views—that the work begins with the *paribhāṣās* and that it does not—are both accepted by their respective authors and remain current;

Nevertheless, how can a difference in intention be possible at the commencement of two commentaries that proceed as a single continuous work? For it has been stated by Kapardisvāmin himself in his own commentary—on page 52, 55, and 61 [of the edition cited], under the sūtras beginning with *dravyasaṃskāravirodhe*—that there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the *yājyānuvākyās*, and that the remainder of the Brāhmaṇa is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) for three reasons.

152. Thus [the text] restates the *paribhāṣā-sūtras* in twenty sections; it refers to the established rule found in the tenth *praśna*, "The duties of the mortar and pestle apply to the nails," as a substitute (*pratyāmnāya*) for those two; it points to what has already been previously determined by stating, "The *rattinas* have been explained"; and it indicates that [the author] will state [later], "He will explain [the ritual] at the *Kaukilī* sacrifice" (18th *praśna*), "The *rattinas* will be explained" (20th *praśna*), and "He will state the designation: 'The kings are those with auspicious names.'"

In such passages as these, how can we refute the position of one who—pointing out that the objects within the scope of future definitions are established by the sequence of the Sūtra text—considers that the twenty-fourth question, "The General Sūtras," constitutes a definition (*paribhāṣā*), and thus disregards the logical necessity of placing it at the beginning while instead placing it at the end for a specific reason? Therefore, since both commentators here are of one voice, [the General Sūtras] constitute the introduction to the *paribhāṣās*.

It should be noted that there is no dispute regarding the fact that the *Kalpanibandha* of Āpastamba consists of three sections: the *Paribhāṣā*, the *Hautra*, and the *Pravara-paṭala*. Herein follows the sequence for understanding the order of the Sūtra recitation: first, in the *Paribhāṣā*, twenty-one forms of sacrifice (*saṃsthā*) are declared as the subjects to be explained; among these, the seven *pākayajñas* have been explained in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*.

The first section consists of the *paribhāṣā* (general rules), as stated by Rāmāṇḍāra according to the sequence ending with the statement that "for the remaining oblation-sacrifices, the seven rites beginning with the *anvārambhaṇīyā* have been explained. Following that is the sequence of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the *yājamāna*, the *agnyādheya*, the *agnihotra*, the *paśubandha*, the *cāturmāsya*, the *prāyaścitta*, and the *praśna* sections; then the *somasaṃsthā*; then the *ukthya* and other modifications of the *agniṣṭoma*; and finally the *pravargya*. Thus the order is established.

As stated by Haradatta, the commentator on the *Dharmapraśna*: "The Śrauta and Gṛhya rites that have been described require the dharmas to be explained hereafter"; as stated by Karavindādhipa: "The *Haviryajñas*, *Somayajñas*, and *Pākayajñas* have been promised for exposition and have now been expounded"; and as stated by Kapardisvāmin: "The rites previously mentioned—beginning with the *Jātakarman* and so forth—apply to those who are living; now, the rite for one who has died is being described."

"The ritual acts pertaining to the *vaitānika* (śrauta) and *gṛhya* (domestic) rites have been explained by the Blessed One, the author of the Sūtras, [in the words] 'Now, therefore, the *paitṛmedhika* (rites for the deceased),' as stated by Gārgya Gopālayajvan; thus, in the *Gṛhyapraśna*, the *haviryajña* sacrifices characterized by the Śruti, along with the *somasaṃsthās* and their modifications, have been explained."

Immediately thereafter, the ritual acts (*karmāṇi*) are taken up; as stated in the *Bhāṣya*, "those which are [derived] from Brāhmaṇas whose textual recensions have been lost, we shall explain them," the fact that the *Gṛhya-praśna* follows the *Soma-grantha* is established. Furthermore, the statement in the *Cayana-praśna-bhāṣya*, "The *Ekāṣṭakā* has been explained by the author of the Sūtras, Āpastamba, in the *Āśvalāyanīya*" and so forth, is also favorable to this conclusion.

From the words of Kapardisvāmin, Gārgya, and Gopālayajvan, it is established that the *Pitṛmedhapraśna* follows the *Gṛhyapraśna*. From the words of Haradatta, it is established that the *Dharmapraśna* follows this [the *Pitṛmedhapraśna*]. Furthermore, from the observation in the commentary on the *Cayanapraśna* stating, "This Brāhmaṇa has been explained in the *Śulba* as the gold plate (*rukma*) consisting of four parts," it is understood that the *Śulbapraśna* precedes the *Cayanapraśna*.

Since the *Kapardibhāṣya* states, "The *Sautrāmaṇī-praśna* is explained [in the section] beginning with 'In all [sacrifices]...'," it is established that the *Cayana-praśna* precedes it. Consequently, the sequence consists of the *Vājapeya*, *Rājasūya*, *Sautrāmaṇī*, the optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*), the *Aśvamedha*, and so forth.

Although, upon examining the *Rāmāṇḍāra-vṛtti* from its beginning—"First, then..."—down to its conclusion—"the *Gṛhya* has been explained," one might suspect that even the *Gṛhya-praśna* precedes the *Darśapūrṇamāsa-praśna*; and although Dhūrtasvāmin, in his division of sacrifices under the heading "Now, therefore, the Darśapūrṇamāsa," mentions the domestic sacrifices (*pākayajña*) first—which might likewise suggest such an order of composition by the author of the Sūtras—nevertheless, [this is not so] because of the *paribhāṣā*.

Following the commentary of Dhūrtasvāmin, which serves as an introduction to the exposition of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices and praises them, it is determined that the Sage composed the section on the Darśapūrṇamāsa immediately after the Paribhāṣā.

This is the intention of the commentary here: having commenced with the statement "we shall explain the sacrifice," and because he provides a definition of those elements required by the sacrifice as understood through Vedic injunctions—namely, that "it is performed with three fires"—the sage Āpastamba has first selected the Śrauta sacrifices themselves for exposition. As for the Gṛhya rites, since their Brāhmaṇa sources have been lost, it is logical that they follow after those [Śrauta] rites which are grasped through Vedic injunctions.

Regarding the division of domestic rites (*gṛhyakarma*), the mention of them first is due to their being the first to be performed. This has been stated by Sudarśanācārya in the *Gṛhyatātparyadarśana*:

"Precisely because these rites are understood through the Veda as inferred from traditional practice (*ācāra*), it is for this reason that the explanation of the Śrauta rites was provided before those [Gṛhya rites], even though they are to be performed later. Furthermore, this is because inquiry regarding those [rites] prescribed by direct Vedic revelation arises first, whereas inquiry regarding the meaning of the Veda as inferred from tradition arises later."

The *Gṛhyasūtra* also intends this same meaning when it states: "The consecration of the *prokṣaṇī* waters is the sprinkling of the vessels; as in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, it is performed silently. For the Sage who composed the Sūtras does not consider an unestablished matter to be something that can be extended by analogy (*atideśya*).

Regarding the tradition of the textual recitation (*sūtrapāṭhasampradāya*) in the *Āpastamba-kalpasūtras*, it is observed that in most manuscript copies of the Sūtras, the text is presented in the form of a *saṃhitā*, with intermediate divisions consisting of *khaṇḍikās*, groups of several *khaṇḍikās* designated as *paṭalas*, and groups of several *paṭalas* forming *praśnas*. Even Sāyaṇācārya, the commentator on the Vedas, refers to this [division] in various places at the beginnings of *anuvākas* and so forth, stating: "here, in the Kalpa... [etc.].

Beginning with these words, they cite various passages; yet these are seen neither as independent fragments nor as standalone sūtras, but rather as consisting of collections of sentences required for each respective topic. When published by the Hūṇa named Kyāleḍ together with Rudradatta’s commentary and translated into the German language, it appears as three volumes, containing the sequential arrangement of the sūtras divided into twenty-four chapters (praśnas).

In the *Kapardibhāṣya* on the section concerning the *Vājapeya* and other rites, an exposition is seen that follows the arrangement of the *Prāyaścitta-sūtra*. From this, it can be understood that even within these *Kalpasūtras*, a reading divided according to the *sūtra* sections is traditional. Thus, the collection of *sūtras*, which was being propagated through instruction in the form of a *saṃhitā*, was followed by the authors of the commentaries (*bhāṣyakāra*) and others according to the very sequence in which the divisions were established by the method of investigating the traditional meaning.

And that [point] has been fully maintained by the commentators as appropriate, as for instance by Rudradatta; thus it is established. Furthermore, this portion is understood from the words of the authors of the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vṛtti*; for instance: "This is the division of the Sūtra. The Sūtra extends up to the word "pādam" as a single unit. In both cases, the *Bhāṣya* is intended to resolve the contradiction between the two mantras. This Sūtra is the prescription of time for what was stated in the section concerning Brahman.

"One should fetch fire from where it is blazing and prepare it"—this is one *sūtra*. The *sūtra* "They should not fetch [fire] from a deficient source" is explained by being displaced due to the logical connection of the meaning; for the sequence of the *mantras* follows the intended order of the *sūtra*-author's recitation. Likewise, "Agni is to be established" does not constitute a single *sūtra*, because there is a prohibition by the *sūtra* "He does not perform those two in the animal sacrifice," and another *sūtra* "Not in the Soma sacrifice. The section ending with "He sprinkles the heart" constitutes a single *sūtra*.

Thus, the statements of the author of the Bhāṣya and the author of the Vṛtti, which proceed in various places to determine the portions of the Sūtras, demonstrate the possibility of differences of opinion therein, their refutation, the necessity of accepting the textual tradition through subtle scrutiny, and the different traditions of its oral transmission that serve as its foundation.

It is understood from the commentary of Kapardi Svāmin that even when there is a fullness of faith in preserving the authentic tradition (*satsampradāya*), the preservation of the tradition regarding the true intent of the author of the Sūtras may, for some reason, become difficult to maintain in certain instances. For instance, in the commentary on the Sūtra (5.2.6.26): "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice with the *Bhūḥ* [verse] accompanied by the *Rathantara* chant," the following passage from the Bhāṣya is seen: "It cannot be explained as not being found among the followers of the Tāṇḍins."

The arrangement of the portions of the Āpastamba-kalpa-bhāṣya: We have observed that the Āpastamba-kalpa-sūtra shines forth, adorned by two portions of commentary—the traditional exegeses composed by Dhūrtasvāmin and Kapardisvāmin—which are intent upon revealing its hidden meanings.

Regarding this, the elder scholar of the three Vedas (*traividyavṛddha*), the author of the *Prayogadīpikā* residing in Tālavṛtta, resolved the doubt as to how many questions were explained by Dhūrtasvāmin and how many by Kapardisvāmin. For he stated at the beginning of his own work: "In accordance with the commentary of Dhūrtasvāmin on the *Āpastamba-sūtra*, having incorporated from other treatises those elements not required [in the former], I compose a manual of performance (*prayogavṛtti*) for the rituals up to the fire-altar construction (*agnicayana*)."

It is asserted within his own work that "the performance of rituals beginning with the Vājapeya and ending with the Viśvasṛjāmayaṇa is described according to the intention of Kapardin"; thus, he makes this promise at the commencement of the Vājapeya. By this, it is indicated that Dhūrtasvāmin began the commentary starting from the Vājapeya, and that Kapardisvāmin composed the Bhāṣya [from that point] onwards.

As for the objection—"Why may it not be postulated that the commentary was composed entirely and separately by both [Bhartṛhari and Puṇyarāja]?"—we refute it, even though it is already refuted by the mere observation of the manuscripts, by means of the corroboration of the statements of ancient authoritative authors who stand apart from this dispute.
