In the commentary on the eleventh verse of the *Adhikaraṇasārāvali*—which is a compendium of the essence of the *Śrībhāṣya* composed by the venerable Nigamāntadeśika—his son Varadanāthācārya raises the objection that there must be a difference between the scriptures (*śāstra*) because their authors differ: Jaimini for the *Karmakāṇḍa*, Kāśakṛtsna for the *Devatākāṇḍa*, and Bādarāyaṇa for the *Śārīraka*. He then refutes this by stating: "For there is no rule that a single effect must have only one author; indeed, it is observed in the case of the preceding and succeeding sections (*vṛtti*) [of the same work]."

It has been stated [by others] that there is a single authorship for both the *Āpastambīya-sūtra* and its commentary, the *Dhūrtasvāmī-nibandhana*, as well as the *Kāpardinī*. Likewise, at the end of the first *paṭala* of the eighth *praśna*, having taken up the commentary beginning with "punarvasantādiniyamāt" on the sūtra beginning with "yo vai vasanto'bhūt," and having commenced an investigation into the meaning of the words, [it is noted]: "In this regard, by Kapardisvāmin, regarding the sūtra 'They are initiated in the cold season (śiśira), they rise [from the vow] in spring (vasanta),' when the two—the twelfth and the first zodiac signs—"

Since Rāmāṇḍāra, while citing the *Kapardibhāṣya* on the Sūtra (21.2.8)—based on the observation of the *Rāmāṇḍāravṛtti* which states, "Because it is said that spring begins at sunrise"—indicates therein that Dhūrtasvāmin did not compose a commentary, it follows that even if Dhūrtasvāmin’s commentary existed there, it was not sufficient to establish the intended meaning; rather, [Rāmāṇḍāra] was seeking a more skillful exposition of all the hidden meanings that were necessarily required. (Srauta Vol. I)

No one who has not fallen into delusion (*nipaka*) would suspect a deficiency in the commentator Paṇapara Dhūrtasvāmin. Nor, considering the unanimity between these two sections of the commentary and the fact that he did not compose separate, complete commentaries for them, could Tālavṛntanivāsin—who preserved the well-attained tradition—have intended either the acceptance or the rejection of these two authoritative means (*pramāṇa*) which had been agreed upon as a path of ritual practice to be maintained with vigilance.

Reflective scholars rightly consider this existing portion [of the commentary] to be indeed the work of Varadanāthācārya based on his own words. Dhūrtasvāmin did not comment upon the *Paribhāṣā* section. We investigate whether Dhūrtasvāmin was the author of the *Bhāṣya* for the first *praśna* of the tenth book; for in the commentary on the *Vṛtti* of the first *sūtra* of the tenth book, beginning with the words "As for this author of the *Bhāṣya*," he states: "And because it has already been explained in the *Paribhāṣā*, he does not explain it here. This is its purpose: [the section] from the *Paribhāṣā* up to the *Prāyaścitta*..."

It has been stated: "Whatever is required here should be understood exactly as it was explained there, just as the word *tantra* was not explained in the passage 'he commences the *tantra* of the *Dīkṣaṇīyā*'; for the word *tantra* has been explained in the context of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices as 'the collection of subsidiary rites (*aṅga-samudāya*)'. By this, it is understood that Dhūrtasvāmin has provided an explanation of this technical definition (*paribhāṣā*).

8. Thus, in the index of the Eastern Treasury (Prācyakośāgāra) located in Tanjore, Dhūrtasvāmin’s *Sāmānya-sūtra-bhāṣya* is indicated. Furthermore, in many commentaries on the *Paribhāṣā*, the notation "Dhūrtasvāmibhāṣya" itself is observed. Likewise, I have seen that the *Āpastamba-paribhāṣā-sūtra-bhāṣya* composed by Dhūrtasvāmin was printed and published in the journal named *Uṣā*. Thus says M., the author of the commentary on the *Paribhāṣā-sūtra*.

Mahādeva Śāstrī wrote thus: "The publisher of the *Tanjore Oriental Library Catalogue* has published his own designated *Sāmānyasūtrabhāṣya* from the Mysore Oriental Library. In that [edition], only a few differences in readings consisting of single letters are seen compared to the manuscript here; therefore, he cites Haradatta’s commentary among the two commentaries published from this [source]."

Furthermore, Haradatta’s commentary on the *Paribhāṣās*, as well as his commentary on the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*—which begins with a significant portion of Dhūrtasvāmin’s *Bhāṣya* on the *Pratijñāsūtra*—might even reinforce the suspicion that it belongs to Dhūrtasvāmin. Nevertheless, if one were to concede that Dhūrtasvāmin composed a *Bhāṣya* on the *Paribhāṣā-praśna*, [the following would apply].

Since the division of sacrifices (*yajñavibhāga*)—which is necessarily required for the phrase "we shall explain the sacrifice" (*yajñaṃ vyākhyāsyāmaḥ*)—and the clarification of the meaning of the word "explanation" (*vyākhyā*) have already been accomplished therein, one might suspect that there would be no further need for them in the introductory sūtra concerning the explanation of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. However, such a suspicion would lead to an insurmountable difficulty for Dhūrtasvāmin, who intends to demonstrate that very division of sacrifices and so forth in that context; therefore, we understand that he is indeed providing an explanation of that [introductory sūtra].

Ahobalasūri, while supporting the view that the *paribhāṣā-praśna* constitutes the beginning of the *kalpa-nibandhana*, clearly states at the outset that it has not been commented upon by the author of the *bhāṣya* and others. He notes that although Dhūrtasvāmin provided a commentary on the *hautra* section at the end of the *iṣṭi-prakaraṇa* and at the end of the *cāturmāsya*, and since Rāmāṇḍāra composed a *vṛtti* thereon, the statement regarding its lack of commentary is indeed justified.

The word "etc. (*ādi*) also indicates that the author of the Bhāṣya did not provide an explanation for certain specific portions of the Paribhāṣās. For if there were an accepted, complete commentary on all parts by a single author, it would not seem particularly appropriate to mention an explanation based on that [commentary] alongside the word "etc. Furthermore, it is reasonable to consider that Dhūrtasvāmin desisted from commenting on the Paribhāṣās because, as the occasion arose, it was possible to point to suitable illustrative examples (*lakṣya*) for those portions requiring explanation.

It remains to be considered who the *bhāṣyakṛt* (author of the commentary) on the *paribhāṣās* was, and who the author of its sub-commentary (*vyākhyākṛt*) was. One might raise the objection that there is no occasion for such inquiry since it is known that these two commentaries have already been printed and published from this very source; nevertheless, for one who observes that the claim of Kapardin’s authorship regarding the *bhāṣya* published here cannot withstand scrutiny, there is indeed room for investigation. To illustrate, in the eighth chapter of the *Āpastamba-gṛhya-sūtra*, the author of the *Tātparya-darśana*, Sudarśanācārya, [states as follows...]

"The feeding of Brahmins, the *homa* offering, and the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍadāna*)—these three are the primary elements in the monthly *śrāddha*, because Dhūrtasvāmin stated this in his commentary on the *Ananyādheya*, and because Kapardisvāmin stated it in the passage 'In the Vaiśvadeva [rite], the Viśvedevas [are the deities]'"; by saying this, the commentator on the *Gṛhyapraśna* clearly identifies himself as Kapardisvāmin.

xxxvi. Having made the formal promise, "We shall explain the sacrifice," Kapardin, the author of the *Gṛhyapraśna*, introduced [his work] as follows: "The forms of the *havis*-sacrifices characterized by direct Vedic injunction (*śruti*), along with their modifications, and the forms of the *soma*-sacrifices have been explained. Now, immediately thereafter, we shall explain those rites pertaining to the domestic ritual (*gṛhya*) which are derived from Brāhmaṇas whose textual readings have become obsolete."

In the *Kapardibhāṣya* as circulated from this source, beginning with the words "The name 'explanation' (*vyākhyāna*)... and continuing with "This explanation, because it is supplementary to all ritual acts, though it logically belongs at the beginning, is placed at the end," [the author] reveals that the inquiry into the *paribhāṣās* constitutes the final portion of the work composed by Kalpa.

Since Kapardisvāmin, introducing [the work] in that manner in the *Gṛhyabhāṣya* while supporting the primacy of the *Paribhāṣās*, would not have introduced the *Paribhāṣās* otherwise, we conclude that someone other than Kapardisvāmin was the commentator there. And in that regard, Rudradatta and Haradatta are renowned as the two commentators on the *Kalpanibandha*.

Since Haradatta also explained those two [sections] following the shadow of Dhūrtasvāmin’s words, it can be surmised that Rudradatta alone considers the *paribhāṣā* section to be the twenty-fourth book (*praśna*), and thus he himself might be the author of this commentary. Regarding the acquaintance with Dhūrtasvāmin’s *bhāṣya-vṛtti*: a commentary (*vṛtti*) on Dhūrtasvāmin’s *bhāṣya* by Rāmāṇḍāra is observed for the portion beginning with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and ending with the *soma*.

Furthermore, because one observes the inscription at the end of the *Somagrantha* stating, "Thus ends the *Rāmāgnicit" [and] *Datti*," it must also be concluded that the commentary (*vṛtti*) was composed only up to that point. Although there exists a manuscript currently circulating from Puṇyapattana under the title *Darśapūrṇamāsaprakāśa*, wherein both the *Bhāṣyavṛtti* and the *Sūtradīpikā* are published for the first four sections (*praśna*).

Nevertheless, we consider the cause for its non-publication to be either the scarcity of the commentary manuscript itself, or the difficulty involved in discerning between these two works—the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vṛtti*. Although it is observed in some manuscripts that the composition of the *Vṛtti* follows the entire sequence of the *Bhāṣya*, there is thus occasion to suspect that this may be a single work consisting of a word-by-word commentary (*svapadavivaraṇa*).

Nevertheless, there are variations in the readings, such as: (5.7) the reading "in some places, when the *caturhotṛ* has been prepared and discarded, there is the *anvādhāna*"; (37.1) the reading "in some places, the awakening by means of a mantra is performed as a regular rite (*nityavat*"); (7.2) the reading "*vikāravadbhyām*"; and (10.1) the reading "or *pitāmahasaṃtatikā*."

(11 pra. "The explanation of the sūtras in an inverted order is due either to a lack of concern or to the error of a scribe"—demonstrating this style of the Bhāṣya and pointing out the commentator separately with the words "As for this author of the Bhāṣya" (*yattu ayam bhāṣyakāraḥ*), etc., Rāmāṇḍāra considers his own *vṛtti* and the *Bhāṣya* which is its subject of commentary to be distinct; this should be noted. 6. Introduction to the Author of the Vṛtti: Now, we wish to provide an introduction to the author of the *vṛtti*.

In that regard, Ahovalasūri states in his *Sūtravṛtti* after discussing the determination of eligibility (*adhikāra-nirūpaṇa*): "The authors of the *Prayogavṛtti* maintain that even one who is ignorant [of the Self] but is virtuous (*sādhu*) has the eligibility; the authors of the *Bhāṣya* and others hold that only one who possesses self-knowledge (*ātmajñānavat*) has the eligibility; and the Advaita Vedāntins say that one who possesses the knowledge of non-duality (*advaitajñānavat*) has the eligibility. By this, it is made known that the intention of both the author of the *Bhāṣya* and the author of the *Vṛtti* is that self-knowledge is the cause for eligibility for sacrifice (*yajñādhikārahetu*).

This is the meaning intended by both the author of the Bhāṣya and the author of the Vṛtti; we shall clarify this position of Aghoraśiva Sūri by demonstrating relevant portions of the respective Bhāṣya and Vṛtti texts. At the beginning of the fourth section (khaṇḍa) of the fourth chapter, the author of the Sūtra prescribes the recitation of the mantra beginning with: *idaṃ śakeyaṃ yadidaṃ karomi ātmā karotvātmane*. Regarding this, Dhūrtasvāmī’s Bhāṣya explains: “The realization ‘the Self acts for the sake of the Self’ is [derived] from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra.”

Regarding that, in the *Vṛtti*: "The cognition must also be formed: 'May the Self perform [the action] for the sake of Brahman. And because of the Smṛti: 'Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give away, and whatever austerity you practice, O son of Kuntī—perform all that as an offering unto Me... Brahman is the vessel of the offering, Brahman is the oblation, in the fire of Brahman it is offered by Brahman; through that, one who is absorbed in the action of Brahman shall attain Brahman alone. Now, how can it be said "for the sake of the Self, for the sake of Brahman"? It is replied:

—because the term *ātman* is applied to the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) who has the individual soul as His body, in the passage: "Dwelling within the self, He controls the self from within; He whose body is the self—that is the Self. And because that [Inner Controller] is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). This is because the Supreme Self is well-known in all Vedic branches as Brahman, as evidenced by the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the terms Nārāyaṇa, Supreme Brahman, Self, and Supreme [Self] in the passage: "Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman; Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Self. Furthermore, it is because Nārāyaṇa is the great object of knowledge, as stated in: "Nārāyaṇa is to be known always."

6. How can one meditate upon even an action performed for other deities as being Brahman? Because [Brahman] is understood from such scriptural passages as "He who alone is the name-giver of the gods," "He is Brahmā, He is Śiva," "Wherein the four officiating priests reach completion along with the gods," and "Wherein all the Vedas become one," as being the sustainer of the names of all deities, the essential nature of all gods, the one to be worshipped by all sacrifices, and the one to be enjoined by all ritual injunctions.

The intention of Dhūrtasvāmin has been described as follows: "For I am indeed the enjoyer and the Lord of all sacrifices; even those who, devoted to other deities, worship them endowed with faith, they too, O son of Kuntī, worship Me alone, though in an improper manner"—so it is stated in the Smṛti.

And on the occasion of commenting upon this sūtra, Ahovala Sūri also follows the commentary (bhāṣya) and the sub-commentary (vṛtti) here both word-for-word and in meaning: "In this mantra, by the indicative mark (liṅga) of the words 'the Self should act for the Self,' one must maintain the realization that 'the Self is Brahman; [therefore] let it act for Brahman'; thus, Brahman alone is the agent and the enjoyer. This is also supported by the Smṛti text: 'Whatever you do... [and so forth]. Now, an objection is raised: "How can the word 'Self' (ātman) have Brahman as its referent? It is replied:

"—because the word 'Self' (ātman) is applied to the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) residing within the individual body, as in the statement 'He who dwells in the self, that is the Self'; because the Inner Controller is established as the Supreme Self; and because it is understood from other sources, such as the Smṛti: 'I indeed am the first'. Thus, in the fifth question, in the seventh chapter: "The formal resolve (saṅkalpa) is: 'I shall begin the Agnihotra and offer it for as long as I live, or I shall desist when I am worn out. The Mīmāṃsakas [hold] that one who desires heaven... [66 XXXIX]... [end of fragment].

The instruction is that because desire is unattached, it is not [considered] "desire" (kāma). Even where there is attachment, it is negated for one who has heard the scripture regarding the destruction of desire; and this is according to the opinion of Vyāsa—so says the commentary of Dhūrtasvāmin. Regarding this, the Vṛtti states: "The Mīmāṃsakas [hold] that for one desiring heaven—because no specific fruit is mentioned—the attainment of heaven is the fruit, as in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice, the Pitṛyajña, and so forth. 'Because desire is unattached, it is not [considered] desire'—the author of the Sūtras [means] that because desire is unattached, there is no assumption of a fruit."

"Even where there is a binding [injunction], such as by the author of the Sūtras regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices, even there the fruit is prohibited for the seeker of liberation who has heard [the scriptures] and is untouched by desire. This is its meaning: since liberation is established through the combination of knowledge and action, a Śrotriya who is untouched by desire should not form a longing for the fruits of ritual actions; for there is no liberation for those possessed of desire. Even though heaven and other rewards are heard of in the scriptures, it is improper for a seeker of liberation to perform rites out of a desire for them.

"Of one whose learning has been struck down by desire"—the meaning is "of one whose learning is [so] struck down. This is also because of the opinion of Vyāsa: "Indeed, being possessed by desire is not praised. And in the *Bhagavadgītā*, this is seen repeatedly: "Having abandoned attachment and the fruit [of action]," and so forth. Now, an objection is raised: "By such Śruti and Smṛti passages as 'Neither by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone some have attained immortality; nothing that is uncreated is achieved by what is created,' the status of action as a means to liberation is prohibited. Likewise [in the passage] 'Him alone...'"

This is because knowledge is understood to be the means [to liberation] through such passages as, "Knowing Him, one transcends death," "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman indeed," and "Knowing Him thus, one becomes immortal here. Furthermore, the difference in the fruits of ritual action (*karman*) and knowledge (*vidyā*) is understood from such texts as, "Having crossed over death by means of ignorance (*avidyā*), one attains immortality by means of knowledge (*vidyā*). Therefore, knowledge and ritual action combined are not the means to liberation.

This is not the essence of the matter—it is the opinion of those who cannot endure the great constraints of the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, who are eager for unrestrained conduct, who cite Vedic passages exactly as they wish out of fear of the censure of the Vedists, and who are devoid of fear regarding the next world. For instance, as for those scriptural statements that prohibit action as a means to liberation, they refer only to action performed in isolation; for [action] accompanied by knowledge is indeed more powerful.

"Whatever one performs with knowledge, that alone becomes more powerful," according to the Śruti; and from such passages as "They attain [the goal] through sacrifice" and "It is He who causes him to perform good deeds whom He wishes to lead up from these worlds," it is understood that [knowledge] is a means for performing action. "The golden bird is Brahman, by whom the sun shines, kindled with splendor; the father is possessed of a son through the son, in womb after womb. One who does not know the Veda does not comprehend that Great One."

Furthermore, after praising Brahman as "the Self that experiences everything in the hereafter," [the text] states, "They attain union with Brahman and residence in the same world who practice this—Om! Thus, it is seen that the Viśvasṛjāmayana sacrifice is a means for attaining Brahman. Moreover, it says, "Having known its very Self as the knower of the path, one is not smeared by evil action. On the contrary, it is understood from the words of the Blessed One that knowledge is the effect of ignorance.

Therefore, according to the *Tāṇḍya* Śruti: "Just as this chariot does not move with only one wheel, or as a bird [cannot fly] with only one wing, so too are knowledge and action for a person," both knowledge and action are to be combined (*samuccita*) in order to avoid mutual contradiction. Smṛti also states: "Relying on knowledge, he performed very many sacrifices, having established himself in the knowledge of Brahman to cross over death by means of ignorance."

And so the Blessed One, having set forth other opinions, said: "O Pārtha, it is my firm and supreme conviction that [these] must be performed. Enough with this elaboration. Furthermore, in the *Yatidharmasamuccaya*, Yādavaprakāśa has also stated: "'Karmayoga' is the combination of knowledge and action; from that, liberation [is attained]. Likewise, there is the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on [Brahma-sūtra 3.3.32]: "Because it exists everywhere."

The commentary on this point states: "Because He, being of the nature of Brahman, abides in all things. In the *Iṣṭihautrakalpa*, regarding Viṣṇu as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all deities, it says: "This indeed is the greatness of the gods that Viṣṇu is the Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhī*). (In the fifth *praśna*, concerning the mantra to be recited into the ear of the horse during the *ādhāna* rite, it is stated that because the term 'horse' (*vājin*) is used, the mantra is excluded from [use with] water-pots and so forth; however, the *bhāṣya* states: "There is no exclusion, for there is a specific instruction [to the contrary]. )

XL. Regarding this, the *Vṛtti* provides the etymological derivation: "The Sun is the steed" (*ādityo vājī*). Since he exists in all things by virtue of being the nature of Brahman, there is no cessation [of his presence] even in objects such as water-pots. This is supported by the commentary on *Maṇḍūkya-praśna*, section 1, which states: "For the path of the gods is the New and Full Moon sacrifices."

On this point, the commentary states: "Because of the scriptural declaration, 'This indeed is the path of the gods, namely the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices,' the knower of Brahman attains the path beginning with light—which serves as the means for reaching Brahman—through the performance of obligatory rites; and because it is said, 'He goes to the highest goal,' the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices have liberation as their purpose, since liberation is attained via the path of light. Thus, by metaphorically attributing the effect to the cause, the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, which are the means for attaining the path of the gods, are themselves designated as the 'path of the gods.'"

And so it is said: in Praśna 9, Section 2, Khanda, the Bhāṣya states, "It is for the purpose of attaining the path to heaven. Here, the Vṛtti comments: "Because of the scriptural indication, 'Now, having taken hold of the deities, he goes to the world of light (suvar),' the word 'heaven' (svarga) has liberation as its ultimate referent; and because the attainment of liberation is mediated by the attainment of the path of the gods (devayāna). In Praśna 12, Section 3, the Bhāṣya states: "Because the word 'heaven' denotes immeasurable supreme bliss (niḥśreyasa)."

Regarding this, the commentary (*vṛtti*) states: "The year is the heavenly world (*svarga-loka*). Because this refers to the bliss of the nature of the Supreme Brahman, which is Time itself, and because effort must always be made for the sake of liberation, there is a sense of permanence (*nityatā*) even when the scripture mentions one who "desires heaven" (*svarga-kāma*).

And thus the commentator Dhūrta-svāmī and the author of the Vṛtti, Rāmāṇḍāra, have stated that there is a relationship of body and embodied between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); that Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, is the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all sentient and insentient beings; that liberation (*mok�ṣa*), which is the unsurpassed supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) and designated by the term "heavenly state," is to be accomplished through the path of the gods (*devayāna-gati*) resulting from the performance of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) conjoined with knowledge by one who knows Brahman; and that the Lord alone is to be propitiated by all ritual actions, and that He alone is the object of all ritual action.

On the one hand, they can be considered followers of the Viśiṣṭādvaita tradition, as they maintain such views as "the continuity of being the enjoyer of the fruits of actions" and so forth. On the other hand, in accordance with the statement of the Vṛttikāra that "liberation is established through the combination of knowledge and action," it is also possible to consider them as not having entered the Viśiṣṭādvaita tradition. Furthermore, regarding the *Tattvamuktākalāpavivaraṇa* on verse 33 of the *Jīvasaṃvāda*: "If he explains the statement concerning the intention regarding the dependence on action, that is the doctrine of their combination (*samuccaya-vāda*)," it says: "Knowledge devoid of action is destroyed; and the action of those without knowledge is destroyed."

In such passages, we observe that the statement regarding the two [knowledge and action] as if they were combined—intending to express the dependence on action—is according to the method supported by the *Sarvārthasiddhi*. For one who asserts that "the scripture states that only that which is accompanied by knowledge is more powerful" and that "it is understood that knowledge is the effect of ignorance," it is possible for the doctrine of the combination of knowledge [with action] to serve as an inciter of the intention that action is subordinate to knowledge. When this is so, we conclude that these two [authors] are indeed adherents of Viśiṣṭādvaita.

We are able [to establish this], and it is indeed reasonable to understand it thus; for—as stated by Bhāskarācārya, the performer of Soma sacrifices, in his *Trikāṇḍī-maṇḍana*: "Either he possesses the occasion known as living during the spring season and so forth, or he performs the Soma sacrifice as a supplement to the knowledge of Brahman" (1.3.8)—this view, handed down through the tradition of commentators on the ancient Kalpasūtras, is restated in the determination of eligibility (*adhikāra*). There is even room to conclude that this very position belongs to these two authors of the Bhāṣya and the Vṛtti as well.

Furthermore, one must explain how such a description of the purport of the *Antaryāmi-brāhmaṇa*—which is the position of the author of the *Śrībhāṣya*—could possibly be consistent with those earlier texts that, under the term "combination of knowledge and action" (*jñāna-karma-samuccaya*), point to the means for attaining liberation. This doubt has been resolved by Maṇḍana Miśra and Vācaspati Miśra themselves. For instance, in the *Vidhiviveka* (p. 24), while introducing the category of injunction (*vidhi*), it is stated: "To say that [injunction] is the intention of the Veda itself is far-fetched."

On this point, Vācaspatimiśra explains: "Even those proponents of Vedānta who, while accepting the non-human origin [of scripture], maintain that the Veda is the body of the Veda and resides within as its inner controller (*antaryāmin*)—referring to the divine realm (*adhideva*)—cite the Śruti: 'He who dwells in all the Vedas, yet is within all the Vedas; whom all the Vedas do not know, whose body the Vedas are, who controls all the Vedas from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal. Thus he explained.

By this exposition, it is established that even the ancient commentators on the Vedas, prior to Maṇḍanamiśra, maintained that the Lord’s having the entire aggregate of sentient and non-sentient beings as His body is the intended meaning of the Upaniṣads.

It is well known in traditional history that they attained great honor, adorned with the title *Bhaṭṭanātha*, witnessed by learned scholars who were delighted by their excellent exposition of the reality of the Supreme Self (*paramātmatattva*). These very Bhaṭṭanāthas are renowned by the auspicious name Periyālvār, whose name is cherished through the meditative inquiry preserved in the lineage of teachers of Viśiṣṭādvaita.

By these very leaders of men, she was adopted as their own daughter; like Jānakī rising from the sacrificial ground, she rose from the surface of a flower garden—comparable to the blossoms of flowers used for the worship of the Lord who sleeps beneath the dense banyan leaves—and having become an incarnation of the venerable Goddess, she is the lady known by the name Godā, adorned with the title *Nātha* bestowed upon her by Him, and graced by her steadfastness in *samādhi* through constant contemplation of the divine and auspicious qualities of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Her divinity...

She who causes hundreds of verses adorned with the Śayyālaṅkāra to circulate, and who is worshipped without distinction from the Goddess Śrī in all the temples of Viṣṇu throughout the entire land of South India, protects the worlds.

And those whom the venerable Nigamānta-gurus designate as *bhaṭṭanāthas* in their own work titled *Maṇipravāla*, the treatise named *Rahasyatrayasāra*, by virtue of their being commentators on the *Kalpasūtra*: "Thus [ends] the commentary on the *Śivakalpasūtra* composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭanātha. [End of quote]

The meaning of this is that the venerable Bhaṭṭanāthācāryas, commentators on the Kalpasūtra, favored the view that the state of being a servant of the Blessed One—which culminates in being a servant of the Lord (Bhāgavata)—must be preserved until its final consummation in sale, as expressed in the words: "Servants of the Lord, who are devoted to the chanting of the Lord's names, are even capable of selling us."

Regarding this, the authors of the *Sārāsvādinī* commentary state: "In this regard, the venerable Bhaṭṭanātha has explained the *Kalpasūtra* after having determined—through sound logical arguments—the relationship between the subordinate and the principal (*aṅga-aṅgin*), the nature of ownership within the sacrifice consisting of the renunciation of one's own property, the nature of purchase and sale within the purchase of Soma, and the modes of application (*viniyoga-prakāra*), and so forth."

It is understood from a verse to be traced through the lineage of gurus that these teachers Viṣṇucitta, adorned with the title of Bhaṭṭanātha, sanctified the surface of the earth with their incarnation more than forty years after Kali [4000]. That is: "When the Kali age had passed its true term, in the year Krodhana, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Mithuna, when the sun was fierce."

"On the day of the Sun, under the asterism Svāti, on the auspicious lunar date named Ekādaśī, the illustrious Śrī Viṣṇucitta, whose greatness is inconceivable and who is free from sin, appeared. (Jayantīmālā). Thus, the attainment of such titles—occasioned by birth into a great family adorned with such epithets—is well-established through traditional succession among the learned, the knowers of the Vedas, and wise men proficient in the Kalpasūtras, as evidenced by the accepted compositions of Rāmāgnicit, the author of the commentary on the *Bhāṣya* of Dhūrtasvāmin.

Rāmāṇḍāra is posterior to Kumārila. This commentator Rāmāṇḍāra, at the beginning of the *Paśubandha-praśna*, cites the *Vārtika* of Kumārila—specifically the verse: "In the section on *arthavādas*, regarding the statement 'By the full oblation one obtains all desires,' the Vārtikakāra has stated: 'There is a distinction between small and great actions and their fruits within their respective spheres; even when the injunction is the same, there is no lack of differentiation based on the commonality of the locus'"—and by doing so, we determine that he is later than him.

Furthermore, because he belongs to the lineage of Bhaṭṭanātha, we ascertain that his role as a promulgator of the sacrificial scriptures—which constitutes the hereditary wealth of that family—was obtained through traditional succession. Although Dhūrtasvāmin and Rāmāṇḍāra were not contemporaries, [Rāmāṇḍāra states]: "Having paid homage to Āpastamba and by the grace of Dhūrtasvāmin, this commentary on his Bhāṣya is being composed according to my ability."

Thus, at the beginning of his own work, the commentator Rāmāṇḍāra, by praising the grace of Dhūrtasvāmin as the cause for the composition of his book, and by describing how he obtained that master’s favor through such means as attending upon and serving him—his very guru—it appears as though he reveals himself to have been a contemporary of the latter. Nevertheless, [he notes]: “In the Sūtra [it is stated] ‘from the *adhidevana* onwards until the end of the *sāda-homa*, this applies only to the Kṣatriya’; the meaning of this [statement] in the Bhāṣya must be investigated. (55–81)

"In this way, in the 177th Sūtra [it says]: 'The description of the subject matter of this Bhāṣya must be made without contradicting other treatises.'"—Likewise, in the tenth Praśna, [it says]: "'This was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya out of disregard, even though it ought to have been mentioned after the joining of the vessels,' or perhaps due to the negligence of a scribe. By such words which indicate the absence of the author of the Bhāṣya, it is determined that the author of the Bhāṣya and the author of the Vṛtti were not contemporaries. And thus:

"The commentary on the Āśvalāyana-sūtra was composed by the venerable one known as Devasvāmin, extensive and free from confusion. By his grace, I, Nārāyaṇa Gārgya, the son of Narasiṃha, now compose such a manual (vṛtti). In this very passage, even in the Rāmāṇḍāra-vṛtti, we conclude that the statement "by his grace" is intended merely to express gratitude rooted in the attainment of clarity of intellect produced by the study of the Bhāṣya text.

**Introduction to Rudradatta, the author of the Śrautasūtravṛtti:** Rudradatta was also a direct commentator on the Āpastamba Śrautasūtras. The title *Rudradattabhāṣya* is seen as a designation for his commentary in the *Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana-ṭīkā*. For example, in the *Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana* (155 Vyā.): "Being restrained by powerful others is *rudhyamānatvam*; that itself is *ārodhana*"—thus it is stated in the *Rudradattabhāṣya*.

Immediately after the statement, "Śabarasvāmin composed his Bhāṣya while disregarding the *Saṅkarṣakāṇḍa*," and following the detailed passage from the *Prapañcahṛdaya* beginning with "likewise [he did so] for the *Devatākāṇḍa*," the fact that he designates the *Devatākāṇṍa* while bypassing the designation *Saṅkarṣa* leads one to perceive that some other collection of Sūtras entirely distinct from the *Saṅkarṣa* must have been intended; furthermore, the author of that [work] was named Saṅkarṣaṇa.

That the term *saṅkarṣa* refers to the *Devatākāṇḍa* is understood from the commentaries of Prakāśātman, Ratnaprabhā, and Ānandagiri. The venerable Nigamānta-guru [Madhvācārya] also points to this very same meaning in the *Śatadūṣaṇī* (Vāda 4): "The *Devatākāṇḍa* has been accepted by the authors of the *Śrībhāṣya* as being supplementary to the *Karmakāṇḍa*; for they cite its sūtras, saying, 'It is stated thus in the *Saṅkarṣa*.'"

The intention [of the author] is that the term *saṃkarṣa*—as indicated by the reference "it was stated in the Saṃkarṣa" in the *Vedāntadīpa*—is a designation for the section concerning the deities (*devatākāṇḍa*), and this usage is also approved by the author of the *Śrībhāṣya*. This is in accordance with the eloquent statement of Bhaṭṭa Parāśarapāda in the *Tattvaratnākara*: "That [treatise] concerning ritual action, the deities, and Brahman appeared threefold from the author of the Sūtras, [namely] from the sage Jaimini, from Kāśakṛtsna, and from Bādarāyaṇa, respectively. This [verse] is kept in mind here.

Indeed, because of such authoritative instruction, this very point was also graciously affirmed by the venerable teacher Meghanādārisūri in his *Nayaprakāśikā*: "The subject matter of the twelve chapters (*dvādaśalakṣaṇī*) is ritual action (*karma*); the subject matter of the subsequent four chapters (*caturlakṣaṇī*) is the deity (*devatā*). This was also stated by the teachers of the Vedānta in the *Tattvaṭīkā*: "Once ritual action has been investigated in the *Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa*, it is precisely those various deities to be worshipped who are distinguished in the four chapters by their essential natures, differences, and excellence of qualities."

And therein, the subjects—such as the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and so forth—have been indicated by the teachers for each chapter. Regarding the derivation of the term *saṃkarṣa* when it refers to the *Devatākāṇḍa*, it has been shown by Ānandagiri: "That which is drawn together—that is, the remaining ritual action situated in the *Karmakāṇḍa*—is stated in summary; thus, *saṃkarṣa* is the *Devatākāṇḍa*. The *Brahmavidyābharaṇa* follows this very view.

Thus, it is established by the consensus of its commentators that the group of sūtras well-known as the *Devatākāṇḍa* was indeed intended to be commented upon by the authors of the Bhāṣya. Since the group of sūtras already renowned by the designation *Devatākāṇḍa* attained its common usage under that very name based on the renown of its commentary, the intention of the author of the Bhāṣya—who designates the *Devatākāṇḍa* by the term *Saṃkarṣa*—and the intention of the *Prapañcahṛdaya* both converge on this point.

Furthermore, in the commentaries (*bhāṣya-vyākhyās*) on the *Devatākāṇḍa* and *Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa*, their identity is clearly established. The eloquent sayings of Bhaṭṭa Parāśara—beginning with "The sphere of ritual action, deity, and Brahman" (*karma-devatā-brahma-gocara*)—as well as the sayings of Ācārya Meghanādārisūri and the venerable Āgamāntaguru, reveal that Mīmāṃsā indeed consists of three sections (*kāṇḍatraya*). This is confirmed by the statement: "It manifested in three ways" (*tridhodvabhau*). (Tattvaratnākara)

"By means of the four characteristics [of the *anantara* section], there is the status of being the subject matter of the deities," as stated in the *Nayaprakāśikā*; "in the *Saṅkarṣakāṇḍa*" and so forth, as stated in the *Tattvaṭīkā* on the three-sectioned *Mīmāṃsā* (*Adhisā*). Indeed, such is their elegant saying. Regarding that, however, the venerable teacher Meghanādārisūri and the venerable Nigamāntadeśikasūri have stated that the *Saṅkarṣakāṇḍa* was simply not in circulation in their own time: "The *Saṅkarṣakāṇḍa*, moreover, has never been seen by me."

Thus [it is said] in the *Nayaprakāśikā* (p. 238): "The middle section (*kāṇḍa*), however, has its status lost" (Mīmāṃsāpādukā, verse 36). Here, the existence of confusion and other doubts based on Ānandagiri’s commentary regarding the subject of *labdhi* (attainment) is indicated. Furthermore, in the *Śatadūṣaṇī*, having introduced the *Saṃkarṣa-kāṇḍa*:

And at the conclusion of that section, having shown the ultimate limit of the deities by stating, "Because he is seen [as such] in Hari," and having established His pervasion as the inner self of all through the statement, "For He is Viṣṇu, so it is said," for the purpose of showing that all forms of worship of deities culminate in Him, the conclusion is made by introducing Him alone as the Supreme Brahman known from the Vedānta with the words, "They call Him Brahman. This is the tradition of those who know the truth, as it has been graciously taught.

The intention of the venerable Ācārya Śrīkaṇṭha and Appayya Dīkṣita, the author of the *Śivārkamaṇidīpikā* on his commentary, is as follows: even though the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*) of the recitation of the Sūtras was interrupted at that time, the non-disappearance of the equipment for reflection required for the unity of the treatise (*ekaśāstrya*) is established; for this is obtained through the teaching—the instruction in the meaning provided by his own predecessors—which itself was obtained from the successive teachings of earlier commentators. In the *Parimala* commentary, he states: "Even though the *Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa* was not composed for the purpose of investigating the deities (*devatāvicāra*)."

However, the *Dvādaśalakṣaṇyā* consists of an investigation into various subjects through the analysis of logical principles (*nyāya*). It is its supplement (*pariśiṣṭa*), composed as a miscellaneous collection (*prakīrṇaka*) by treating both direct instruction (*upadeśa*) and extended application (*atideśa*) in a general manner, much like the relationship between a primary system (*tantra*) and its incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*). Indeed, there is neither an opening nor a conclusion in that work concerning the investigation of deities; for its opening investigation begins with the statement: "The *anuvaṣaṭkāra* is enjoined by the rule 'he performs the *anuyāja*'"; and [its conclusion] exists in the form of the *ājyasaṃpraiṣa* (the call for the *ājyā* offering), since it occurs at another time, just like the *ājyasaṃpraiṣa*.

—Thus concludes the treatise through this inquiry. 1. In the *upāṃśuyāja* and other rites which lack an explicit injunction regarding a deity, does a deity exist or not? In the *prayāja*s and other such rites, do the words *samit*, *barhis*, and so forth—which denote deities—refer to the well-known *samit*, *barhis*, and so on that are established as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, or do they refer to something else? 2. [The third point follows.]

Or not? 9. 10. Regarding the word *devān* in the first *anūyāja* initiation-call (*praiṣa*), "Sacrifice to the gods" (*devān yaja*): does this term refer to the deity of the first *anūyāja* alone, or to the deities of all the *anūyājas*?

Because of the abundance of deliberations on deities in such passages, the *Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa* itself is frequently referred to as the "Deity Section" (*Devatākāṇḍa*); thus, the non-dualists, including the author of the *Ratnaprabhā*, accept that this collection of aphorisms—which is designated primarily by the term "Deity Section"—is included therein. Yet, while they themselves deny this, they attempt to justify their position based on the consensus of the statements of the direct disciples of the author of the *Śrībhāṣya*, which is accepted in all the authoritative treatises of the Viśiṣṭādvaitins.

Those who know the tradition maintain that, because Dhūrtasvāmin provides an illustration from the discussion in the *Saṃkarṣa* [Kāṇḍa], and because Śabarasvāmin, in the commentary on sūtra 10.4.32, states "it will be explained in the *Saṃkarṣa*" regarding sūtra 12.2.11, there is no dispute whatsoever that the investigation of ritual action (*karma*) exists within the *Saṃkarṣa*. However, whether or not an investigation of the deities (*devatā*) exists in the *Saṃkarṣa* cannot be understood from the words of Dhūrtasvāmin alone.

The citation of that [work] by Śaṅkarācārya and the author of the *Śrībhāṣya*, as well as the statement in the *Prapañcahṛdaya* within the *Devatākāṇḍa* regarding Saṃkarṣaṇa’s composition of a commentary (*bhāṣya*), further demonstrate that the *Saṃkarṣa* is devoted to the investigation of deities (*devatāvicāra*). Having stated that Śabarasvāmin composed his commentary while disregarding the second section, the *Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa*, within the two-sectioned *Dharmamīmāṃsāśāstra*;

Likewise, regarding the phrase "in the Devatākāṇḍa," it is quite clear that the author of the *Prapañcahṛdaya*, by using the term *Devatākāṇḍa* to refer to a certain portion [of the text], intends precisely that portion which was disregarded by Śabara; for if he intended anything other than that, it would contradict the statement that [the work] consists of twenty chapters. And thus, the *Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa* consists of the mantras concerning ritual action (*karman*) and the deities (*devatā*).

In this regard, the investigation of ritual action (*karmavicāra*) is merely subordinate to that which is investigated in the twelve chapters [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*], being rooted in a desire for excellence; however, the investigation of the deity (*devatāvicāra*) is primary, because its essential nature and other attributes have been previously determined. Therefore, its name "The Section on the Deity" (*Devatākāṇḍa*) is significant, as it is based on the fact that it primarily investigates the deity.

In that regard, the designation "Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa" is based on the fact that it was composed as a commentary by Saṃkarṣaṇa; and it is precisely this usage, adopted as the basis for the commentators' terminology, that accounts for the terms "Saṃkarṣa" and "Sāṃkarṣaṇa" used by Śrī Śaṅkarācārya and Śrī Rāmānujācārya.

In this regard, since the term *saṃkarṣa* does not by itself convey the subject matter directly expounded in the text, Śrī Rāmānanda and the author of the *Prakaṭārtha* undertook the composition of the *Devatākāṇḍa* as a commentary in order to clarify what is being propounded therein.

Even though Śabarasvāmin composed a commentary on the *Devatākāṇḍa* within the *Saṃkarṣa*, due to his disregard for it, and because of the decline in its circulation at that time, as well as the lack of support from renowned and wise teachers such as Bhartṛmitra and others, the acceptance and dissemination of the *Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa* gradually dwindled. Among those parts, the section concerning the investigation of ritual action (*karmavicāra*) continued to be practiced to some extent, owing to its connection with the twelve chapters (*dvādaśādhyāyī*) of the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā*.

Regarding the section on the investigation of the deities (*devatāvicārabhāga*), however, those who took pleasure in the doctrine of non-theism (*nirīśvaravāda*) exerted themselves almost exclusively in its destruction by their own and others' hands; and when that section on the investigation of the deities had somehow persisted until the time of Śrī Rāmānuja and then vanished by fate, it was Ānandagiri himself—who perceived a deficiency in the *pravṛttinimitta* (the ground for application) regarding the status of being denoted by the term *saṃkarṣa*—who, despite having demonstrated the etymological analysis (*vigraha*) with the words "by whom [is it] drawn? (*kenaiva saṃkṛṣyate*), [resumed it] out of a desire to preserve established tradition.

Although the *Devatākāṇḍa* has indeed been commented upon, it is understood from this that at that time only the portion concerning the investigation of ritual action (*karmavicāra*) was extant, while the portion concerning the investigation of deities (*devatāvicāra*) had already been lost. For this very reason, the venerable teachers Meghanādāri Sūri and Nigamānta Sūri—who were born subsequently and were masters of the entire science of ritual inquiry—stated with the intention of consolation regarding the missing section on the investigation of deities: "The *Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa*, however, has never been seen by me."

This is supported by the *Nayaprakāśikā* and the *Mīmāṃsāpādukā*, which state: "Thus, the middle section (*kāṇḍa*) has its existence lost" (*luptasthiti*). Furthermore, in the *Mīmāṃsāpādukā*, although the Teacher should have simply said "lost" (*lupta*), his mention of "having its existence lost" (*luptasthititva*) is intended to refer specifically to the disappearance of the portion concerning the investigation of deities (*devatāvicāra*); therefore, the continued existence of the portion concerning the investigation of ritual action (*karmavicāra*) at that time is also intended.

Likewise, in the *Śatadūṣaṇī* as well, the section concerning the deities (*devatākāṇḍa*) has been refuted by the commentators on the grounds that it is a supplement to the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*). This is stated in the *Saṅkarṣa-kāṇḍa*, where they cite the passage: "For it is said [in the scripture], 'Thus it should be'"; and by pointing to the final sūtra therein with the words, "And because at the conclusion of that section, in the case of Hari, that [divinity] is seen," and by the phrase, "This is the tradition of the knowers of reality" (*tattvavid-sampradāya*), it is established through instruction that this much alone [is required]. However, the apprehension of each individual portion to be explained is accomplished only by the existence of those [scriptural passages].

It has now been made manifest that this is possible. For in the *Tattvaṭīkā*, based on the observation of the venerable Sūtra-author’s statement: "In the *Saṅkarṣakāṇḍa*, concerning the ritual actions investigated by the four chapters (*caturlakṣaṇī*), the very deity to be propitiated through each respective action is drawn forth [as the subject] by means of distinctions in essential nature, differences, and excellence of qualities," it was summarized by his sons, the teacher Varadanātha: "In the *Devatākāṇḍa*, the essential nature [of the deities], their distinctions, preceded by the enumeration of their qualities, and their fruit are declared for the deities."

Thus, while reflecting upon the actual state of affairs, those who were examining Ānandagiri’s analysis of the compound *saṅkarṣa-pada*—noticing that it did not include a section on the investigation of deities (*devatā*) and striving to determine its status—proceeded to establish the basis for the well-known designation of this section as the "Deity Section" (*devatākāṇḍa*) by selecting only certain deliberations from within the "Karma Section" (*karmavicārabhāga*) of the *Saṅkarṣa* and attributing the status of a separate section to that much alone.

They maintain that it is not appropriate to reject the section on deities (*devatākāṇḍa*)—which is traditionally accepted and intended to conclude with an inquiry into the deities—merely because of that much [disagreement]. Regarding the subjects commented upon by Dhūrtasvāmī: 1. Among those, the portion concerning "the maintenance of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* fire" is stated in the fifteenth chapter, second quarter (*pāda*), of the *Saṅkarṣakāṇḍa*, by the sūtra beginning with "of the consecrated fire" (*dīkṣitāgneḥ*). 2.

The portion stated by the author of the *Saṅkarṣa* as "the *prājahita* [fire]" is expressed in that very *Saṅkarṣakāṇḍa* by the sūtra "It should be the same" (*savaiva syāt*). 3. However, the portion stated by the author of the *Saṅkarṣa* as "of the entire *Saṅkarṣa*" is not seen in the *Saṅkarṣakāṇḍa*. Furthermore, it is understood from the commentary that the portion stating "the *paridhi* is encircled with a mantra" is discussed in the *Saṅkarṣakāṇḍa*, in the fourth pāda of the thirteenth adhyāya. 5.

6. That other portion where there is a repetition of words is not found among the sūtras in the *Saṅkarṣakāṇḍa*. However, the portion stating "the placing [of the fire] is with the preceding [mantra], the touching is with the following" is found in the *Saṅkarṣakāṇḍa*, in the first section (pāda) of the fourteenth chapter. Here we reflect upon this: the *Saṅkarṣakāṇḍa*, together with the commentary by Bhāskaradīkṣita, is currently available in printed form.

Moreover, in that work, not only very many, but indeed all the sūtras are seen to be incomplete in their sequence. For the inclusion of sūtras there is seen to be in such forms as *yo 'gnim* (13.7), *abhitaḥ* (13.10), *aindram* (13.2.5), *uttarasmin* (11), *teṣām* (13.4.19), *gaṇeṣu* (14.1.19), *udite* (15.1.4), and *yasyai* (16.4.6). And in its commentary, the meaning of the sentences is demonstrated, preceded by clear and extensive explanations of the subject matter.

No philosopher accepts that the full meaning of each sūtra—as indicated by the sūtra itself—is complete without the necessary supplementary elements such as implied ellipses, grammatical supply, and so forth. Nor can anyone compose a treatise by superimposing upon the sūtras meanings fabricated from one's own imagination or constructed from various plausible interpretations, devoid of even a fraction of support [from the original]. Furthermore, authoritative scholars do not hold such a treatise in high regard.

Therefore, we consider that this [work] was either an exposition based on the mere citation of a sūtra fragment; or an exposition written following the transcription of the complete sūtra due to a lack of faith in transcribing it, thus presenting only the fragments; or a discovery of such a partial portion resulting from an era in which the recitation of the complete sūtra had become difficult to obtain.

This is because [this point] is demonstrated by Appadīkṣita in his *Parimala* commentary on Śaṅkara’s *Bhāṣya*, through the presentation of several complete sūtras from the *Saṅkarṣakāṇḍa*. Furthermore, in the *Bhāvaprakāśikā*, a commentary on the *Śrutaprakāśikā*, taking up the pratīka "Or they are separate, because the deities are distinct," it presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "their offering is separate because the portions (*avadāna*) are one," arguing that like the portions, the offering itself must also be performed simultaneously; therein, this is the sūtra for the final conclusion (*siddhānta*): "They are separate..."

This is determined by the adoption of the sūtra, "Or [it is so] because of the distinctness of the deity," and by the exposition of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) and the established conclusion (siddhānta) by the venerable Raṅgarāmānuja Muni. Therefore, it is entirely reasonable to conjecture that the Saṅkarṣakāṇḍa was indeed not perceived by some due to its rare circulation, and that it existed in an incomplete form somewhere.

"Tomorrow it will be full" refers to the case where there is a slight fifteenth lunar day (*alpapañcadaśī*) in the forenoon. "One should fast on the third, the *kharvikā*," is the alternative view: in the case where the conjunction (*saṃdhi*) occurs before the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*), or in the case where the *pratipad* occurs within the *saṅgava* period on the following day.

Regarding the *sadyaskālatā* (immediate performance), it occurs only when there is a conjunction with the final portion of the fourteenth day (*pañcadaśī*) in the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*), and [the new moon] arises solely during the first part of the first lunar day (*pratipat*). For the *vikṛti* sacrifices, however, if the junction (*saṃdhi*) falls at night or in the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), the performance takes place on that same day; or else, starting on the previous day, it is performed immediately (*sadyas*). If the junction occurs in the forenoon, one performs the *prakṛti* sacrifice first, and afterwards the *vikṛti*, which is indeed immediate (*sadyaskāla*). In that case, there is no fasting (*upavāsa*) for the *kharvikā*. According to the rule, "on the day the [moon] is not seen, that is the *amāvāsyā*," this applies when the junction occurs after midday.

"Tomorrow we shall not see [him]"—this refers to the junction of the latter part of the day and the former part of the night (*uttarapūrvāhasandhi-pakṣe*). The word *yajña* is used here in its general sense with the intention of referring to the twenty-one types of sacrifices. He states another reason for the eternity of all [these rites]: "Because of the injunction for repeated practice"—as in, "This dharma, indeed, is unceasing; it is performed day after day, namely the Agnihotra"; "Thereupon, he offers [the animal] constantly during the latter half of the month; when the time arrives, he sacrifices; it is performed every half-month"; and "By means of these two, one should sacrifice as long as life lasts. The meaning of the word *darśa* is as follows: that moment in which the moon is seen conjoined with the sun by the perfected ones (*siddhas*) is *adarśa*; by association with that [moment], the day-and-night period is so called. Because it occurs at that time, the primary collection [of rites] is designated as such. What, then, are those primary elements? The instruction is that they are the oblations (*homa*) of the *āgneya* and *aindrāgna*, or the *āgneya* and *sānnāyya*. This is because the principle is that the property accomplished by the oblation is the means for producing the fruit. Therefore, the meaning of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*)—as in "it is said"—is the sense of the term *ataḥ*.

It is observed that [the term] *ahorātra* (day-and-night) is used for this purpose; one adds fuel in the morning [of the following day]. The reason for the secondary (*gauṇa*) application of the word *darśa* is understood from its application to a period spanning two days, as seen in such injunctions as "one sacrifices on the [day] after [the new moon]" (*bhūte yajate*). Since it is impossible to perform the sacrifice at the primary moment of the conjunction of the lunar phases (*parvan*) on the new moon day itself—according to the rule "one should sacrifice with the new moon [offering]" (*amāvāsyayā yajeta*)—it is understood through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to refer to the two days consisting of the two lunar dates (*tithi*) joined with that [conjunction]. Consequently, since the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*) also possesses the character of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), the metaphorical application is justified in the sense of the action occurring at that time.

The moment in which it is filled is the *pūrṇamāsa* (full moon) moment; by connection with that, it constitutes a day-and-night (*ahorātra*). Because it occurs at that time, it is a collection of primary rites (*pradhāna*). What, then, are those primary rites? They are the offerings (*homa*) of the Āgneya, the Upāṃśuyāja, and the Agnīṣomīya. According to the principle that "the determination of the fruit [of the sacrifice] applies to all offerings," this is the fulfillment of the constituent elements of the *pūrṇamāsa*. As for the analysis of the compound *darśapūrṇamāsau*: it is a *dvandva* compound meaning "the New Moon (*darśa*) and the Full Moon (*pūrṇamāsa*)."

According to the rule that "that which has fewer syllables is placed first," the word *darśa*, though used later [in the sentence], appears first in the compound. (Commentary) He explains the word *pūrṇamāsa*: "Month" and "sacrifice. The explanation is as before. Regarding the term *sarvahomanyāya*—the *apūrva* is that by which the fruit is produced (*kalpyate*) or accomplished (*sādhyate*). This refers to the intention of the word "all" (*sarva*). [The mention of the *āhavanīya* fire] is for the purpose of indicating the taking [of the fire], so that the carrying forward (*nayana*) of the *dakṣiṇāgni* may also take place, provided that the *dakṣiṇāgni* has the same source as the *āhavanīya*. Because it is observed that the *dakṣiṇāgni* is deposited after the *āhavanīya* has been drawn out but not yet established, some maintain that [the rule applies] "in all cases."

Regarding the mention of "another": after the morning *agnihotra* has been offered, there is no carrying forward (*praṇayana*) of another [fire] for the evening *agnihotra*. When the sacrifice is performed at night, the *āhavanīya* fire is maintained; [the result of the term *āhavanīya* is that] no other fire is carried forward. If the taking of the *āhavanīya* were not performed, even those fires maintained by one who has attained prosperity (*gataśrī*) would have to be carried forward to another location; therefore, this is done, because of the governing rule stating "he should follow the fires" (*agnīnanvādadhāti*). (Vṛtti)—Thus, because the fruits are identical, [the fires serve as] the primary elements.

In response to the doubt that there might be a dependence on the constituent parts (*aṅga*), the following solution is stated: due to the difference in time—since the performance of the *sāṅga-pradhāna* (the principal rite with its subsidiaries) must be carried out at each respective time, there is a distinction of fires: namely, the *Āhavanīya* and the *Dakṣiṇāgni*. At that time, these two are brought forth (*āhārya*) because they have been observed to be drawn out (*uddhṛta*) and because they depend on a specific sequence; even though they lack the status of being the original archetype (*prakṛti*), they possess the commonality of being Vedic. [The absence of the term "some": Some say that [this applies] everywhere (here too)—because of the mention of "some," one may either establish the *Āhavanīya* or lead forward the *Dakṣiṇāgni*.

Because the sequence beginning with the lifting (*uddharaṇa*) and ending with the placing (*sthāpana*) constitutes a single ritual act (*ekapadārtha*), since nothing else can occur in between them except by explicit scriptural statement (*vacana*). The mention of "another" (*anyagrahaṇa*) refers to cases such as the *niśīṣṭi* sacrifice after one has offered the oblation, or when one should eat at night (*naktamāyateta*). Furthermore, the mention of "another" is intended to demonstrate what is established by logical principle (*nyāya*). The mention of the *āhavanīya* fire is made because it is prepared [at that time].

The summary of the meaning there is as follows: having offered the *agnihotra* and having carried forth [the fire], one should perform the morning *anvādhāna* for the *āhavanīya*. There are three points here: the distinction in the sentence-meaning (*vākyārthabheda*), the natural sense of the word "other" (*anyaśabda-svārasya*), and the meaning of the term *anvādhāna*. These three sūtras end with the words "having offered," "having carried forth," and "he performs the *anvādhāna*. Is it because they express a different matter? This is the resolution of the objection regarding the instruction (*upadeśa*). By the word "other," the rule for the carrying forth (*viharaṇa*) of the *agnihotra* becomes silent; or rather, it is "other" because of the statement, "having purified with the *yajus*. The *anvādhāna* is the act of making [the fire] powerful.
One who has not attained prosperity does not lead another fire [into his house]. ||3||

"One whose fortune has departed" (*gataśrī*) is one who has lost his prosperity; he will be explained further below. For him, there are no others—[specifically] not in the *someṣṭi*s such as the *prāyaṇīya* and so forth. These three [sentences], though their sequence is established, have distinct meanings because they are independent, being intent upon injunctions since their objects are not already established. Because they express different things—that is, because each expresses a distinct meaning.

"Because of the mention of another [alternative]" (*anyaśa-vacanāt*): This refers to the state of the words of instruction (*upadeśapada*). By means of the view of the instruction (*upadeśamata*), he removes the suspicion of meaninglessness (*ānarthakyaśaṅkā*) regarding the word "other" (*anya*) as being a restatement established by logic (*nyāyasiddhānuvāda*). By the inclusion of the term "Yajus," although there is an exclusion of the *mantra*, the intention is that the properties of the *praṇītā* water still apply when it is done silently (*tūṣṇīm*). This is stated in the passage: "Three indeed are those who have attained prosperity... (*trayo vai gataśriyaḥ*). The silent recitation (*japa*) is also a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the fuel-adding (*anvādhāna*). [Variants: *japo'pyanvādhānāṅgam* (ka, ja); *japo'gnayanvādhānasya* (ga); *japo'pyamanvā-* (kha).]

Having led forward another Āhavanīya fire—[variants: *praṇīya* (kha), *praṇīyāhvanī-* (ja)]—following the *ramīnām* [variant: *anvā* (4)]... three of those [are mentioned]—[variant: *anyārtha-* (kha), *tvānupadeśa-* (ja)]. Because of the absence of instruction regarding [the word] *tvā*, there is the refutation of the instruction—[variant: *parihāra* (ka)]. Here, in this manuscript, it is seen written with the indication of the words for the refutation of the instruction under the heading "Sūtra-abandonment" (*sūtratyāga*). [Variant: *gatādhāryasya* (ka), *gatā yasya śrī-* (ja)]. It is said here: [variant: *ratrocyate* (ka)]. "[The fire] other than this"—[variant: *syānyamaniṃ* (pra)]. Rudradatta does not accept this, because the author of the Sūtra himself will explain it later.

Regarding the statement "it is so said" (*ityuktam*), [the commentary] says: "He leads forward the fire. Because of the scriptural injunction, "The fire of one who has attained prosperity (*gataśrī*) is permanently maintained," it should not be commenced here. [The meaning of the term *gataśrī* and the purpose of the compound are as follows: The prohibition against one who has attained prosperity applies to others; [furthermore, the purpose is] so that there may be a distribution of the Āhavanīya fire for the Pratiprasthātṛ during the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices. Thus he says. [Note: This passage appears to be a commentary on the ritual procedure concerning the leading forward of the sacred fires (*praṇayana*). It discusses the specific case of the *gataśrī*—one who has attained worldly or ritual eminence—and the necessity of distributing the fire for the assistant priest (*pratiprasthātṛ*) in the Varuṇapraghāsa rites.]

The mention of "another" is intended so that there might not be a prohibition of water that has been brought forward by someone else when it is extremely well-prepared. The mention of "fire" is intended so that even when another person is observing, there may not be a prohibition of the bringing forward of water and other substances that have already been prepared.

Having murmured, "O gods who know the way, find the way for the sacrifice; let the sacrifice be set in motion by the god Vāta, the lord of mind," he kindles the Āhavanīya fire with the verse, "Mine, O Agni, be splendor in the invocations," the Gārhapatya fire with the following verse, and the Anvāhāryapacana fire with the next verse. 4.

The place for recitation and the tone: one recites to the north of the sacrificial hall (*vihāra*). All recitations are performed with the fourfold intonation (*cātussvarya*). Regarding other mantras, if it is said that there is a permanent prohibition—namely, "it should belong to Varuṇa"—then this prohibition is applied to those who have lost their prosperity (*gataśrī*). Because of the absence of two *āhavanīya* fires, the restriction of the prohibition applies specifically to this *vihāra*. The placement is divided and set down in two parts. As for the prohibition of others—it is a prohibition specifically of that which is designated as "one should lead forth another."

The prohibition of the *praṇītā* waters does not apply to the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, nor to one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), nor to one whose prosperity has departed; for this prohibition refers to the subject matter of the previously mentioned *praṇayana*. [This is stated] so that the prohibition of the *praṇayana* of the *praṇītā* waters and others might not apply even when the word "fire" (*agni*) is used as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for other things. (3) He murmurs [the mantra], because of the statement: "The ritual movement (*vihāra*) is performed from the north. According to the fourfold hearing (*cātuśrutyā*), it is because of the traditional law (*smṛti*): "In sacrificial rites, except for *japa*, *nyūṅkha*, and *sāman*."

Some perform the *japa* before the *viharaṇa*, because it serves the purpose of the sacrificial application (*yajñayoga*); however, this alternative view is untenable, as the sequence follows the *viharaṇa*. Furthermore, by them, the *samiṣṭayajus* must be employed at the very end. Fuel capable of sustaining the fire is "kindling" (*upasamindhana*), which is the placing of large logs. Having first performed that for the *āhavanīya*, the kindling of the *gārhapatya*—the fire associated with the householder (*gṛhapati*)—follows immediately thereafter. "Cruel" (*krūra*) refers to that which is connected with the destruction of seeds and so forth.

*Viliṣṭa*—the etymological explanation (*nirvacana*) of the word *anvāhārya* and others has been incorrectly formulated. He explains it as follows: it is called *anvāhārya* because one brings (*anvaharati*) [food] to it, that is, one causes it to be destroyed [by cooking]; thus, that in which [the food] is cooked is the *anvāhāryapacana*. That which exists in the *āvasatha* (dwelling) is *āvasathya*. Regarding these two, the fueling is done silently, because we observe the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) of the sacrificer. (Vṛtti): However, some do this based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) [in the text]: "Let the Vāta-sacrifice be performed," and because the spreading of the fires (*viharaṇa*) is for the purpose of engaging in the sacrifice, and because [the Vāta-sacrifice] is not a subordinate element (*apadārtha*) of the primary sacrifice.

That is untenable, because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the completion of the sacrifice in the passage: "having found [the path] for the sake of the sacrifice" (*yajñāya vittvā*). Therefore, the performance follows the order of the recitation (*yathāpāṭha*). As for the term *dhāraṇa* (maintenance), its application to the *gārhapatya* fire—even though all fires are connected with the householder (*gṛhapati*)—occurs in a single instance, just like the word *paṅkaja* (lotus) and others. Now follows the etymological explanation (*nirvacana*) of the term *anvāhāryapacana*: it is the "cooking of the crude" (*krūra-pacana*), which is the explanation of the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with, "Whatever in the sacrifice is crude, whatever is disjointed... It is the cause for taking more [food] in the assembly (*sabhā*).

Although the Sūtrakāra has not mentioned the *āhavanīya* and *gārhapatya* fires here, since the worship (*upasthāna*) by the sacrificer is observed for them, their kindling (*upasamindhana*) must be performed silently; for that purpose, the etymological explanation of those two terms is also provided here. For they are seen to be silent—[as stated]: "At the end of the *vyāhṛtis*, the kindling of those two is silent. [The fire] is to the south, facing east. (4.1) [Variant readings: *muktvopari-ka*; *vya syān-ka*; *hisāsa-ja*].

Regarding the recitation (*japa*), there is a rule for the conclusion (*apavarga*) in the *Vihavya* [section]: "In all the *vikalpa*s, the conclusion is with each set of three [verses]. Because of this restriction, the recitation of the final verse (*uttamā*) occurs only in this specific case.
(Verse) Some prescribe the placing of the firewood with the *vyāhṛti* formulas.

(Bhā) The *anvādhāna* is performed with each individual *vyāhṛti*. In the case of the laying down of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks, the reason for taking them all together is that they are divided according to their assigned portions (*diṣṭa*). However, here [the procedure concerns] the *gārhapatya* and other fires. According to the Vājasaneyins, there are three [verses] for each direction; the position of the *ṛṣi* is that the conclusion of the section beginning with "O Agni, [grant] splendor" (*māgne varcaḥ*) consists of three verses. Here, however, the meaning is that one should recite the final verse as a silent prayer (*japa*).

She should not be pleased with either alternative alone; rather, she should place all the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) into the *āhavanīya* fire, even if there are only five. The number [five] is for the purpose of indicating all the fuel-sticks, and does not apply to the others. Although, in the case of the *vyāhṛtis*, the plural number—being inherent in the items to be employed—is obtained as a non-intentional expression (*avivakṣā*), nevertheless, because they serve different purposes, [the rule applies].

Regarding "by oneself" (*svayam*): the Sūtrakāra has taught the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks by means of the *vyāhṛtis*—"Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Suvaḥ"—and by teaching them individually with the words "He lays down [the brick] with this *vyāhṛti*, 'Bhūḥ'. However, in this case, the *vyāhṛti* option is due to a specific scriptural statement (*vacana*). But in that other case, Rudradatta holds that there is a separate Sūtra ending with "tisābhas tisabhivāḥ."

In the opinion of some, one should kindle the fire with the ten verses of the *vihavya* section and the three verses beginning with "abhipanāminde" (*iti tanmate*). According to others, however, in all ritual manuals (*kalpa*), one should recite the three *vyāhṛtis* once for each of the three fires, because of the use of the word "but" (*tu*) and the word "and" (*ca*). Furthermore, according to the statement in the *Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra*, first book, first chapter: "In one case, [the fires are addressed] together; in another case, [they are addressed] individually. (*ekasmin pakṣe saha; anekasmin pakṣe ekaikam*). This is established by the explicit scriptural injunction (*vacana*).

The instruction for each [of the three] is by means of three [verses] each. Now, regarding the ritual procedure (*kalpa*): previously, after having commenced the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is: "By means of these two, I shall sacrifice as long as I live and attain the heavenly world," or else the desire for all objects of desire. This is because the *sārasvata-homas*, the *anvārambhaṇīyā-iṣṭi*, and the *caturhotṛ-homas* serve the purpose of all *darśapūrṇamāsa* rites.

But when there is a separation of the offerings (*hārapṛthaktva*), O Kāma, even then, because of the fulfillment of the intention regarding the two *Sārasvata* oblations, one should sacrifice at the *darśa* [and *pūrṇamāsa*]. [The state of the plural number] is due to the fact that, according to the Vājasaneyins, before the division of those taught as a whole, there is no statement of their separate establishment; thus, even in the case of the *vyāhṛti*s, by the principle of intending plurality as previously stated, it is directed toward the *āhavanīya* fire alone.

The mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) follows the sequence of the ritual acts; although this resolve is essentially a mental operation, it extends only as far as the utterance of the words that express it. This is because it has been stated, "one does not sacrifice after having spoken," which indicates that the act is defined by its culmination in utterance. [This applies to both obligatory and optional rites. Even in the context of obligatory duties (*nityādhikāra*), the mention of a result is for the sake of liberation (*mokṣa*). There is no contradiction even in that case regarding the mention of heaven (*svarga*), for it has been stated previously that the word *svarga* denotes liberation, which is of the nature of an immeasurable and certain state.

One who seeks the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) should not intend even that; such are these positions regarding the desire for all [the rites] simultaneously. Now, why is the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) made first for both the Sārasvata and the Agnihotra, when it is the Full Moon sacrifice? It is said: because of its being the commencement of the purpose. Having made the resolve common to the entire performance, those [rites] must be carried out. However, when the resolve "I shall begin" is made, it is appropriate at the time of commencement. This is the conclusion.
Wherever one accumulates craving, there action follows as its consequence. [The reading in the printed edition is: "Thus I have reflected upon you."]

(Bhāṣya): Having said, "I shall begin the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices; I shall sacrifice with them for as long as I live, or for thirty years, or I shall desist when I am worn out," and having offered four oblations into the fire after they have been set aside, [he declares] the desires such as, "I shall sacrifice with the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa; may I attain the heavenly world. Etcetera.

[Time for shaving: Shaving takes place at the full moon and other such occasions. [Its specific variations depend on the distinction between the first, second, and subsequent performances,] because of the scriptural injunction "Then, when lightning appears... (Vṛtti). There is no mention here of the results of desires (*kāma-phala*). "I shall perform these two"—this much is common to both. Thus far—desires—at the beginning of the performance of the full moon sacrifice and so forth, [there is] the *sārasvata-homa*... [the difference in the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and its purpose]. Having formulated the resolve regarding the obligatory entitlement (*nityādhikāra*), at the beginning of the performance, one formulates the resolve regarding desires (*kāmasaṃkalpa*).

In that case, by the occasion of the discussion regarding the optional (*akāma*) entitlement, the entitlement for the obligatory (*nitya*) rite is also established. [Regarding the fruit of shaving and its once-only performance: Shaving is a refinement of the person (*puruṣa-saṃskāra*), because it effects the fitness of the person as the locus of the transcendental result (*apūrva*). Since a single *apūrva* is accomplished through the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), that fitness is established by shaving performed just once at the Full Moon sacrifice and so forth; therefore, there is no shaving on both occasions.

For this very reason, the shaving of hair is taught as an optional practice for every ritual period (*parvan*) according to the opinion of the Vājasaneyins, in accordance with the rule: "He shaves even a small amount of hair. Following the shaving—after which the touching of water is prescribed—the text states: "You are lightning" (*vidyud asi*). Thus, after the shaving, there is the touching of water with the mantra "You are lightning.
