Having offered oblations in other fires, one says, "I shall sacrifice with this," and performs the shaving of the hair for the sake of specific desires (*kāma*). Then follows the ritual of spreading the fires (*viharaṇa*) and so forth, beginning with the formula "Thou art lightning" (*vidyud asi*). Regarding the fruit prior to the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): if, during a season for which no resolve has been made, one were to perform [the rite] with the formulas "Thou art lightning" or "Desire," it would not be known which sacrifice is being commenced. The instruction is that the shaving, the formula "Thou art lightning," the resolve regarding the season, the desire, and the spreading of the fires constitute the sequence.

(Sūtra 1.1.7) "For one who is about to perform the *saṃnaya* sacrifice, he brings a branch of the *palāśa* tree or a branch of the *śamī* tree—one that has many leaves, many twigs, with unwithered tips, and without holes."

[The meaning of the word *sānnāyya*. (Bhāṣya): Because Indra’s sensory power (*indriya*) was brought together (*sanīta*) within himself from the animals and the plants, therefore both the curd (*dadhi*) and the milk (*payas*) are called *sānnāyya*. Since they were brought together (*sam-anayat*), that is the reason for the *sānnāyya* being called *sānnāyya*. Thus, he who sacrifices with it is called "one who brings together" (*sannayan*). For that one who brings together (*sannayataḥ*), the resolve (*saṅkalpa*) is the commencement of the performance of the *palāśa* [leaf]. From the word "about to sacrifice" (*yakṣyamāṇaḥ*), its priority to the commencement of the performance is understood. Therefore...

It is logical that [the *sānnāyya*] exists even prior to the mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*), because the resolve consists in the commencement of the ritual performance (*prayoga*). Regarding the etymological definition (*nirvacana*) of the *sānnāyya*: "Because Indra slew Vṛtra with the cattle... and so forth. However, in other cases, [the term refers to]: *viharaṇa*, *japa*, etc. *Viharaṇa* is the act of spreading out [the fires]: taking the fire from the *gārhapatya* and placing it in its proper place for the sake of the *āhavanīya* on the southern altar. [End of section 1. *Karma*... [fragmentary text].

The first sequence among the others: [the verses] *vidyumatī* and *gavyūti*. If here the *manas* is performed, [it is] *kha-ga-a*. *Vidyutvatī*—in this [verse], *ga*. *Vidyut-kā-sa*. 7 Or, having first spoken to the sacrificer, the *viharaṇa* [is performed]. 3.8.9.21 – 5 kha 1, sūtra: *Śākhā-palāśa-śākhā* means a branch with leaves; *śamyā-śākhā-śamī-śākhā* means a branch of the *śamī* tree. He brings that [branch]. *Parṇāni* means leaves. [The word *sanayata* indicates the purpose: because of the statement "he brings together" (*sanayata*), the branch is for the sake of the *sānnāyya* offering, not for the sake of the *upaveṣa*. "Not dried at the tip" means not dried out at the end. "Without holes" means that which has no cavity inside.
(Sūtra): "If one should desire that [a person] be without cattle, for him he should fetch a branch with dry tips; he indeed becomes without cattle. 1.1.8.
"If one should desire, 'May he be possessed of cattle,' for him one should fetch a branch with many leaves and many twigs; thus it is known that one makes him indeed possessed of cattle."

[According to the *Sūtrasamata*, the state of being based on scripture (*śrutibhāva*): Prohibitions such as "not hearing" and so forth exist because they are undesirable; for one should not contemplate what is impure, like a sacrificial priest (*ṛtvij*). Furthermore, the intention of the author of the *Sūtra* is the prohibition of the repetition of words. (Vṛtti: The meaning is that the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the word *sānnāyya* has been stated in the *Brāhmaṇa*. Regarding "leaves" (*parṇāni*), which means "foliage," the word *parṇa* signifies "many leaves."

[The Taking of the Upaveṣa]: Because it is taught as something well-known in the world and because no specific detail is taught here, the wood for the *upaveṣa* and so forth is to be taken at the full-moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*), even in the absence of a branch. One should consider that this applies to the sacrificer, since there is no mention of an animal sacrifice.

The intention of the author of the Sūtras regarding the prohibitive nature of the statement is as follows: "He who desires that there may be no cattle [should take] the *parācī* [verse]"—he brings it; he fetches it; he brings it together. [This applies] to substances and actions. He who desires that there may be no cattle [should take] the *aguṇā* [verse]; this is for the purpose of avoiding [the quality], and not because of the desire of the Adhvaryu priest that specifically that [verse] be taken.

Rudradatta, however, maintains that because it is impossible for one who has been hired by the sacrificer to be directed toward what is not for his benefit, this is a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*). [In the *Āpastamba Śrautasūtra*, First Praśna, First Paṭala, Section 10: [Bhāṣya: The instruction is that the desire belongs to the Adhvaryu. The logical principle (*nyāya*) is that it is for the purpose of breaking through many leaves.
[Sūtra: That [branch] which is facing east, north, or northeast—one cuts it with the formula: "For food thee! For strength thee! (TS 1.1.1). 1.1.10.

The northern branch of the tree is the one to be taken, and that alone is to be used, and not any other that has grown; for the eastward or northward direction of the tree is intended for the Brāhmaṇa, as stated by the author of the Sūtras in the rule: "One should offer the *iḍā* after [the sacrifice] has been performed," which, being prohibitive in nature, implies a prohibition of repeating the steps. [This is the application of the principle. Regarding the teaching: because of the teacher's instruction on desire. Regarding the principle of the many: the censure of the former is for the purpose of praising the subsequent injunction.

Therefore, even if it has many leaves, it should be taken in times of distress. [Explanation of the specific branch to be accepted: "Situated to the north"—the mention of "that which is toward the east and north" is for the purpose of indicating that only that [branch] which is not situated otherwise should be accepted. "To the north" (uttarā) means, having stated "one with many leaves," it is superior to what was previously prohibited. [The directional limit: Since the tree is the subject under discussion, and having introduced the topic with "Brahman indeed is the leaf," the understanding of "east" and so forth is relative to the tree when it says, "if one were to bring [a branch] facing east."

One cuts off that branch of the tree whose qualities extend toward the directions such as the east and so forth. This [concluding] sentence must be supplied. "On the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), on that day when they do not see the moon, they perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña in the afternoon (*aparāhṇe*). [Piṇḍapitṛyajña Times] (Bhāṣya): Because of the statement, "on that day when they do not see the moon," [the time is] in the afternoon of the first lunar day (*pratipad*) when the moon is still visible. This is because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the text: "Therefore, it is performed for the ancestors every month. [1]

[The specific rule regarding the time for the Piṇḍapitṛyajña. (vṛ)—Regarding the statement "on the day when the moon is not seen in the afternoon": if there is a mixture with the fourteenth day, it is on the preceding day. If the moon is visible in the morning, then when the junction of the lunar phases (*parvan*) occurs in the afternoon on the following day, the performance takes place precisely in that afternoon. This is because of the scriptural injunction, "on the day when they do not see the moon," since the moon is entirely invisible at the junction of the phases; therefore, it is specifically in the afternoon of the day-and-night (*ahorātra*) associated with that junction.

— 7. Therefore, [the argument] "on account of the indicative mark" (*liṅga*) means that the Sūtra must be explained in accordance with that indicative mark. The meaning of the Brāhmaṇa passage, "It is performed for the ancestors when the month is complete," is as follows: the month is complete at the final moment of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). Therefore, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is indeed performed during the afternoon of the yogin’s day-and-night (*ahorātra*). Consequently, even when there is a mixture with the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*) due to the waning of the moon, if the junction of the lunar phases (*parvasandhi*) occurs within that day-and-night, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is performed in its afternoon.

Even in the absence of the fourteenth day, if there is an increase [in the lunar days], it occurs on the afternoon of the conjunction (*saṃdhi*) of the following day. The reason for mentioning the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* within this context is that, although the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* is independent, its mention here—within the performance of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*—is for the purpose of fixing its position among the constituent elements of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* which are bound by sequence on the day of preparation (*aupavasathya*). Therefore, if due to negligence or other causes the ritual actions up to the smearing of the cooking pots (*kumbhyālepana*) have not been performed, the expiation for an omission (*antarita-prāyaścitta*) takes place.

[And there is a difference of opinion regarding the fruit: Regarding the *adhivṛkṣa* [rite], it is said, "In the *pitṛyajña*, he offers three oblations and pours out [the remains] three times; thus six are produced. The view of the author of the Sūtras, however, is that because one extends the sacrifice after having ransomed it from the ancestors, this [Piṇḍapitṛyajña] is obligatory since its purpose is the ransom for the New Moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*). For this very reason, the Commentator, having stated "I shall perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña," said "Vidyut asi" (Thou art lightning), and did not mention a specific fruit. In the view of the Mīmāṃsakas, however, there is no fault in not commencing the Piṇḍapitṛyajña; rather, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) applies only when there is an interruption of what has already been commenced.

Because the word *gārhapatya* is based on the purpose of consecration (*saṃskāra*), how then can there be an absence of those [consecrations]? This is an inquiry into the propriety of the elision of the word *gārhapatya*. [The answer is: "Due to the absence of the word *gārhapatya*"—this very [fire] is indeed prescribed for one who has not performed the fire-consecration (*anāhitāgni*), because it is prescribed as being devoid of the consecratory rites (*ādhāna-saṃskāra*). Consequently, in the accompanying mantra "That which is the atmosphere... (*yad antarikṣam...*), the word *gārhapatya* is elided. However, this is not a case of the elision of the entire mantra, as in the case of [the elision of the mantra] for a vessel made of clay (*mṛnmayam*) when it is used silently (*tūṣṇīka*).

In that case, when the primary sense of the word *gārhapatya* is excluded from the *kāṃsya* vessel and the earthenware vessel, it is logical that the other words are also excluded because the primary sense has ceased. However, here, since the mantra "O Fire, do thou protect me" (*agnirmā*) is intended to reveal the fire as the substantive (*viśeṣya*), the subordinate term *gārhapatya*, which expresses a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), cannot possibly apply and is therefore excluded. The distinction is that [the subordinate] follows the lead of the primary.

Regarding the mantra "abhi gṛhṇāmi," because the word *śvas* (tomorrow) is predominant, there is an elision of the word *sadyas* (today) from that mantra. The phrase "he sacrifices when [the day] has become tomorrow" (*śvobhūte yajate*) is for the purpose of praying for the pleasure of [the deity]; thus, in other cases as well, the elision of mantra words is to be inferred based on the designation of the reason, namely, "because it is the disposal of the consecrated materials" (*saṃskārapratipattitvāt*). This is the justification for its being directed toward the kindling of the Gārhapatya fire. In the phrase "in that [case], of the word..."—the remainder is "the application" (*pravṛttiḥ*). It is not merely due to the connection with the householder (*gṛhapati*).

Alternatively, the word *gṛha* refers specifically to the Vedic ritual, as seen in such passages as "He who knows the house of the sacrifice" (*yo vā adhvaryo gṛhān veda*) and "He goes forth with his house" (*sa-gṛhaḥ prayāti*). The intention is that the *gārhapatya* fire is so called because it is the master (*pati*) of that [house], due to its connection with it. But how is there an absence of those [fires]?—for this is the meaning: the absence of the letter *s* [in the derivation] is indeed due to the non-manifestation of the two [suffixes] *ka* and *jha*, and because the operation follows the predominance of the primary element (*prādhānya-anurūpa-pravartana*). This is the remainder [of the argument].

The remaining portion [of the text] beginning with *pravartate* (is performed), *varaṇa* (the choosing), and *lopa* (omission) of the word *gṛhapati* (householder)—[these apply] even by one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*). For those [rites] are prohibited; if they were performed, he would indeed become one who has established the fires (*āhitāgni*). Therefore, because of the prohibition of the consecration (*saṃskāra*), there is the omission of the word *gārhapatya*. Thus ends the third chapter in the commentary of Dhūrtasvāmin, accompanied by the gloss of Śrī Rāmāgnicit.

And the modifications of the *Āgnīṣomīya* do not apply to one who has not performed the Soma sacrifice. However, by virtue of a specific scriptural statement (*vacana*), they do apply, as in the case of the animal sacrifice and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, according to the sequence. (Vṛtti): The conclusion of the laying down of the bricks (*upadhāna*) occurs at the end of the act of placing the fire-wood (*adhyūhana*). 7.

[The establishment of the rule stated in the Bhāṣya. Regarding the phrase "from the fear of the assembly" (*asabhayat*), its meaning is as follows: the modifications (*vikāra*) of the *sānnāyya* and the *āmīṣomīya* [offerings] occur after the *soma* sacrifice, according to the principle that "the modified form follows the archetypal form" (*prakṛtivad iti nyāyāt*). Furthermore, because of the scriptural statement, "Only one who has performed the *soma* sacrifice should offer the *sānnāyya*; for a Brāhmaṇa is by his very nature connected to the gods through *soma*, and he becomes connected to the *āmīṣomīya* [deity] through *soma*," the time following the *soma* sacrifice constitutes the subsidiary period (*aṅgakāla*) for the *sānnāyya* and *āmīṣomīya*. Consequently, the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to those modifications belongs only to one who is capable of performing them within that specific time.

"Even in the case of modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), [the rule applies] only to one who is capable of performing them at that time. Although it should have been stated as "for one who has not performed the *soma* sacrifice," the expression "for one who does not offer the *sānnāyya*" is used because even for one who has not performed the *soma* sacrifice, the *sānnāyya* offering is prescribed. The meaning of this is: "But by virtue of a direct statement (*vacana*), they occur out of sequence; the modified sacrifices occur by virtue of a direct statement. For example, the *Āgrayaṇa*, the animal sacrifice, and the *Cāturmāsya* occur [out of their natural order] because they are taught according to the sequence following the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*)."

It should not be said that this sequence is not authoritative for the performance because the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are taught even prior to the Ādhāna (fire-consecration); for while only the mere nature (*svarūpa*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa was mentioned previously, their actual performance is taught in the passage "one who is about to begin the Darśapūrṇamāsa. Thus says Āśvalāyana: "Having sacrificed with the Darśapūrṇamāsa, then with the Iṣṭis, Paśus, and Cāturmāsyas, and then with Soma," and so forth.

[Khaṇḍa 14, Sūtra 9] [The Rule Concerning the Association with Indra and Mahendra] One who has not attained prosperity (*agataśrī*) should not sacrifice to Mahendra; for it has been stated: "There are indeed three who have attained prosperity" (ŚB 2.2.2.6). [Commentary: "One who has heard" (*śuśruvān*) means one who has mastered the three Vedas—the *Ṛg*, *Sāman*, and *Yajus*—for that is indeed prosperity (*śrī*). Thus says the Śruti. (Sūtra, Bhāṣya, Vṛtti) 4, 5. (Vṛtti) 1.35.135.

For one who has performed the *Soma* sacrifice but whose wife has died, after taking a new wife, the *Āgnīṣomīya* and *Sānnāyya* offerings indeed continue; they do not cease because of the wife’s lack of qualification [in the primary rite]. This is because women depend upon the qualification conferred by their husband. Thus, the qualification of a Kṣatriya wife is observed in the *Āgnīṣomīya*, as she is not the primary agent. Furthermore, it is seen that the wife is a limb (*aṅga*) of the sacrificer, according to the rule: "Or when he should be deprived of a limb."

Likewise, during the thirteen-night sacrifice (*trayodaśarātra*), the sacrificer, having fasted for twelve days, should himself offer the *agnihotra*. Not departing, he should perform the *soma* sacrifice right here, or the *paśu* sacrifice, or even the *iṣṭi-paśu*. [The meaning of the items beginning with *gataśrī*, and the justification for the arrangement stated in the Commentary: The explanation of the passage "There are indeed three who have attained prosperity" (*trayo vai gataśriyaḥ*) is as follows: "One who has heard" (*śuśruvān*). Regarding the term "prosperity" (*śrī*): according to its etymological derivation, one whose prosperity (*śrī*) has gone to, or been attained, is called "one who has attained prosperity" (*gataśrī*). Furthermore, by the word "prosperity," the three Vedas are indicated.

And [the word] "learned" (*śrutavān*)—according to the statement, "The sages (*kavayaḥ*) are indeed those who have heard," and "The sage (*kavi*) is one who has far-reaching vision," [it follows that] "one who has heard" becomes one who has attained prosperity. By this, the meaning is that he alone who possesses the three Vedas is one who has mastered the meaning of the threefold Veda. Now, Rudradatta introduces [the following section] by stating that it demonstrates the arrangement of the deities of the *sānnāyya* offering as declared in the Brāhmaṇa.

Regarding the phrase "for she is Śrī," Rudradatta himself states that there is no evidence to support the inclusion of a collective reference to the *Ṛg* and other Vedas; furthermore, by citing the worldly expression of being wealthy through each individual possession such as cattle or gold, he asserts that one should not place undue confidence in the meaning intended here by the author of the Bhāṣya. However, he maintains that even one who knows a single Veda is entitled to the goal, whereas one who knows three Vedas (*trivedī*)—that is, a Brāhmaṇa—is [qualified for] the sacrifice, and not otherwise. The son of a consecrated Kṣatriya (rājanya)—for him also, the state of having attained prosperity (*gataśrī*) arises from the acquisition of wealth. As for the statement "one's own [deity] indeed," this refers to Indra for one year, because it is supplementary to the injunction regarding the rule (*niyamavidhi*). Regarding *vrātapatīm*—it is Mahendra; the word "should be sacrificed to" (*ijyeta*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. Thus is the meaning of the scriptural passage "then he should sacrifice with the *adhika* [offering]": after sacrificing to Indra for a year, he should sacrifice to either Indra or Mahendra at a later time. There is no fixed rule between those two. For the other—that is, for one who has attained prosperity (*gataśrī*)—it is Mahendra alone.

Because of the rule that for them, Mahendra is the deity [of the offering]. When this rite—beginning with the *anvādhāna* (adding fuel to the fires) and ending with the *paristaraṇa* (strewing of grass around the altar)—has been performed, the sacrificer observes the fast (*upavasati*). Or rather, the meaning is: having performed this *paristaraṇa*. The fast (*upavāsa*) consists of staying near the fire for the sake of the sacrifice on the following day, characterized by specific observances (*niyama*).

These observances will be stated [later]: [he eats] forest-grown food... [omitted] ...he does not eat domestic [food]. [The rites are: the *anvādhāna*, the driving away of the calves (*vatsāpākaraṇa*), the *idhma* (fuel), the *barhis* (sacrificial grass), and the *vedi* (altar).

Having performed the preliminary enclosure on the previous day, one should, on the following morning, pour out the water for moistening and perform the final enclosure and the strewing of grass. On the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), these acts—the addition of fuel (*anvādhāna*), the strewing of grass, and the fasting (*upavāsa*)—are performed on the preceding day; however, on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), they are performed on that very day. [The arrangement of the sequence of time regarding the altar and other elements. (Commentary): The altar and the strewing of grass take place on the previous day during the new moon sacrifice.

Regarding the preparation of the altar (*vedi-saṃskāra*): having performed the preparations for the altar prior to the northern enclosure (*parigraha*), one pours out the water-residue (*āpyalepa*) and performs the northern enclosure. (Commentary: "The altar and the strewing [of grass] on the day before the new moon"—this is the syntactical connection of the sūtra stating "the altar and the strewing on the day before. "Having performed the preparations for the altar prior to the northern enclosure"—this indicates the limit for the construction of the altar, which was previously referred to by the term *vedi*. "Pouring out the water-residue"—this is a restatement of what is already established by logical necessity (*nyāya*).

1. Thus, having first explained the manner of fasting according to the Brāhmaṇa, he now introduces [the following] by showing the injunction from another Vedic branch (*śākhā*). 2. Here, by the term *vatsāpākaraṇa* ("driving away the calves"), there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the entire previously mentioned ritual procedure for milking. 3. Although *barhis* (sacrificial grass) comes first, the word *idhma* (fuel) is placed first because it begins with a vowel and ends in a nasal (*ajādya-antatva*). Immediately after the Veda, the rite of the altar (*vedikarma*) follows; having performed that and then paused, one should perform the remainder on the following day, after the pouring out of the water used for smearing (*āpyalepaninayana*).

Thereafter, at a later time, the spreading of the grass (*paristaraṇa*) takes place. On the day before the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), however, only the threefold *anvādhāna* is performed. All else—the fuel (*idhma*), the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), and so forth—is done on the following day. Having performed the tracing of the altar (*parigraha*), he [proceeds].

7. Here, one might raise the objection: "Why are these two options explained as optional? It is more appropriate that these two be mandatory due to the fixed nature of their respective subjects, since there is no indication of optionality. Anticipating this, [the author] replies: because the *vedi* was not mentioned previously; because it would contradict the indicative mark (*liṅga*) stating "before the fetching of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*); because it would contradict the postponement of the *vedi*—which is mentioned immediately after the mantra and brāhmaṇa—to the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*); and because it would contradict the advancement of the *idhma* and *barhis*—for which no specific time is heard—to the following day of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*).

Because the presentation of all four ritual procedures (*kalpa*) occurs through both the rules for performance in another ritual manual (*kalpāntarakṛti*) and through optional alternatives (*vikalpa*), the aforementioned explanation is more correct. [Having omitted *parigrahādi*—as noted by Rudradatta in the Āpastamba Śrautasūtra, First Book, Fourth Chapter, Section 14, Sūtra 17]—it says: "On the previous day, the *anvāhārya* and so forth; on the following day, the fuel (*idhma*) and sacrificial grass (*barhis*), and the altar (*vedi*). *Bhāṣya*: On the previous day, the *anvāhārya* (the guest-offering) and so forth are performed; on the following day, the fuel, the sacrificial grass, and the altar are prepared.

And the instruction [is as follows]: because of the general statement, "On the previous day he prepares the *ṛc* and the *barhis*," and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that "prior to the fetching of the *barhis*," these [acts] also are performed on the previous day. However, in the case where the preparation of the altar (*vedi-karaṇa*) is done on the previous day, the placing (*sādana*) and the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) [of the *sphya* and the *veda*] do not take place; for this would subvert the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) regarding the *sphya* and the *veda*. Or rather, on the same day, everything is performed in the case of a sacrifice completed in a single day (*sadyaskālā*). Thus ends the fourteenth section (*khaṇḍikā*) of the fourth chapter (*paṭala*).

[The Meaning of the Term *Sadyaskāla* and the Arrangement of Ritual Duties] (Bhāṣya): *Sadyaskāla*—that day on which the time for the *parvan* occurs while the sun has not yet turned back; this is "immediate" (*sadyas*). [The Sequence of Duties for the Following Day] (Vṛtti): The duties beginning with the *anvādhāna* and the construction of the altar (*vedi*)—on the following day, prior to the washing of the hands, having prepared these sacrificial grasses and the altar, one performs the washing of the hands and so forth, pours out the remnants of the water used for rinsing (*āpyalepa*), and constructs the altar. [The Reason for Supersession] The reason for supersession is that the instruction follows the sequence of the texts; for the placement of the vessels (*pātrāsādana*) and their sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) are recited later in the subsequent sections.

Regarding the *sadyaskālā* (immediate-performance) rites, such as the *aparyādhūrvā*: the ellipsis is that the acts beginning with the *anvādhāna* (the placing of fuel) are performed [as an object of option]. Therefore, the temporal option applies only to the *anvādhāna* and subsequent acts, not to the sacrifice itself. [The determination of the scope regarding the *sadyaskālatva*: If, through negligence, the *aupavasathya* day is passed, yet the time for the principal sacrifice is not exceeded, then the *anvādhāna* and subsequent acts are indeed performed on that very same day, as there is no contradiction.

However, because the curd is excluded on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), [the term] "on the full moon day" (*paurṇamāsī*) alone is connected here due to proximity, the singular number, and because it is explicitly stated by Bharadvāja and others. By way of restating the *sadyaskālā* (one-day performance), the injunction for the *sadyaskālā* from another branch is indicated.

When the time for the principal rite is the same—that is, on the day of sacrifice—the entire procedure beginning with the kindling of the fires (*agnyādhāna*) is performed; nothing at all is done on the preceding day. Some, however, call the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*) when the moon is waxing the *sadyaskālā*; in that regard, the authority must be sought. (Khaṇḍa 14, Sūtra).

[17] In the commentary adorned by the *Bhāṣya* of Dhūrtasvāmin together with the *Vṛtti* of Śrī Rāmāgnicit: (Bhāṣya) On the same day when the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) and the first lunar day (*pratipad*) coincide, these [sacrifices] are performed on that very day (*sadyas*). (Vṛtti) Due to the contradiction with the primary [rule], even in times of distress (*āpad*), there is no performance on the same day. According to the opinion of Bharadvāja, "the milking is in milk already drawn" (*dugdhe dohanamaśrāḥ*); thus, since the application of the mantra is possible even in ordinary curd, the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) sacrifice is also obtained as being performed on the same day (*sadyaskālā*).

1.2 [Objection regarding the stated meaning: But surely, since it is heard in scripture that "one should sacrifice near the junction (*saṃdhi*)," the sacrifice must be performed during the middle of the ritual action just as at the junction of the lunar phases (*parvan*). Moreover, because of the injunction to sacrifice on the full moon with the full moon and on the new moon with the new moon—which prescribes the sacrifice at the junction of the first day (*pratipad*) and the lunar phase—the performance [of the sacrifice] at that precise moment is impossible; therefore, the sacrifice is possible at another time connected to that [junction]. True; [the intended meaning of the cited statements: these statements refer to the lunar days (*tithi*) preceding and following those marked by the junction.

For sacrifices such as the *iṣṭi* and *paśu*, although the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) and so forth are the prescribed times, even when there is the possibility of performing them "on the following day" (*śvaḥ*), if the conjunction (*sandhi*) occurs during the commencement or the middle of the procedure, there is a contradiction in the performance; therefore, these do not refer to a day-and-night (*ahorātra*) that contains the conjunction. Likewise, since it is observed that after the turning point (*āvartana*) of the day, if the conjunction occurs, one performs the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) and then begins the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*), even in the absence of the conjunction during the middle of the procedure, they do not refer to a day-and-night containing the conjunction.

On the day of the fast (*aupavasathya*), when the junction of the lunar phases (*parvasaṃdhi*) occurs, even if the sacrifice is to be performed on the following day, the expression "the full moon for the full moon" would be inconsistent if the conjunction were not present. [The Determination of the Time for Sacrifice: Therefore, since the performance of the sacrifice on the fifteenth day is authorized only when the junction of the phases occurs before midday, and because the sacrifice is prescribed for the following day when the junction occurs by even a single digit (*kalā*) after midday, the time for the sacrifice consists of the fourth part of the *parvan* day and the first three quarters of the *pratipad* day.

[The distinction regarding the other half of the fortnight: In the case where [the moon] will not be visible on the following day after the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), even though the *aupavasathya* day has already passed, the primary time (*mukhyakāla*) continues to apply because the juncture (*saṃdhi*) exists on the following day. (1) They are performed—(ka); 2. only in the curd—(kha, ga). 102. In the fourth chapter of the first book of the *Āpastamba Śrautasūtra*: (Bhāṣya) They may be performed [on the following day], or the previous day from the kindling of the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*) onwards; and everything is performed.

The *śayvantā* and other [rites] are performed in separate sections (*khaṇḍasaṃsthā*). Regarding the instruction that it may be "immediately" (*sadyas*) or otherwise, there is an option (*vikalpa*) in all cases; the modified form (*vikṛti*) is of immediate duration (*sadyaskālā*). And in that [modified form], everything is performed up to the release of the potsherds (*kapālavimocana*). Thus ends the fourth chapter in Dhūrtasvāmin’s commentary on the Āpastamba Śrautasūtra. [Special rule for times of distress: According to the principle that "when there is a conflict between a subsidiary (*aṅga*) and a quality (*guṇa*), the former prevails because it exists for the sake of the latter," [the rites] should be performed on the following day.

If there is the apprehension of a royal decree, a regional upheaval, the destruction of the body, or similar calamities, or if the four-part time (caturthāṃśa) and so forth of the fifteenth day cannot be obtained, the sacrifice may be performed on the preceding day as well. Furthermore, if in times of distress (āpad), even though the sacrifice has begun, the proper time does not arrive, one should desist; once the distress has passed, the performance should be carried out according to the prescribed rule. [This is to be considered as an option. Everything is performed—since there is an option in all cases—even in the "immediate" (sadyaskālā) ritual, all the various sacrificial sessions (khaṇḍasaṃsthā) are optionally available.

[The cause for the adoption of a specific rule: Regarding the statement "the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) is one performed on the same day" (*sadyaskālā*)—since it would have been sufficient to say simply "in that [sacrifice] everything is performed," the fact that the term "on the same day" (*sadyaskālāyām*) is mentioned again implies that those modified sacrifices which are optionally performed on the same day—such as "if by means of an *iṣṭi* or if by means of an animal sacrifice"—are not included. [The contraction of all constituent elements: And in that case, the phrase "everything" (*sarvam*) excludes eating at the end of the night, eating both [morning and evening], eating in the forest, and so forth. The plurality of the agent refers to the plurality of the priests themselves, not the plurality of others. Because of the mention of the number "four priests" (*catvāra ṛtvijaḥ*), no other person—neither the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) nor the wife (*patnī*)—is to be brought in. Furthermore, it is not completed by only three, according to the principle that "the first [mentioned] must be restricted. [This is for the sake of illustration: Just as in the case of "the priests eat the remnants of the oblation" (*ṛtvijo haviḥśeṣān bhakṣayanti*), by the mere statement "there are priests," the priests who are already established by the sense of the matter are indeed restricted. The same applies here to the Brahman priest.

The selection (*varaṇa*) of a human [officiant] is done silently; however, that of a divine one occurs later, according to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra beginning with "O Lord of the Earth" (*bhūpate*), just like the *hotṛ*. The sacrificer causes [the fire] to proceed by means of the *adhvaryu*; here the suffix *ṇic* is used in the sense of the root itself (*svārthika*). This is because the root is listed in the *curādi* group under the rule "roots meaning 'to go' (*gaty-artha*)," etc. In that regard, even for one who has already kindled the fire, the commencement on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) takes place before sunrise. However, the *agnihotra* sacrifice is to be offered at its own proper time even in the midst of the ritual procedure (*tantra*).

Thus, elsewhere, by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) "having departed" (*viprakrānta*), [the text] states that the sacrificer and the others should not sit together for the sake of the *asamāsa* (non-compound) meaning, or for the purpose of imitating the Brāhmaṇa [text]. Regarding the verses enjoined [in the *Ṛgveda*], [the variants] *kha* and *ga* are not seen in the *Mūlarāja* manuscript. [The forms, measurements, and other views regarding the *sruva* and other implements] (Bhāṣya): The *sruva* should be the size of an *akṣa* (an eye); its belly should have the appearance of a hollowed palm (*saṃpuṭa*). Its length should be divided into five parts, and two parts are said to be the vessel (*pātra*). The cavity (*bila*) of the vessel... [the handle (*daṇḍa*) should be one-third of that]. The ninth part [of this work] is for the sake of detailed exposition. One should make the cavity (*bila*) one-eighth of the width; this is the characteristic of the vessel (*pātra*). According to another scripture, the height of the cavity is one-twentieth [of the width]. The cavity of the *sruva* ladle is the size of a thumb-joint. "There is no occurrence of those desiring subsidiary benefits (*guṇakāma*) in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*)."—For those desiring subsidiary benefits, there is not even an attainment through implication based on the existence of a substratum (*āśraya*) in the modified sacrifices; this is because the *godohana* vessel and others lack a substratum.

From the ultimate standpoint (*paramārthatas*), however, the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) alone are the substratum (*āśraya*), according to the statement of the Mīmāṃsakas. For instance, it is because the *godohana* vessel and so forth possess the capacity to produce the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the animal sacrifice only by means of the *praṇayana* (water-carrying) and other rites which are themselves connected to the primary sacrifices such as the *āgneya*. In the modified sacrifices (*vikṛtis*), since the *āgneya* and others are absent, there is no substratum for the *praṇayana* and other rites that are connected to them. But this is not a matter of direct injunction (*upadeśa*). This is because even a substance (*dravya*) can be enjoined as the object of the transcendental result, provided it is colored by the mere action of *praṇayana* and so forth.

Even in the case of the *godohana* vessel and others, [the text] says "he washes with the mind" (*manasā*), and thus one does not mention speech. Furthermore, because the *anupaṅga* (supplementation) is characterized by expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*) and other such features, if one were to admit a division of the mantra, it would follow that the *Sāvitra* [mantra] would also have to be supplemented. And it will be stated later: "Those things which can be accomplished [simultaneously] are performed once. With the formula, "Thou art the skin of Aditi," he spreads [the hide] to the north of the Gārhapatya fire, or in the place of the rubbish heap (*utkara*), with its neck facing west and its hair side up. Therefore, the sense is that one must not be deluded. Regarding the mantra *śundhadhvam* ("be purified"), because it designates the vessels, there is modification (*ūha*) according to the actual object in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*). Some claim that because it designates water, there is no modification; however, that is incorrect, because the action is explicitly stated in the scripture (*śruti*). This is because the transitive verb *śundhati*, which expresses a purifying substance, is heard everywhere [in the Vedic texts], and furthermore, because the active voice (*parasmaipada*) is generally observed.

Likewise, because the word *śundhati*—which denotes substances that are to be purified—is intransitive, there is a reversal [of the case ending], as in "May the mothers purify themselves from this" (*asmānmātaraḥ śundhantu*) and so forth, and "O world, be purified" (*śundhatā loka*). Therefore, the modification (*ūha*) must be according to the actual meaning. And for items located in the same place, the mantra is recited once, as before. The placing of the remains of the *prokṣaṇī* water is for the purpose of sprinkling the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the fuel (*idhma*), and the altar (*vedi*). [Response: Not so. The action would not come into being if she were not an auxiliary (*aṅga*), but it would indeed come into being if she is an auxiliary. Why? Furthermore, because she is mentioned in close association with well-known auxiliaries—such as rice, barley, animals, clarified butter, milk, sacrificial vessels, and the wife herself—it is established that she is an auxiliary.

Likewise, the injunctions regarding ritual acts (*karmacodanā*) also apply only to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) and not to his wife. And in that regard, because the word *madhu* is seen to denote clarified butter (*ghṛta*) in the mantra, "This indeed is divine honey, O tree, with divine honey," and because of the observation [in the ritual texts] that "he makes it honeyed" (*madhumat*), some say that the *praṇītā* waters are like clarified butter. And that [mantra], like the mantra for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth, must be modified according to the deity, as is prescribed for each specific deity; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the indicative mark (*liṅga*). Nor can it be argued that it is merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), because it denotes that which is inherent [in the ritual]. This is also evident from the Vedic revelation: "He says, 'To Agni thee' and 'To Agni-Soma you two,' by way of distinction. Nor should it be said that there is no modification because of the expression "according to the deity," since that applies to the nature of the *prokṣaṇa* mantra and so forth, and the same logic applies to these cases as well.

Because Bodhāyana has explained it as a modification and because he uses explicit words—namely, "Just as 'For Agni thee, for Agni-Soma thee, for so-and-so,' so [it is] according to the deity"—others, however, having concluded the *saṃyavana* mantra with "For the progenitor thee, I mix," offer an alternative for the remainder of the mantra during the touching of the divided portions, using the mantra from the Sūtra. This, however, is not the intention of the author of the Sūtra, because there is no separate application [of the two mantras].

And how can we conceive that this teacher, while assigning the entire collection of mantras (*mantra-samāmnāya*) [to their respective rites], has omitted even a single mantra? Therefore, it is well said that one must not alter the unity of the mantra. Thus, this [formula] consisting of the performance itself is: "For Janayatrī thee; for Sayuj Agni thee; for Agni-Soma thee; for Indra Vaimṛdha thee," and so forth.

Having made the entire [cake] into a single lump with the formula, "Thou art the head of Bhakha," he then divides it, makes two equal portions, and applies them to the touching of both the Āgneya and the other [portion]. However, when there is a common ritual procedure (*samānatantra*) for the group of sacrificial cakes including the Vaimṛdha, one performs the assignment of deities only for the last two [portions], according to the principle of "according to their respective shares" (*yathā-bhāgam*), and not for the Āgneya. Thus, there is no touching of the Āgneya alone, because of the absence of division [into separate portions].

With the mantra, "I push away this face of the attacking army," he pushes the embers away from the potsherds with the *veda* grass-bundle. Regarding the removal [of embers] from the potsherds (*kapāla*), because of the general statement "from the potsherds" and because of the specific statement regarding the placing [of the oblation] upon eight potsherds, one should remove the embers even from the northern potsherd and then place the *Āgneya* offering upon it. Those preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as spreading [the flour] and so forth, which occur after the placing on the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*), must also be performed for these *puroḍāśa* cakes in this same manner—namely, according to the order of their origin (*utpattikrama*) as stated regarding the placing on the fire. The plural number in "for these" (*eṣu*) is used with reference to the Aindrāgna offerings. This principle is the same for all sacrificial oblations (*havir*), because there is no distinction between them. Therefore, even when there is an intermixture of *caru*, milk, and other substances within a group of oblations (*havirgaṇa*), the preparatory rites for those oblations occur strictly according to the order of their origin.

The phrase "from this point onwards" (*ata ūrdhvam*) was stated because prior to this there was no differentiation, and thus no possibility of a sequential order (*ānupūrvya*). It was not stated, however, because it was logical (*nyāyyatva*) in that earlier context. When that [action] is performed many times, because of the diversity of individual instances, there arises the notion of belonging to the same class. (Śūtra): "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa [offerings] accompanied by abundant clarified butter (*ājya*)," so it is known. (End of the fifth section. (Śūtra): 171.3. Therefore, the worship of the wives of the gods (*devapatnī*) is performed while standing right there, as is the worship of the *gārhapatya* fire. (Ru) Many authors of ritual manuals (*kalpakāra*) have stated that when cow’s ghee is unavailable, the ghee of a goat or a buffalo may be used as a substitute, and in its absence, oil; for example: "In its absence, cow’s ghee; in its absence, buffalo ghee; in its absence, oil," and so forth. In that case, because oil functions as a substitute, its ritual properties (*dharma*) should be understood to be like those of ghee.

And this has been stated by Āśvalāyana: "Having placed it on the Dakṣiṇāgni with the formula 'For food thee,' having placed it on the southern half of the Gārhapatya fire with 'For strength thee,' having taken it down and supported it with the Veda-grass-bundle, he offers it to the wife. || 1 || 58 || 308 ||

[The removal of doubt arising from the multiplicity of mantras and its cause: (Bhāṣya) The entire mantra for pouring out (*nirvāpa*) applies only to the clarified butter (*ājya*), and not to honey or water, because of the statement: "having poured out the clarified butter" (*ājyaṃ nirupya*). || 308 || [Special rule regarding the plurality of wives: (Sūtra) Having closed her eyes, she looks at it while not breathing out, and gazes upon it with the mantra: "Thou art the milk of the earth" (*mahīnāṃ payo 'si*). || 2 || 59 || 309 || (Bhāṣya) This gazing is performed by each wife individually, because it is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of that [butter]; or rather, it is a consecration of the clarified butter itself, like the gazing at the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśīya*). || 309 ||

Having first performed the closing and the looking, one should subsequently look at the clarified butter (*ājya*) while exhaling, using the mantra ending with "thou art clarified butter" (*ājyamasīti*). [This addresses the doubt and its resolution. (Commentary): Because of the specific mention of "clarified butter alone," even though honey and water are modifications of clarified butter in the passage "curd, honey, clarified butter, water, and parched grains," the mantra does not apply to those two. [The examination and approaching by the wife, and the production of the clarified butter]—Because of the wife’s participation, as indicated by the mantra-marking (*mantra-liṅga*): "I examine it for good progeny"; and because of the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*): "He examines it for union and procreation," the examination is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the wife, just like the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*). Therefore, there is an examination by the wife. Consequently, in the event of a mishap, there is re-examination after the pouring out of the clarified butter again. Like the examination of the clarified butter—in this view, there is no repetition for that which has been submerged, just as in the case of the *sapatnīya* offering.

Closing the eyes and looking [at the clarified butter]; this is the same even when looking at the wife again. [Note: *patnī* is used in place of *patnyāḥ*]. Looking silently while closing the eyes, he subsequently looks [at the clarified butter] with the mantra. Regarding the case of there being more than one wife, the procedure has been stated by Baudhāyana. Because it occupies that position, [the singular form is used]. In that [context]—[variant readings: *ka*, *khaṃ*].

173 (vṛ): "Thou art semen" is the first; "Thou art light" is the second; "Thou art brilliance" is the third. || 1 || 65 || 315 || [The justification for the omission of the words "light" (*tejas*) and so forth as stated in the Sūtra: "In the absence of the wife, 'light' and the others are omitted"—the intention of this is as follows: because of the scriptural direction, "He makes it impure when he lets the wife look at it; he places it on the Gārhapatya fire for the sake of purity. In states such as when the wife is menstruating (*rajasvalā*), if the wife is absent, the placing on the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*) with the mantra "Thou art brilliance" (*tejo 'si*) and the taking down (*apādāna*) with "For brilliance thee" (*tejase tvā*) are omitted. This is stated in the Brāhmaṇa. But after the placing on the fire, it certainly takes place.

"The two firebrands are drawn forward for the sake of the after-offerings (*anūyāja*)," so says the Vājasaneyaka. According to the Vājasaneyin tradition, one may optionally lead the two firebrands forward.

[Establishing the cause and effect regarding the status of the enclosing-stick as a subordinate element] (Vṛtti): "Sūryas tvā... and "...liṅgāt dhīye ca"—this is the intended meaning: because it is stated that "he lays down the enclosing-sticks for the destruction of the Rākṣasas," laying them down has the purpose of slaying demons; therefore, one does not lay one down in the east, because of the mention of the Sun as the slayer of demons in the passage, "For the Sun indeed, rising, [drives away the demons] from the east. Since it is specified that "May Sūrya protect you from the east," Sūrya is designated as the protector; thus, [the mantra] is a subordinate element of the laying down of the enclosing-sticks.

Regarding the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) of the *āhavanīya* fire: consequently, in the absence of the act of encircling with the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), there is a cessation [of this consecration] at the *avabhṛtha* bath and other such rites. However, in the case of the *upasat*, according to the view that "the enclosing-sticks are those very sticks used for the encircling," there is a cessation because of the absence of the act of encircling, even though the enclosing-sticks themselves are present; yet, according to the view that there is an act of encircling, it does indeed take place. "The enclosing-stick is a subsidiary (*aṅga*)" means that it is a subsidiary to the act of encircling. "He prepares the fire" means by means of the fuel-stick (*idhma*).

1. The consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) is for the purpose of wrapping [the fire] forward (*purobhāga-paridhāna*), because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, as well as from the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) beginning with "not so in front," and from the statement of Baudhāyana. Therefore, in the absence of enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) in the *upasad*, the *avabhṛtha*, and other such rites, the consecration does not take place. 2. At the two *āghāra*s. (Note: *vā* is read as *ca* in manuscript *ka*).

"In the middle of the fire" (4)—at that point, having touched [the fire] once in one place (7), he places two fuel-sticks with their tips pointing upward around the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). Because it is impossible for it to have any other purpose, the *svāhākāra* occurs only at that specific time in the middle [of the formula]. Therefore, regarding the *yajus*: here, among the expiations (*prāyaścitta*), the deities (*devatā*) for the first four mantras are Brahmā, Yajña, the Maruts, and the divine Ṛbhus; for the next three, Sūrya; for the next two, Varuṇa; for the next two, Agni and Varuṇa; for the following one, Agni; then Prajāpati; then the deities mentioned in the mantras in the dative case; then Agni; then the gods; then Agni Jātavedas.

For the two [oblations], [the deities are] Abhi and Sviṣṭakṛt; for the latter, Indra Vṛtrahan, then Harivant. For the triad beginning with "anājñātam," Agni; for the next, Agni and Śraddhā; then Agni Jātavedas. For the next, Varuṇa, Indra, Savitṛ, Viṣṇu, the Viśvedevas, and the Maruts; for the next, Rudra—or according to the measure of the syllables (mātravarṇika). Then Agni; then Varuṇa. For the Vyāhṛtis, [the deities are] Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, and Prajāpati. In all cases, the deities are expressed in the dative case.

Some say that the *samiṣṭayajus* offering and the *devāgātuvid* formula are drawn forward [to the beginning], as is the *brahmán*. Regarding the "middle" (*madhyama*)—in the manuscript *kha*, it is intended that the second position here is considered "middle" in relation to the technical term *svāhākāra* at the end of the mantra.

For this very reason, we understand from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that the *svāhā*-utterance occurring at the end of the mantra serves the purpose of offering, and not one situated in the middle. Although we shall demonstrate in the section on the *parivapya* that the *svāhā* occurring at the beginning also serves the purpose of offering in certain cases, what is the meaning of "the *svāhā* in the middle"? It means [the *svāhā*] in the mantra "Svāhā to Speech" (*vāci svāhā*). Therefore, even when there is an increase in the *samiṣṭayajus* offerings for the animal and soma sacrifices, one should still cast [the grass-bundle] onto that same sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

Regarding the *śaṃyuvanta* rites: there are three specific ritual acts here, namely the *iḍā*, the *sūktavāka*, and the *śaṃyuvāka*, which are connected with the recitations (*nigada*) of the Hotṛ priest. Among these, the *iḍā* is fixed for both fires—the Āhavanīya and the Gārhapatya—according to the difference in the substance: the *iḍā* of the oblation (*havis*) is at the Āhavanīya, while the *iḍā* of the clarified butter (*ājya*) is at the Gārhapatya.

Likewise, the Sūktavāka and Śamyuvāka are also accepted by other authors of Sūtras as being applicable in both places, through either restrictive rule or option. Now, however, he says that they should take place in the Gārhapatya fire immediately after the *ājyeḍā*, and not in the Āhavanīya. The *darvihoma* and *āgrayaṇa* are performed [1.297], [the justification for the occurrence of other remnants in the absence of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, according to different views]. (*Bū*) Because the *darśapūrṇamāsa* is their archetype—this applies also to its modifications such as the *āgrayaṇa*. This is the intended meaning: one who has been consecrated by the *anvārambhaṇīyā* is qualified for the modifications of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*. For instance: the *anvārambhaṇīyā* would not occur in a modification (*vikṛti*), because it falls within the interval of the archetype (*prakṛti*). (Jaimini Sūtra 12.2.20).

In this view (*sū*), the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) subsist upon the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) acquired through the *anvārambhaṇīyā* rite connected with the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). Therefore, when those two [the New and Full Moon sacrifices] have ceased, since the purificatory rite performed for their sake has also perished, the modified sacrifices that depend upon it are likewise not to be performed. Or rather, they may be performed, because the time [for them] has not yet fully elapsed [Jaimini Sūtra 12.2.20].

In this view, since the *anvārambhaṇīyā* is consecrated only for the primary rite (*pradhāna*) together with its subsidiaries (*sāṅga*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the eligibility (*adhikāra*) for the subsidiaries depends upon the eligibility prompted by the primary. Consequently, when the eligibility for the primary ceases, there is no eligibility for the subsidiaries either; thus, like those subsidiaries, there is no eligibility for the modified rites (*vikṛti*). Therefore, when the archetype ceases, the modified rites are also not to be performed. This is just as it has been stated that in the performance of a modified rite, the modifications of the *sānnāyya* do not occur for one who does not maintain the *sānnāyya*.

This [Āgrayaṇa, including its causes for non-performance, etc. is twofold—it is performed as follows: even upon the conclusion of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the Āgrayaṇa is performed in the form of cooking a *sthālīpāka* on the *gārhapatya* fire, according to the rule: "Having cooked a *sthālīpāka* of new grain on the *gārhapatya* fire" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.30.16). Now, the distinction regarding the application for one who desires supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) through these two rites is demonstrated. One who should desire, "May I sacrifice," should perform both the Full Moon (*paurṇamāsī*) and the New Moon (*amāvāsyā*) sacrifices twice each at their respective times. What is meant? One should repeat the Full Moon sacrifice within a single year—performing one on the fifteenth day (*pañcadaśī*) and the other on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*). Likewise, one should perform the New Moon sacrifice at its own time. In this context, the word "first" (*prathama*) should be understood as being supplied immediately after the word "thus" (*iti*).

Having been addressed thus, she said: "Having spoken of repetition (*abhyāsa*) in this manner, she says to the Brāhmaṇa: 'One should sacrifice with only one [verse]. The meaning is that one should sacrifice with only one [verse] that has not been repeated, and not with two [verses] each. Thus, repetition is stated to be optional (*vaikalpika*), because its purpose is non-mandatory (*aniyatārthatvāt*). Furthermore, even there, since the performance is non-mandatory, there is no absolute necessity regarding the mere ritual action; [therefore] the oblations are [performed] as such."

[Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra, Third Praśna, Fourth Paṭala: Time and Measurement in the Optional Performance (Kāmyaprayoga)] (Commentary): The sacrifice on the first and second days is for one desiring prosperity (*ṛddhi*), according to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) "whomsoever he may sacrifice. Even a single day is permitted for one desiring prosperity. According to the *Upadeśa* school, it is the full moon day and the first day of the lunar fortnight (*paurṇamāsī-pratipad*), because of the contradiction regarding the *Sākamedha* offerings.

299. (ghṛ) Thereafter, there is also the performance of the *somayajña*s, which are modifications (*vikāra*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). [Establishing the specific details for the optional ritual application] regarding the first new moon day: "On account of the indicative mark" (*liṅga*)—on whichever day the sacrifice is completed, on that very day the appearance of the moon is perceived behind [the sun], as expressed by the phrase "the moon rises behind. Therefore, for the first [application], the worship begins on the fifteenth day and the sacrifice is performed on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*). For the second, however, the worship begins on the first day and the sacrifice is performed on the second day. [Establishing the specific details according to the *upadeśa* school: This is the instruction regarding the full moon.

—Based on the statement "there are two full-moon days," the instruction is that the sacrifice begins on the fourteenth day and is performed on the fifteenth, or it begins on the fifteenth day and is performed on the first day of the new moon. —2.3.5 Regarding the Sākamedha sacrifices, because of the contradiction—it is understood that in the Sākamedha sacrifices, only the fifteenth and the first days possess the status of the full-moon day.

Regarding the statement "with the Sākamedhas," it refers here to the full-moon sacrifices; having begun on the fourteenth day and completed the Sākamedhas by the fifteenth, on the first day (pratipad) there are two full-moon sacrifices because of the injunction for the full-moon sacrifice. Thus, on the fifteenth and the first day, there is the performance of the sacrifice. It is also stated that one may perform only one: "one should sacrifice to only one. One [result] is obtained for one desiring prosperity. The Sākamedha concludes in two days. By the statement [of the text], [it is established]. On the first day, the full-moon [sacrifice].

300. (Sūtra) Even for one who desires only a single object, the desire for prosperity (*ṛddhi*) is also obtained; thus there is a renewed commencement. This concludes the fourth chapter in the third book of the *Āpastamba Śrautasūtra* with the commentary (*bhāṣya*) of Dhūrtasvāmin. [Section 15, Sūtra 2] Having completed the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*), he subsequently offers a cake on eleven potsherds (*ekādaśakapāla-puroḍāśa*) to Indra Vaimṛdha. 1.1.607.

Some authorities recite this as a *samānatantra* (common ritual procedure). [The possibility of desiring prosperity even for one who desires only a single object: It was stated that for one who desires only a single object, heaven alone should be desired first at the outset. However, although prosperity (*ṛddhi*) is established by the view of separate offerings (*āhārapṛthaktva*) for one who desires prosperity alone, because of the further injunction "one should sacrifice with only one [offering]," the desire for prosperity indeed arises for one who desires only a single object, and it is not restricted to heaven alone. 135 || 558 ||

Thus ends the fourth chapter of the third book in the *Āpastamba-Śrauta-Sūtra* with the commentary (*bhāṣya*) of Śrī Dhūrtasvāmin. Now, by means of the subsequent chapter, [the author] teaches the obligatory and optional offerings to be prepared for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), as well as their modifications through secondary qualities (*guṇavikāra*). Because of the scriptural statement, "He prepares the *Vaimṛdha* after the Full Moon sacrifice," the *Vaimṛdha* is a subsidiary (*anunirvāpya*) belonging to the collective whole; therefore, it does not occur in the modifications (*vikāra*) of the Full Moon sacrifice.

The *tantra* (ritual procedure) for this [offering] is that of the *āmāvāsya* (new-moon sacrifice), because it is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *aindrāgna* (offering to Indra and Agni)—[as stated in] the *ru* 2; [the text reads] "merely desiring prosperity" (*ṛddhikāmamātra*)—[variant readings: *āhāra* in *kha-ga*; *vṛddhirhānirbha* in *kha-ga*; *vṛddhikāmanā* in *ka*]. Here, after the completion of the full-moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsyā iṣṭeḥ*), one offers a cake on eleven potsherds (*ekādaśakapāla-puroḍāśa*) to Indra Vaimṛdha; or else, from the time of the fire-installation (*ādhāna*) until the conclusion of this sacrifice, the procedure is that of the new-moon sacrifice because it is a modification of the *aindrāgna*—such is the commentary (*vṛtti*) seen [in the manuscript *mu-raI*].

Āpastamba Śrautasūtra, Third Praśna, Fifth Paṭala (Bhāṣya): [The distinction regarding whether the Vaimṛdheṣṭi has the same or different *tantras*, and the view of the direct instruction (*upadeśa*). In the case of the Vaimṛdheṣṭi performed with a common *tantra* (*samānatantre*), for one who has performed the Soma sacrifice (*somayājin*), there is no modification of the ritual elements belonging to different seeds (*nānābījadharma*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*), because that would contradict the rules of adaptation (*ūha*). Furthermore, it is a modification of the Aindrāgna offering. Therefore, the *tantra* belongs to the Āmāvāsya sacrifice. According to the direct instruction (*upadeśa*), however, it should be performed according to its respective portions (*yathābhāgam*).

Even in the *samānatantra* (the common ritual manual), there is modification (*ūha*) because it relies upon the modified form (*vikṛti*). [The justification for the presence or absence of modification (*ūha*) in the two *vaimṛdha* offerings] (Commentary): Regarding the phrase "because of the contradiction with the oblation" in the *Samānatantra*: since the *abhīṣomīya* sacrifice of one who has performed the Soma sacrifice also exists, there is a plurality of sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*). Consequently, the plural form in the mantra "Separate yourselves according to your respective portions" would necessitate a modification (*ūha*). However, such a modification is improper in the archetype (*prakṛti*). Therefore, when the *vaimṛdha* is part of the same ritual framework (*samānatantra*), it possesses the characteristic of having multiple seeds (*nānābījadharma*).

Regarding the *aindrāgna-tantra*: in the view that it is distinct from that [tantra], the instruction is "according to their respective portions" because of the act of mixing (*āśrayaṇa*). Since the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) shares the same *tantra* as the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*), and because the modified sacrifice is adventitious while the model sacrifice must be accomplished both with and without its specific qualities, it is logical that the performance should follow the *tantra* of the model; thus, modification (*ūha*) is appropriate. This position was stated by the Commentator (*Bhāṣyakāra*) according to the Mīmāṃsaka view, under the alternative that the *anvāhārya* is not included in the *aprayaṇa*.

[Consideration of the specific times for the duties to be performed under the view of separate performance] (Commentary): In that regard, when there is a separate performance of the evening milkings, we must consider this: does the postponement of the evening milkings result in a postponement of the common *tantra* (ritual framework), or is it to be performed at its own proper time? Regarding this, some maintain that it should be performed at its own time, because the *Āgneya* sacrifice is the primary one.

[The objection that the Āgneya sacrifice lacks primacy has been stated. That is untenable; because the evening milking (sāyadoha) is performed first, the primacy of the Āgneya is set aside. [By establishing the primacy of the milking, postponement alone is logical. The two milkings themselves are what possess primacy.

Furthermore, regarding those rites characterized by the evening milking (*sāyadoha*), which were previously the subject of investigation: when it is asked whether, due to the displacement of the evening milking, there is a displacement of the common ritual framework (*tantra*) such as the washing of the hands and so forth, or whether they should be performed at their own time—[the explanation of one school's position]—some say they should be performed at their own time, because the *Āgneya* sacrifice is primary and because the morning milkings (*prātardoha*) belonging to the *Āgneya* are more numerous.

Because the Sāka-prasthāyīya sacrifice consists of the Darśa, and because the Āgneya offering is primary within the Darśa, and because it occurs at dawn when performed together with that [Darśa], and because of its greater frequency, the *tantra* (ritual framework) belongs to its own time on the subsequent day. [The reason for the cessation of primacy: That is untenable; [the cessation] occurs precisely at night due to the performance [of the sacrifice then], and because of the primacy of those two [offerings], there is a cessation of the primacy of the Āgneya.

[The justification for the primacy of the evening milking: The evening milking is the proper course—(1) because Prajāpati created the sacrifice and its two vessels (*ukhā*) were shattered; (2) there would be a displacement of the ritual sequence; (3) there is a displacement of the *tantra* (the main body of the ritual); (4) there is a cessation of this particular rite; and (5) because the two milkings are performed together. (ŚB 5.3.1.1–5)

[The specific characteristic of the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*) and its displacement from the common ritual procedure (*tantra*): But for the animal sacrifice, which is enjoined by one separate scriptural statement, the animal-cake is enjoined by another separate statement: "Having immolated the animal, [he offers] the cake. Therefore, because the common procedure (*tantra*) begins simultaneously with the two milkings, when there is a displacement of those two milkings, there is a displacement of that [cake-offering]. And this constitutes a different ritual procedure (*tantrabheda*).

[In the absence of a statement regarding postponement, there is no connection with the subsidiaries performed on a later day. Nor can there be a connection between the principal act already commenced—which is observed to have occurred at an earlier time—and the subsequent substrates and other elements being employed. [The resulting specific mode of performance in our own position: Therefore, there is a postponement (*apakarṣa*) of all the common subsidiaries belonging to the principal acts. Thus, in the subsequent [section], [it is argued that] the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*) is appropriately incidental (*prāsaṅgika*). (Vṛtti: But as for the animal sacrifice, it is questioned—[is it] by way of being a subsidiary?

"Having immolated the animal, [one prepares] the *puroḍāśa* (cake)"—from this it follows that the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the animal sacrifice is incidental (*prāsaṅgika*) to the *paśupuroḍāśa*. [When the objection has been resolved, the established position is: Therefore, in this case, there is a difference in ritual procedure (*tantrabheda*); there is no other cause for a difference in procedure such as a difference in place, time, or qualification (*adhikāra*). As for the statement "by means of both the evening and morning milkings," that too is a prescription for the postponement of two [acts] within the very same ritual procedures (*samānatantreṣu*).

[The demonstration of the lack of connection: Nor is there a connection for that which has already been employed; for when there is a postponement of the auxiliaries (*aṅga*) prior to the primary (*pradhāna*), such postponement is indeed logical. However, in the absence of a statement of postponement, those performed subsequently would provide no assistance [to the primary].

Because of the fall [of the rule] into the middle [of the procedure], therefore the principal acts—such as the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and others—must be performed on the following day as well. This is because another *sūtra* statement is accepted, namely: "In the removal of the calves, the pot is at the end" (*vatsāpākaraṇe kumbhīparārdhya*). Furthermore, by another scriptural passage... In the *Āpastamba Śrautasūtra*, third book, fifth chapter: (Commentary) For the Rāmeyī [offering], having performed the specific rites such as the carrying forward of the fires (*praṇītāpraṇayana*) for both the morning milking and the [other] milkings, the *Pārvaṇahoma* and subsequent rites are performed. 2. [Specific rule regarding the milk-offerings: The milk-offerings (*doha*), however, are indeed entirely offered (*sarvahuta*). There are no remaining portions (*śeṣakārya*) from them. 3. Regarding the placing [of the vessels]—[the procedure applies to the specific vessels and the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), etc., while there is no modification (*anūha*) of the specific mantras]—there are two jars (*kumbhī*) and two covers (*apidhāna*).

The other [rites] follow the *tantra* [procedure]. And because the mantra expresses a single [action], [the rites] beginning with the *śākhāpavitra* and the *atyāghāna*, and ending with the pouring out (*ninayana*), are performed in a single pot (*kumbhī*). This is also due to the absence of modification (*ūha*). Having performed [the rites] from the *śākhāpavitra* and *atyāghāna* up to the washing and pouring out for one [cow], the same is done for the second pot; this is because the act of milking is a single unit and the *pavitra* is impossible [to use twice]. (Vṛtti) From those [cows], there is the removal of many; thus there is an increase in the number of pots. This is the application according to the method of performing the evening milking at the time of sunset.

[The subject matter of the *tantra* as stated in the *Bhāṣya*: At the setting down (*āsādana*), there are two pots together with the *śākhāpavitra*. There are two covers together with the milking vessel (*dohana*). The other *tantra* elements are the vessels, beginning with the *śākhāpavitra*. Even when the pots are separate, these remain undivided. The sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), the heating (*niṣṭapana*), the taking up of the *upaveṣa*, and the extinguishing of the embers (*aṅgāranirūṇa*) constitute the *tantra*. The placing of the pots on the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*) and the scattering of ashes around them (*paryūhaṇa*) are performed alternately; they are done simultaneously with the right hand only if one is unable [to do so otherwise].

Because the washing of the hands occurs after the evening strewing (*sāyaparistaraṇa*), and because one who is incapable is unfit for the ritual action on the right side; and because of the absence of modification (*ūha*) of the mantra—since there is no modification in the archetype (*prakṛti*) for mantras such as "Thou art the heat of Mātariśvan" (*mātariśvano gharmo'si*); and because of the impossibility of the branch-strainer (*śākhāpavitra*)—since it is impossible for a single branch-strainer to be placed simultaneously in both places, nor can there be a performance of the common procedure (*tantra*) for subsequent rites by means of succession.
