(Bhāṣya): Because of the washing and pouring out, and because of the state of being mixed.

By way of the sequence beginning with the removal [of the curdling agent]. All substances intended for curdling are poured into one [vessel], and then into another, because the act of curdling is a single unitary action. (322) [Repetition of the mantra denoting the substance in the singular: Because of the singular ending in the word "amṛnmayam" (not made of clay), there is a repetition of the mantra; and because the two substances are present together, the specific distinction [between them] is not known through the use of the pronoun "idam" (this). [No repetition of the mantra for the wife: At the time of the *praiṣa* (direction), the wives are not present.

(Vṛtti) And because of the impossibility of washing and non-contact—due to the impossibility of performing the acts of washing and pouring out—the entire process should be performed within a single pot. [The justification for the unity of the action in the case of curdling: Because the actions beginning with the removal from the fire constitute a single unit; thus, even though there is a difference in the substances being curdled, there is a unity of the action delimited by the result of producing curds, just as in the case of the cooking of rice and so forth. Therefore, having divided the remnants and the bark-leaves, they should be placed in both locations.

[The occurrence of repetition as a cause for recurrence: It is not a case of non-repetition (*amṛnmaya-vṛtti*), because the subject under discussion is the designation of a substance. This is because the term "devapātram" (the vessel of the gods) designates a single substance. Regarding the phrase "due to the cognition of what is proximate": since a word denoting a single substance cannot produce a specific cognition that one or the other of two proximate substances has been designated, there must be a repetition for the purpose of designating the second.

[Non-returning rebirth: The meaning of this is that the wives are not present at the time of the *praiṣa* (ritual summons). Even for one who has no wife, there is no modification in the application of the phrase "sanayā patnīm" (with the wife), nor in the phrase "amṛnmayam" (not made of clay); for the word "tulya" (equal) applies equally to both. [The reading] "amṛnma" [is found in] Kha, Gha; "tattulyaśam" [is found in] Ka; "tattulyālana-ninayana" [is found in] Ka, Gha; "ninayanasya" [is found in] Gha; and "viśeṣavijñāna" [is found in] Kha, Gha. This is for the purpose of refuting [any] doubt regarding the specific understanding [of these rules]. [End of section] Kha, Gha. Kaṃ.

[Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra, Third Praśna, Fifth Paṭala, Sūtra 14. And there is no separate consecration for them, as in the case of the designation by genus. [The mantra for the branch-strainer is common: The mantra "These two leaves... is used in common because of their unity. [Specificity in the driving away of calves, etc.: The driving away of the calves is performed individually for each calf that has been marked. [Commonality in the consecration of the cows: Likewise, for the cows intended for the evening milking, the consecration is performed in common.

(Vṛtti) A specific qualification is stated in order to remove this doubt: "the wife prepares" (*patnī sanoti*). At the time of the *praiṣa* (direction), the wives are not present, because their presence begins from the time of the girding (*sanahana*) onwards. Therefore, since there is no capacity for knowing a specific [individual] through the singular number in the mantra, it is a designation of something not currently present (*asamavetābhidhāna*). Nor is there a consecration (*saṃskāra*) for them as there is in the case of a generic designation; nor is the *praiṣa* for the purpose of consecrating them. Rather, this [consecration] is for the sake of the [main] sacrifice, because that is the nature of a *praiṣa*.

For this very reason, at the time of the *praiṣa* (the call for action), because the wives are not present, there can be no consecration (*saṃskāra*) for them, even by means of denoting their genus (*jāti*), nor even on the mere basis of the possibility of connection with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), as is the case with the mantra regarding the noose (*pāśamantra*). "As in the case of denoting the genus" means: just as a consecration occurs through the denotation of the genus even when the specific purpose of the statement is absent, so it is not possible here. [The driving away of the cows marked with signs] — "Separate driving away" refers to those cows that have been marked for the purpose of milking.

Likewise—having assigned distinct characteristics to the cows as well—one separates six calves at most from those intended for evening milking at the time of morning calf-separation. In both cases, this means that at the time of calf-separation, the calves are separated from their mothers after having been individually marked according to each milk-pot (*kumbhī*). [The accomplishment of the cow-consecration (*go-saṃskāra*): However, the consecration is performed by a single ritual procedure (*tantra*), namely, the consecration of the cows' departure and so forth.

[Special Rule for Milking] (Commentary): Three separate [milks] each are for the purpose of curdling; two are to be given beforehand. [The Method of Curdling]: A means must be employed so that it becomes curd at that very moment. Immediately after the end of the strewing of grass, or after the eating of forest-food, the washing of hands and other rites follow.

(Śulba-sūtra) 324. At the time of arranging the vessels, he sets out four vessels made of *udumbara* wood. 15 || 36 || 632 || The ritual procedure for these is like that of the *juhū*. 16 || 37 || 633 || [The vessels to be set out, their location, and the manner of setting them out: To the west are the wooden sword (*sphya*) and the *agnihotra-havaṇī*; to the east are the *patnī*, the *prāśitra*, the *anvāhāryasthālī*, the *iḍāpātra*, the stone, the *upaveṣa*, and the *madantī*—excluding these last ones.

[Explanation of the specific types of *doha*] (i) "Separately" (*pṛthak-pṛthak*) refers to the three [types of milking] as a demonstration; that is, [milking] one, two, or three [cows] individually. Likewise, "on two days" (*dvyahe*) is a demonstration for cases such as "on one day" (*ekāhe*), "on two days" (*dvyahe*), and so forth. When the curdling (*ātañcana*) has been performed, [the distinction regarding the curdling in the present context] is to be understood as immediate—such as the depositing of silver and so on.

—[The alternative regarding eating forest-food] At the end of the *paristaraṇa* (strewing of grass)—that is, after the washing and so forth, and according to the view that the milking (*doha*) follows the *paristaraṇa*—if one ceases immediately after the milking, then there is the eating of forest-food. [The reason for the avoidance, etc. 5. "The *sphya*, the fire, and [the vessels] excluding the *madantī* [water], because there is no consumption [of them]. 1. "Both [vessels] are placed in front for the purpose of curdling (*ātañcana*). (Ga. 2. "Having combined the four vessels used for the oblation (*homa*) with the *juhū* ladle, he employs them according to the previously stated rule. (Ru. 3. "Its ritual procedure is like that of the *juhū*. (Ka.)

4. Their cleaning and other preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) should be performed as in the case of the *juhū* ladle. In that context, the mantra "Speech [is] breath" (*vācaḥ prāṇam*) is modified to "the victor, the subduer of rivals" (*vājitvā sapatnasāham*), because it is a modification based on a specific quality (*guṇavikṛti*). 5. [Regarding the *sphya* and the *agnihotra-havaṇī*: according to Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra, Book 3, Chapter 5, Section 16, the two *audumbara* spoons are used together with the *juhū*. There are no *praṇītā* waters, because they are for the purpose of cooking the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). Some say they should be present, because their purpose is transcendental (*adṛṣṭārtha*). [Silence (*vāgyama*):]

And there is a difference in the ritual procedure (*pakṣabheda*): having said, "O sacrificer, restrain your speech," he remains silent regarding the vessels and so forth; as in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), they do not perform the "joining of the sacrifice" (*yajñayoga*). This is the instruction for the sake of the plant-offering (*auṣadha*). [Regarding other duties and specific details: the act of circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*); the command (*praisha*) "Place the sprinkling waters" (*prokṣaṇīr āsādaya*) and so on, which is unmodified; the taking up of the two vessels together during the path of the *sruk*; and having wiped the *juhū* ladle, then [using] the *juhū* mantra without modification regarding the two vessels.

[The non-intentionality of gender and number; their causes. Gender is not intended to be expressed because of the denotation of a universal. What is the universal? Some say it is the *audumbarī* posts—because, as in the case of the *praṇītā* waters, they serve the purpose of destroying demons through the statement, "Water indeed is the slayer of demons; for the sake of driving away the demons," and thus have an invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose.

[Establishing that it is for the purpose of the sacrificial oblation (auṣadha): "The sacrificer is for the purpose of the sacrificial oblation"—this is because, having introduced the sprinkling of the oblation being prepared with the words, "O Agni and Hotṛ, come hither," and having uttered that, he restrains his speech, thinking, "Now he yokes the sacrifice"; since this occurs within the section concerning the sacrificial oblation (auṣadhakāṇḍa), it is indeed for the purpose of the sacrificial oblation.

[The results of not intending to express gender and number: Regarding gender (*liṅga*): because of the mention of "possessing vigor" (*vājinīṃ tvā sapatnasāhīm*), since the intent is to denote the common property of possessing vigor (*vājitva-sāmānya-abhidhāna-paratvāt*), when the word *pātrāṇi* is in the neuter gender, there is no modification even for the vessel (*pātra*) due to the non-intention to express the feminine gender. Likewise—what is the common property? It is the state of possessing vigor; just as among the wives (*patnīṣu*) there is the state of being a wife (*patnītva*), by denoting merely the state of being a wife through the term *patnīm*, there is no intention to express plurality (*vacana*). (Variant reading: *avivakṣayā*) [Mu Rā].

[The word] *vājita* [denotes] the state of being a wife (*patnītva*), just as the word *patnī* denotes the state of being a wife among wives. If it is asked how the expression for "femininity" can apply to a generality, [the answer is: it is just like the expression for "masculinity. Generality is devoid of gender and number. In that regard, just as the word *puṃs* [is used], so too is the word *strī*. [This is seen in the mantra: "He drags with a frog; O female frog, come with them."

[The reason for the intention to express a general term: Furthermore, in a given context, a general expression is employed so that there may be no loss of the ritual refinement (*saṃskāra*) among those things that share a common purpose. [Non-intentionality regarding specific number: This same principle applies even when there is a contradiction with the grammatical number (*vacana*). For example, in the case of the *āgneya* [offering], where the mantra "this for the gods" (*idaṃ devānām*) is used even when the portion cut off (*avadāna*) is singular.

—(Vṛtti: If it is asked, "How is there femininity?"—that is, if it is asked how there can be femininity when the word expresses a universal (*sāmānya*), [the answer is: when the universal is the expressed meaning, why is there femininity in the word *vājinīm*? There would indeed be only neuter gender. He provides the rebuttal: "Just as in the case of a word expressing masculinity."

He explains the illustration: "By the frog *aliṅgarāgahī*"; for when there is the application of the masculine form *maṇḍūka*, one sees the feminine ending in *maṇḍūki tābhirāgahī*. Thus, because such words denote only a general meaning, gender, number, and so forth are not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣā*). [An analysis of the reasons for intentionality stated in the Bhāṣya: "And in a context, the same [form] is resorted to"—because those belonging to the same context and having the same function are to be treated equally, the expression of the general form is resorted to.

Regarding contradiction with number: for example, in the case of the *āgneya* [offering] alone, it is said, "This is for the gods" (*idaṃ devānām*), where the touching of the portioned-out [oblation] uses only the plural ending. And in the mantra for the cutting-off (*avadāna*), "I shall cut off portions for you" (*avadānāni te pratyavadāsyāmi*), because we observe the mention of the genus (*jāti*) of the cuttings, the plural ending is used even when there is only a pair of cuttings. [Notes: 1. Because it is an action of consecration (*saṃskāra-kāryatvāt*). 2. Only the ending... (as in *mūlarāja*). 16, Sūtra.

17] Āpastamba Śrautasūtra, Third Praśna, Fifth Paṭala [In some cases, there is the position of modification (ūha)]. (Commentary): Some say that modification (*ūha*) occurs in the case of changes in secondary qualities (*guṇa*). In that case, it becomes "having caused to fly down" (*avājitvā*). This is the division of the Veda and the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). [Regarding the release of the strainers (*pavitra*), the milking, and the placing of the vessels]:
(Sūtra 6): 3. [He performs] the release of the *pavitra* strainers; having consecrated the clarified butter (*ājya*), he performs the placing of the two milk-pails.

Having performed the ritual with the two *ājyabhāga* offerings and having offered the *āgneya* cake, he hands over the two ladles (*srucau*) while reciting the *āśīḥ* (benediction). When it is established by the designation (*samākhyā*) that all mantras belong to the Adhvaryu, the following is stated: those mantras in the Adhvaryu ritual that express self-blessings (*ātmāśīḥ*) and salutations (*abhivāda*), and which are employed as instruments (*karaṇatayā*), the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) mutters them, stands near with them (*upatiṣṭhate*), or seeks permission with them; it is not the Adhvaryu. This is because self-blessings are directed toward the fruit to be attained, and because the fruits of all ritual actions belong to the master (*svāmin*). Thus, the sense is that the designation is set aside by the force of the inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*). This was also stated by Jaimini (PMS 3.8.15).

The *karaṇa-mantras*, such as "May I be... (*māmāma*), although containing blessings directed toward oneself, belong exclusively to the Adhvaryu. Even in those cases, the blessing is for the sake of the sacrificer; the word "we" (*asmad*) is used figuratively. He will demonstrate the specific application of *japa* and other rites in passages such as "He mutters when the fires are being added. The recitation of the mantra beginning with *vediṃ samṛjyamānām* is an *anumantraṇa* (consecratory recitation). Even in the absence of an explicit blessing, they possess the character of being recited by the sacrificer (*yājamānatva*), just as there is the consecration (*abhimantrya*) of rain and so forth. Those which assist by coming together (*sannipatyopakāraka*) belong to the Adhvaryu alone, even if they contain internal blessings (*pratyagāśis*), such as the kindling of the fire with the *samidh* fuel-sticks during the *anvādhāna* rite. [The reason for not depending on other means of knowledge: Regarding "internal blessings"—this refers to their belonging to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), because the invocation of the fruit is for the sake of the sacrificer. [The meaning of the sūtra beginning with *pratyagāśiṣaḥ*: "Japa, upasthāna, and anumantraṇa"—the meaning of this is: one mutters (*japati*) mantras containing prayers for oneself (*pratyagāśiṣaḥ*), performs *upasthāna* (standing near), and performs *anumantraṇa* (reciting after). That is to say: one mutters mantras containing prayers for oneself; with such [mantras], one performs *upasthāna* and *anumantraṇa*. Those mantras, being prayers for oneself, belong to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*).

355. Because they are to be employed [as a reason for their belonging to the *ādhvaryava* class]. Those formulas of the *karaṇa-mantras* which are indeed connected with the performance of the ritual action belong to the *ādhvaryava* [class], as do the *pratyagāśis-mantras* (mantras containing blessings for oneself), such as "O Agni, may there be splendor for me" (*mama agne varcaḥ*) and so forth, [used] at the establishment of the fires (*agny-ādhāna*). [He] mutters [them]... as in the case of kindling the fire (*upasamindhana*). In the absence of a specific instruction, one stands near (*upatiṣṭhate*) or consecrates with a mantra (*anumantrayate*) [the objects] located at a distance. (Ga. 1; Ṭa; Mu. Rā. 4. [This refers to] the action performed while standing at a distance. (Kha. Ga.)

[The rule governing the application of *japa*, *upasthāna*, and *anumantraṇa*: (Bhāṣya) Where there is an indication by the locative case (*saptamī*), there it is a *japa* (muttering), as for example: "when the *hotṛ-pravara* and the *adhvaryu-pravara* are being performed. But where there is the accusative (*dvitīyā*), there it is either an *upasthāna* (approaching/standing near) or an *anumantraṇa* (consecrating with a mantra). The repetition [of the rule] is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*). (Sūtra) And on the festival day (*parvan*), he has his hair and beard shaved. 4.4.675.

[The restrictive nature of the injunction for shaving and its result as the literal meaning of the word] Since shaving is already established by the requirements of the situation, if it were to occur at another time, it would be restricted [to a specific occasion]. Therefore, [the example of restriction shown in the Bhāṣya]—(ḍa)—where, however, the particle *vā* is for the purpose of restriction—as in "He worships the Gārhapatya fire with the two Āgnipāvamānī verses"—there, the act of worship itself is what is intended; the repeated instruction "with the mantra" is for the purpose of restriction.

[The nature of the injunction as a restriction of time alone, and the presence of the word "yadi" (if): That which is already established by implication is being restricted. Since the statement "and on the full moon day one shaves the hair and beard" is intended to prescribe the time for shaving—which is already undertaken as a matter of fact because there is no other purpose for the statement—it is an injunction restricting the time alone for that shaving which is already prompted by desire. Furthermore, because of the subsequent statement "only a little," the restriction applies to this time only if the hair is very long and if the desire to shave exists.

Just as *homas*, *yāgas*, and other rites performed with specific instruments—such as cutting or splitting—are subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) of those actions associated with their respective occasions (*nimitta*), so too, shaving which is performed when there is a desire [for it] or when the hair is excessive is occasional (*kādācitka*). Because shaving is optional (*aicchikatvāt*), its performance on the *parvan* days is merely one possibility; therefore, it is restricted by the rule: "One must indeed shave on the *parvan* day. Consequently, there is no restriction for non-*parvan* days.

And that [shaving] is not an auxiliary (anaṅga) of the sacrifice, because it is prescribed for its own specific time, like the *pitṛyajña*; therefore, even if it is omitted, the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices must still be performed according to the alternatives such as "for thirty years" or "one may desist when aged. Alternatively, the shaving is an auxiliary (*karmāṅga*) to the ritual, based on indicative marks (*liṅga*) such as "she is as if dead. Even in that case, because of the mention of the *parvan* (the new or full moon), it is not desired in the archetypal (*prakṛti*) rites beginning with the *pathikṛt*, nor in the modified (*vikṛti*) rites which do not have the *parvan* as their time, just as in the case of occasional (*naimittika*) *iṣṭi* sacrifices.

The shaving of body hair (*lomavapana*) should be understood as optional (*aicchika*), because of the mention of shaving the hair of the head and beard (*keśaśmaśru*). [In the case] of Soma sacrifices and the like, it is not performed again and again when there are multiple *iṣṭi* offerings; by the word "and" (*ca*), its prohibition elsewhere is inferred. [Sūtra]: "One may also shave even a small amount of hair," so says the Vājasaneyaka. [Commentary]: "Even a small amount" (*apya-lpaśaḥ*).

Even though the body hairs are few and the beard is incapable [of performing the function], [it is still required]. (Commentary: This refers to its being a constituent part (*aṅga*). Since it is contingent upon desire, it must certainly be performed when there is a desire; and even in the absence of desire, it is fixed by the abundance of hair. "This skin—namely the hair of the head and the beard—is indeed dead and impure. Having cast off this very dead and impure skin, one becomes fit for sacrifice and approaches the rain-cloud. Because it is a constituent part by way of being a refinement of the person (*puruṣasaṃskāra*), [the shaving of hair is required].

"Because of the indicative mark (liṅga) stating 'this skin is as if dead,' it cannot tolerate even an abundance of hair, just as it does not tolerate an abundance of nails. [This explains the meaning of the word *ca* (and), the various views regarding its being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the ritual, and how the nails are indicated by the sūtra. By the word *ca*, it is inferred that one should perform the rite even at a time other than the prescribed juncture (*parvan*), provided there is a desire to do so, even if the ritual has not commenced. Some hold that because it is an auxiliary to the ritual by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is not an auxiliary to the ritual itself due to the mention of the *parvan*.

Others, however, say that this should be performed even at a time other than the prescribed parvan for the commencement of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, based on the indicative mark (liṅga) stating, "Having become fit for sacrifice, he approaches the cloud. In the opinion of Keśavasvāmin, however, the particle *ca* is intended to include the shaving of the body hair and nails. In my own view, the mention of "hair" (*keśa*) and "beard" (*śmaśru*) is an illustration that includes the nails as well, since they belong to the same part of the body. Furthermore, the mention of "hair" (*loman*) in the Sūtra is for the purpose of illustration; the meaning of the Sūtra is that even if there is only a small amount of hair, it is still an occasion for the rite.

The meaning of this is as follows: the body hairs (*lomāni*, *tanūruhāṇi*) should be shaved even if they are few, provided they have reached the state of hair on the head and beard (*keśa-śmaśru-kalpa*); otherwise, they may be left as they are. Alternatively, the word "hair" (*loman*) in the text is intended to refer specifically to the beard (*śmaśru*), since the beard is a particular kind of body hair. One should indeed shave even a small amount of beard. However, the hair on the head, even if it is sparse, should not be shorn (*nopyeran*). [Note: 2. As with the nails, there is an abundance of body hair on the palms and soles. — Gha. version.

[There is] an abundance of nails, teeth, skin-parts, and growing hair (Muṇḍaka Rāṇāyaniya 3; cf. Gopatha Brāhmaṇa). Also, even when engaged in ritual action—(variant: *karmapravṛtto'pi*—Ka). 4. "In the state of being a limb, having established the joints"—(variants: *ṅgatveparvaka*—Kha, Ga; *jñatve siddhe parva*—Ka). 5. "Formerly"—(variant: *pūrva*—Kha, Ga). 6. Accompanied by the commentary of Śrī Rāmāgnicit and adorned with the Bhāṣya of Dhūrtasvāmin: [Section 1, Sūtra 7] "You are lightning; strike away my evil; from the Untrue I go unto the True"—thus, one who is about to sacrifice touches water. 6. 6. 677. [The optionality of shaving.]

After the shaving, there is a bath. Regarding the presence of the term *yakṣyamāṇa* ("one who is about to sacrifice"): having said "I shall sacrifice" (*yakṣye*), the desire is for the shaving. After bathing, there is the touching of water (*apām upasparśanam*), because of the statement "one who is about to sacrifice. Therefore, even on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), [the rite is repeated] due to the difference in time. (Sūtra) All this touching of water occurs at the sacrifices. (Vṛtti) He has his hair shaved little by little; he should have his body hair shaved little by little. The word *api* is for the purpose of including the beard.

Thus is the application of the Sūtra. Even on this view, the shaving (*vapana*) occurs only at each full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), not at the new moon (*darśa*). This is because it is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the qualified performer (*adhikārī*), and because the qualification is unitary. [The purpose of the word *kāma*]: "I shall sacrifice" (*yakṣye*)—the inclusion of the word "desire" (*kāma*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*). [The intention behind indicating the time of touching water]: "Having bathed"—this is because the touching of water (*upasparśana*) is prescribed as occurring after the shaving. If the touching of water were to occur even before the resolve, then the shaving would necessarily take place even earlier.

Because of the statement "one who is about to sacrifice" (*yakṣyamāṇa*), which indicates that the intention (*saṅkalpa*) "I shall sacrifice" is understood as being immediate; [the reason for repetition is] therefore: due to difference—that is, due to the difference in performance—the contact with the purpose of the performance is repeated. "One who is about to sacrifice" means one who has formed the intention to sacrifice. And since intention is a unique function of the mind, it is mental. There is also another view that it is verbal, based on the indicative mark (liṅga) in the passage: "He who, having said 'I shall sacrifice,' does not sacrifice. According to Bodhāyana, one forms the intention three times mentally and utters it three times aloud.

One who desires to perform a sacrifice (*kratukāma*) must have a desire; however, the various types of such desire have been described by Bodhāyana: "Even while setting aside a [worldly] desire, one should seek to please the Supreme Deity; the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) is properly expressed as 'I shall see [the deity]' or 'I shall sacrifice,' and so forth. This applies to *iṣṭi*, animal sacrifices (*paśu*), and *soma* sacrifices when enjoined with the prefix *pra* and the root *yaj*. Consequently, it does not apply to *darvihoma* offerings. Having made the resolve for the sake of non-interruption, one should approach the water... [end of fragment].

[Sūtra 1, 7. Regarding the ritual acts to be grasped as being accompanied by this touching (*upasparśana*), there is the view of the *Upadeśa* and the measurement (*māna*). (Commentary: Thus it is also the case in the modifications of the *iṣṭi*. All sacrifices (*yajña*) are together with the *darvihoma*s. The *Upadeśa* applies only to those connected with the *yajña* and *kratu*, because of such a statement in the *Brāhmaṇa*. [Regarding the touching in the *agnihotra*: ] But it is not so in the *agnihotra*, because of the re-enjoining of it in that *homa*.

[The time for the preparatory sipping of water (upasparśana) when about to sacrifice: When one is about to sacrifice during the seasonal sacrifices (yajña-ṛtu), or when performing a *veṣṭi* sacrifice, or in the modifications (*vikāra*) of the *iṣṭi*, the sipping of water takes place prior to the carrying forward of the fire (*praṇayana*).

[The time for touching in the case of animals, etc. (Vṛtti): Thus it occurs in the *iṣṭi*: when there is touching after the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) in the case of animals and so forth, then, because the word "one who is about to sacrifice" (*yakṣyamāṇa*) refers to one desiring to undertake the first ritual act, and because the bringing forward of the fire (*praṇayana*) is the first ritual act, the touching takes place before the bringing forward of the *āhavanīya* fire for the animal sacrifice.

[The rule establishing the requirement for touching water as common to *darvihoma* offerings: Having prescribed that "one who is about to sacrifice touches water together with all sacrifices and *darvi*-offerings," it is stated again, "this applies to all sacrifices. Thus, there is an explicit teaching based on the scriptural statement: "Moreover, they say, 'in all sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*)'. [The justification for its absence in the *agnihotra*: However, this does not apply to the *agnihotra*, even though the requirement would otherwise obtain for *darvi*-offerings at their commencement.

In that case, because of the re-enactment of the injunction regarding the *homa*—namely, "Having touched water, being about to offer, having offered a fuel-stick (*samidh*) of *pālāśa* wood, and having touched water again," followed by the injunction for the extension and contraction [of the ritual space] with the words "within the altar" (*antarvedi*)—there is no [separate] commencement or conclusion [of the *homa*]. For this very reason, in the *agnihotra* as well, those two [the commencement and conclusion] belong to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*).

6. [The justification for touching water prior to the carrying forward of the fire] Regarding the sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*): "touching" (*sparśana*)—the meaning of this is that after the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), there is the touching of water. In one view, since the intention to perform the sacrifice with all its auxiliary parts (*sāṅga-pradhāna*) has ceased, and because the intention to perform the sacrifice regarding the primary rite alone (*kevala-pradhāna*) must be maintained, it would follow that the touching should occur before the portions are cut off (*avadāna*). However, [it is argued that] prior to the carrying forward of the fire (*praṇayana*)—in the case of the horse and other animals?—[this is not so]. After the time of the resolve—*kha*, *ga*; after the time of the resolve—*gha*.

5. At the time of the *śana* sacrifice, when one is about to commence the *Sāṅga-ṣaṣṭha-tīrtha*—[variants: *kha*, *ga*: *antarvedyutkarṣā*; *ka*: *sāśaṃ prati*]—(Bhāṣya) (Sūtra) (Sūtra): In the *someṣṭis*, [one recites]: "I seize Agni, the good chariot, who is the source of bliss, who mounts the rising sun; the Āditya, the highest light among lights—may the horse delight in the sacrifice for the sake of the deities. 1. *agniṃ gṛhṇāmi surathaṃ yo mayobhūrya udyantamārohati sūryamadde | ādityaṃ jyotiṣāṃ jyotiruttama-iśvo yajñāya ramatāṃ devatābhyaḥ |*

The Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, and the deities together with Indra—I first encompass them within my own abode through my wisdom. Those gods who have entered this fifteen-fold nourishment (*ūrj*), I first encompass them. May Agni, the bearer of oblations, bring them here; let this full-moon offering be for them, and let this new-moon offering be for them within me. Thus he mutters according to the respective signs while the Āhavanīya fire is being prepared. The cattle have come from between the two fires to the assembly of the gods.

Standing between the two fires, he mutters: "I first enclose them with wisdom in their own abode. "May offspring of every form delight here, dwelling together around Agni the householder. I first enclose them with wisdom in their own abode. May cattle of every form delight here, dwelling together around Agni the householder."

I accept them first, because of the injunction for the *anvādhāna* and *japa* following the ritual touching (*upasparśana*) with the thought "it must be done"; thus, in the *Soma* sacrifices, there is an extension (*prasaṅga*) of the purpose of the *Soma* following the ritual touching. The carrying forward of the fire (*praṇayana*) is likewise [extended]. On the full-moon day that coincides with the new-moon time, the first [offering] is omitted due to the restrictive force of the indicative marks (*liṅga*) such as "for one's own sacrifice" and so forth. However, when even a small portion of the fifteenth day remains, then there is no omission of the third [offering]. In the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), however, there is modification (*ūha*) everywhere according to the specific requirements.

Likewise, in sacrifices (*iṣṭi*) that have specific names, the ritual action is designated by those respective names. However, those sacrifices that are nameless are to be designated by a general name, such as "the oblation according to one's wish" (*yatheṣṭaṃ haviḥ*). (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra, Fourth Praśna, First Paṭala, Sūtra 10. "In its own place, with the mind..."—with these words, [one should worship] the Gārhapatya fire. (Sūtra 10. [First Khaṇḍikā] [On the occasional omission of the recitation prescribed in the Sūtras]: In the case of a sacrifice performed on the same day (*sadyaskālā*), if there is, however, a sequential recitation (*paripāṭha*); [then the recitation is not omitted]. (Bhāṣya)

If it were said, "For the sacrifice today," on the full moon day, then in the verse "I take Agni," the word "today" (*adya*) would be omitted; [in the alternative case where omission does not occur, there would be modification]. [The reason for the omission of the recitation mentioned in the Bhāṣya]. 2.3. Regarding the *sadyaskālā* (immediate performance): there is an omission. Since the connection of the sacrifice with "tomorrow" (*śvaḥ*)—as in "May they rest for the sacrifice tomorrow"—is absent in the *sadyaskālā* rite, and since modification (*ūha*) is impossible in the archetype (*prakṛti*), there must be an omission of the principal term itself.

And because it is impossible [for it to apply], there is no non-intentionality (avivakṣā) on the grounds that it is common to both types of verbal root usage (*prakṛti*), like the word *saṃnatī*. In that case, the non-intentionality of the number is due to the possibility of the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) being realized. Here, however, since the connection with the verbal root is possible during the two-day performance—just as in the expression "being well-disposed toward the rice" (*vrīhīṇāṃ medhaṃ sumanasyamānaḥ*)—and because it denotes something actually present (*samavetābhidhāyitva*), there is simply an omission (*lopa*) in the one-day performance (*sadyaskālā*), just as in the case of rice when barley is used.

If, however, it were to be recited [as it stands], it should be modified (*ūha*). For example, one might say "yajñāya" today—just as one says "sutyām" when there is modification (*ūha*)—but one would not say "śvo yajñāya," because that would contradict the *sadyaskālā* (immediate) rite. Furthermore, [the word "patnī"] lacks connection [in this context]; for while there is a connection [to the sacrifice], there is no connection [to the wife] here. Because it is not common to both, there is no intention to express it there; thus, it is established [that it should be modified].

[The manner of indicating the intended meaning in modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*)] (Bhāṣya): In a modified sacrifice that is to be performed on the same day (*sadyaskālā*), there is indeed modification (*ūha*). And the indication of the specific day on which it is performed is as follows: "This nourishment, the eleventh. [Specific indicative words in certain cases]: Furthermore, for those [sacrifices] that have a change in their name, the indication is by means of that very name; for example, "the Caitra oblation" (*caitraṃ haviḥ*).

"Beyond the fifteenth day, the first, the second," and so forth. [This establishes that the term is an indicator by resolving the apparent contradiction. (Commentary): In the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) performed on the same day (*sadyaskālā*), the phrase "this fifteenth day of *ūrj*" serves as an indicator for the date of the fire-kindling (*anvādhāna*). Since its purpose is the formal selection of the deities to be worshipped, it does not intend to refer to the specific time; therefore, there is no insistence on the fifteenth day itself. Consequently, it is an indicator for the date of the fire-kindling.

For example: "This [is] the eleventh [day], the *ūrja*"; "On the *parvan*, what is the initiation (*dīkṣā*)?"—in this context, regarding the initiation sacrifice (*dīkṣaṇīyā*), there is the omission of the word "fifteenth" (*pañcadaśī*) when the modified qualities (*guṇavikṛti*) proceed on the fourteenth day of the preceding full moon or the preceding new moon. And in the case of the *pathikṛt* [sacrifice], it is at the beginning. [This is a mark for determining the indicative sign: "The name is 'oblation' (*havis*)," for they call those sacrifices "offerings" (*iṣṭi*) by way of indirect designation (*parokṣaṇa*). Of the fifteenth [day]...

"—the sixteenth and the seventeenth. Because of the observation that "months consist of thirty [days] and half-months consist of fifteen," it follows that even the sixteenth [day] would be implied in a calculation based on thirty; thus, it is prohibited. Furthermore, since in the archetype (prakṛti) the new moon day (amāvāsyā) is indeed designated as the fifteenth, and because of the observation, "In the half-month the gods are worshipped; you, O Hotṛ, have sacrificed for the half-months," it must be understood as a designation referring to the half-month in general.

10. Āpastamba Śrautasūtra, Fourth Book, First Patala [Concerning the meaning of the word *antarā*]: (Commentary) *Antarāmī* refers to the space between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires. [The *anvāhitajapa* as a subsidiary of the *anvādhāna*]: The *anvāhitajapa* is a subsidiary element of the *anvādhāna* rite. [Omission of "imām" etc. in certain cases]: 363. Some teachers maintain that the formula beginning with "imām ūrjām" is to be omitted in the case of modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*). [Indication by collective names]: In some instances, there is indication by means of collective terms; those [sacrifices] which have a collective name are indicated by that very collective term.

Just as in the case of the *daivaśyanika* sacrifice, where the oblation is to be offered after it has been prepared (*āpādhyam*). [The view of the Upadeśa school: However, the instruction for the sacrificer regarding the *anvādhāna* ritual ends with the words "this am I" (*idamaham iti*), because that collective [formula] does not exist [in this context]. [Regarding the authority for the two specific fires being the limits in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*): (Vṛtti: "Between the two fires"—that is, between the *gārhapatya* and the *āhavanīya*—[the rule applies], because of the Sūtra-author’s direction: "He does not move between the two fires; if the former has gone out, he should move [to the latter]," and because of the predominance of those two.

[The justification for the primary status of the *anvādhāna*: The recitation (*japa*) following the *anvādhāna* is established as a primary act because it is taught immediately after the *anvādhāna*, despite its being already obtained through that very sequence; furthermore, the rule "he recites when the fires have been piled" (*anvāhiteṣu japatīti*) constitutes a restatement. Therefore, it does not occur in the *someṣṭis*. In the *prāyaṇīyā* and other such rites, because of the absence of *anvādhāna*, one sits to the north of the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) and performs the fourfold recitation (*cātuvarya*).

[The phrase "imām ityādi" serves as the reason for the omission in the *vikṛti* sacrifices. Regarding the mantra "imām ūrjam," some maintain that there is an omission in the *vikṛtis*, because the mention of the ritual acts connected to both lunar phases—namely, "the oblation of the full moon" (*paurṇamāsa-haviḥ*) and "the oblation of the new moon" (*āmāvāsya-haviḥ*)—indicates that, like the *pārvaṇa-homas*, the reference is intended to denote the collective whole. This collective indication applies to those [mantras] such as "divaśśyenāpāghāt" and so forth.

[The intention regarding the position of the instruction: However, there is no such instruction here because of its absence; for the *anvādhāna* (the placing of fuel) in the primary rite involves a single mantra that denotes two collections, which is impossible in the modified rites (*vikṛti*). Another [mantra], however, is connected to the time of the following day. (Sūtra 364) [He says: "This is for the fathers, the oblation for the fathers; I first enclose it so that it may provide us with harmless food"—with this, he places [fuel] on the southern fire.

"May the guardians of the assembly kindle you perpetually, O Agni, as a sharer in victory! O Agni of the assembly hall, shine for me for a hundred autumns for the sake of conquest!"—thus for the *sabhya* fire. "May I bring food to the household for a hundred autumns! May the Lord of the House bestow prosperity and sacred knowledge upon this dwelling!"—thus for the *āvasathya* fire. [Section 2, Sūtra 3]

"I announce this sacrifice to the Vasus, with Agni as their chief; I announce this sacrifice to the Rudras, with Indra as their chief; I announce this sacrifice to the Ādityas, with Varuṇa as their chief"—thus he mutters when the fires have been established. "Rich in milk are the plants"—this [verse] is recited before the *barhis* grass is brought forward. Before the calves are driven away, and before the fire is carried forward, on the new moon day. (Vṛtti): Because of the restrictive rule.

For there is the scriptural observation: "He who indeed grasps the deities beforehand sacrifices to them on the following day. Since the formula "The Vasus, the Rudras... also serves the purpose of grasping the deities to be sacrificed to on the following day, and since formulas such as "The Antarāmīs... have the same meaning as this one, there is the omission of all [of them]. (The remainder is: "In every case, he stands by [the fire] while the anvādhāna is being performed," or "he consecrates [it] with a mantra" (according to the *Rudra*).

2. Here, having begun with the phrase "while the [fires] are being added" (*anvādhīyamāne*), the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) for the five fires are stated; since the conclusion is made with the words "when they have been added" (*teṣvanvāhiteṣu*), it should be understood that for the *sabhya* and *āvasathya* fires, there is a silent addition (*tūṣṇīkam anvādhānam*), even though it is not explicitly mentioned in the *Ādhvaryava* section. Furthermore, there is a Vedic mantra-text: "May the portion of victory kindle [them]" (*vijayabhāga samindhatām*). 3. From the bringing forth (*āharaṇāt*).

Likewise, the phrase "of the one who removes" (*apākartuḥ*) is a definition of time; therefore, when the *anvādhāna* and *parisamūhana* have been performed on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), that is the time for the husband and wife to eat at the *darśa* and other sacrifices, as well as the various alternative views regarding that matter. (Bhāṣya): "Before"—that is, prior to the bringing of the *paristaraṇa* grass-bundle; this applies even to the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*). Or else, it is according to the rule: "On the previous day, the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*idhmābarhis*)."

Having performed the cutting of the branch, one then eats, because the branch is for the purpose of driving away the calves. The instruction is that eating, cutting the branch, and driving away the calves [are to be done together], since the cutting is mentioned separately. (Bṛ) "Previously shown" means it has been demonstrated.

[The specific rule for the full-moon day regarding the meal of the couple: "On the full-moon day as well"—because of the rule that "on the full-moon day there is the placing of the firewood (anvādhāna), the strewing of grass (paristaraṇa), and fasting," and because there is no sacrificial grass (*barhis*) on the preceding day, the phrase "before the fetching of the grass" uses the word *barhis* as an indicator of time; thus, it refers to the strewing of grass. Since eating is a mandatory duty, there is no prohibition against it in this case.

—[Fulfilling the meaning stated in the Bhāṣya beginning with "api vā"]: The instruction "prior to the fetching of the *barhis* grass" proceeds together with the injunction. In the alternative view, there are other options such as eating or performing the *upasad* rites. [Establishing the reason for the specific time of eating at the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices]: Regarding the phrase "having separated the calves from their mothers"—since this is not an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of the mere separation of the calves, there is no eating prior to the cutting [of the grass].

How is it said that "to the Self, to Brahman"? It is explained as follows: because the word "Self" (ātman) is applied to the Inner Ruler (antaryāmin) who dwells within the self, who rules from within the self, and whose body is the self—that is, to the Self residing in the body of the individual soul (jīva)—and because He is the Supreme Self (paramātman), and because the Supreme Self is established as Brahman in all Vedic branches; for it is said: "Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman; Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Self."

Thus, because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the terms Nārāyaṇa, Parabrahman, and Paramātman; because [Nārāyaṇa] is "the great object of knowledge" (*mahājñeya*) and is therefore always to be known; and because of the Vedic revelation: "Whatever one performs with knowledge, that alone is more powerful. How could one meditate upon an action performed for other deities as being Brahman? He who alone is the name-giver of the gods—he is Brahmā, he is Śiva. Therein the four *hotṛ*-priests reach their fulfillment along with the gods.

This is because, in such scriptural passages as "wherein all the Vedas become one," He is understood to be the bearer of the names of all the Vedas, the essential nature of all the gods, the one to be worshipped by all sacrifices, and the one to be enjoined by all injunctive statements. Furthermore, by the term *caturhotṛ*, all sacrifices are denoted, as in the text: "He saw these *caturhotṛ* [formulas] which are for the protection of the self. And the word *veda* refers to both the Mantra and the Brāhmaṇa, according to the statement: "The name 'Veda' applies to the Mantra and the Brāhmaṇa."

The phrase "of Agni and Soma," however, serves the purpose of setting aside [the general rule]. [Explanation of the justification based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) as shown in the Bhāṣya]: There is a recitation of the *anumantraṇa* mantras for other deities, such as "O Agni, you are well-sacrificed" (*agneḥ sviṣṭakṛd asi*). These are the *anumantraṇa* mantras. According to their respective indicative marks (*yathāliṅga*), they apply to the modified (*vaikṛta*) rites because they are specifically assigned to particular deities. In the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice and the *upāṃśuyāja*, however, there is only the mantra "You are the destroyer" (*dabdhir asi*), according to the scriptural statement.

Nor is there a contradiction with the indicative mark (*liṅga*), because it denotes a sacrifice. In the recited collection of post-offering consecrations (*hutānumantraṇa*) belonging to the *upāṃśuyāja*—which has the *darbha* grass as its archetype—some followers of a particular recension (*śākhin*) record certain sacrificial formulas (*yajūṃṣi*) intended for deities other than those of the archetypal rite, prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* mantra. However, since those [deities] are impossible in the archetype, they must override the context (*prakaraṇa*) and be inserted into the modified rites (*vikṛti*) in accordance with their indicative marks.

It might be argued: since the formula "of Indra, the possessor of sense-power" (*indrasyendriyāvataḥ*) is a modification of the *aindrāgna* [offering], the fact that "sense-powers" (*indriyāni*) and "eater of food" (*annāda*) are established [therein] means that the repeated recitation is for the purpose of making it a mantra; otherwise, this would not be a mantra. That which exists in a modification is "modified" (*vaikṛtī*); the consecration by recitation (*anumantraṇa*) refers to the deities of the modification.

Some, however, maintain that the *viṣṇvatikrama* and *atimokṣa* rites are also obligatory—just like the *viṣṇukrama* rites—and that there is only an option between their being performed in conjunction with the main sacrifice or separately; this is incorrect, because their essential nature is not established from any other source in the same way as the *viṣṇukrama* rites. For their establishment does not arise from scripture (*śruti*), since only the *viṣṇukrama* rites are recorded in the context of the *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa* sections of the Darśapūrṇamāsa.

In the Sūtra as well, those very [acts] are prescribed immediately thereafter and are restated in other sections, such as "He pours out the full vessel; he performs the Viṣṇu-steps," and so forth. Even in other ritual manuals (kalpas), the Viṣṇu-steps and the like are not mentioned at all; thus, we do not see the establishment of their essential nature from any source whatsoever. Therefore, it is well said that here their very nature, characterized by the interconnection (vyatiṣaṅga) and so on, is subject to option (vikalpa). This means that there exists a ritual manual for the Viṣṇu-steps alone (ka). Regarding the term *viṣṇukrama*: [ka].

[Explanation of the "Separated" Method (*vinirūḍha-pakṣa*)]: The performance of the "separated" method is as follows: having performed the four *viṣṇukramas* without interruption, and having uttered the three *viṣṇvatikramas*, one should recite the three *atimokṣas*.

(Sūtra): In the *Āpastamba-Śrautasūtra*, this is the *Iṣṭihotrakalpa*: "Thou art the guardian of the vows of the gods. Whatever we have violated of yours, whether with a simple mind or otherwise—since thou hast been generated as the bright banner and the face of all sacrifices—do thou, O Rbhu-like one, perform the sacrifice for us according to the lands rich in men. Svāhā! May there be nourishments that bring wealth and are beneficial to all people."

"O Heaven and Earth, you who have come to you; O Waters, you who have come to you; you whom Tvaṣṭṛ, the well-born, has generated—knowing the path traveled by the fathers, kindling yourself in the exhilaration of the sacrifice, shine forth! Of this hymn, [recite] six verses or the whole of it. "O All-Gods, instruct me as I have been chosen here as the Hotṛ-priest, so that having sat down, I may think what is right for men. Speak to me of the portion to be given, according to you, by which path I shall carry the oblation to you."

He whom I desire with my mind has arrived; he knows the joint of the sacrifice, being wise. May he, the most skilled sacrificer, worship among the deities for us; may he sit down within us, sitting down before us. Today, may I utter that first word of speech by which we may overcome the Asuras through the gods. O eaters of strength, worthy of sacrifice, you five tribes, be pleased with my oblation! Homage to the great, homage to the small, homage to the young, homage to the aged!

(Gha) Regarding the *agnihotra*, the *srugādāpana*, and the *prayāja* formulas: because of their immediate sequence, the author of the Sūtra provides a mere application (*viniyoga*) for the *iṣṭi-hautra* mantras without citing the actual mantras, following the established procedure, as in the passage beginning with "having recited the *sāmidhenīs*," etc., because of the statement that "the others [are taken] from the direct instruction."

The specific application is established according to the *viniyoga* (prescribed usage) stated by Āśvalāyana. Therefore, "O Agni" (*amite*) is the formula for taking up the offering-ladle (*srugādāpana*). Because it is not recited [in the standard sequence], the phrase "O Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, you have sacrificed" (*amiṃ sviṣṭakṛtam ayāḍ agneḥ*) is used in the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering as an indicator of the deity. If it were performed—on account of the statement of Baudhāyana and the statement of Bharadvāja—it may be performed optionally everywhere; if it were performed, then the *vyāhṛtis* would be recited even in the absence of the *yeyajāmahe* formula, prior to the *yājyā*.

Regarding the instruction "in those [offerings]"—the author of the Sūtras has stated that the *vyāhṛti* follows the utterance of *yeyajāmaha*. Because of this instruction of immediate sequence, the designation of the deity occurs after that. However, there are no *vyāhṛtis* in the *anūyāja* offerings, because of the absence of *yeyajāmaha* there. [The *vaṣaṭ* call is high-pitched: The loud utterance of the *vaṣaṭ* call is prescribed by two scriptural passages (*śruti*) as being higher than the *yājyā* verse. For one whom he desires should become wealthier, he should pronounce the *vaṣaṭ* call higher than the *yājyā* verse.

In the *Yukteṣu*, the *Iḍā* is explained as being both directed forward (*parācī*) and backward (*praticī*). (Sūtra 19): But there is a prohibition of the repetition of the word. (Bhāṣya): "Repetition of the word" (*padābhyāsa*) and "prohibition" (*pratiṣedha*) together constitute "the prohibition of the repetition of the word. This is established by two scriptural texts (*śruti*). (Sūtra 20): It is known from scripture: "When it says 'iḍopahūtā' (the *Iḍā* is invoked), that is directed forward; when it says 'upahūtā' (invoked), that is directed backward. 883.

By these two [statements], "the *iḍā* is turned away" (*parācīm*) is a prohibition for a word that is the same [in form], while "turned toward" (*pratīcīm*) is an injunction for repetition regarding a word that is not the same. How is this established without doubt from another scriptural passage? From the subsequent [text]: "The *iḍā* has been invoked; the *iḍā* has been invited. Since the *iḍā* is recited for us in the sequence beginning with "turned away," it is prohibited [from being repeated]. The *iḍā* turned away and turned toward shall be explained: "He who should desire, 'May I have cattle,' for him the *iḍā* is turned toward"—this is the explanation based on such scriptural authority (*śruti*).

And there is the repetition of the word—of this word, the meaning is as follows: since even those who know the path (adhvavādibhiḥ) ought not to desire for themselves a fruit that is non-animal-like (*apaśutva*) and of an inauspicious nature, which is the result of the *yajamāna-iṣṭi*, the prohibition of its being "turned away" (*parācī*) is made by the words "its *iḍā* [is] turned away. "Of the same word" (*samānasya padasya*) means "of a similar word. The word "invoked" (*upahūtā*) is similar to the word "invoked" (*upahūtā*) in the phrase "the *iḍā* is invoked," because they are to be performed as a single action through transposition.

Because the syllables are identical, similarity exists merely due to a difference in sequence, while the word remains the same; therefore, there is a prohibition against using two similar words such as "parācīm" and "tasya. The rule "of a non-identical word" (asamānasya padasya) is an injunction for the repetition of a single dissimilar word, such as "upahūteḍā. [The variants are: "prohibition of that month" (a. and "for the sake of the ritual procedure" (a.).]

— How so? Regarding the meaning of the words *parācīṃ* and *pratīcīṃ*, he says: "It is for the sake of the modification (*vikṛti*); the application [of the rule] that was prohibited is for the sake of the modification, because of the instruction of the prohibition in the archetype (*prakṛti*). If it is asked, "How can there be an insertion of what was prohibited in the modification?", [the answer is: "It is for the sake of the modification. (Bhāṣya) It is for the sake of the modification. [Note: This passage refers to Āpastamba Śrautasūtra, Dṛṣṭihautrakalpa, Khaṇḍa 14, Sūtra 20.]

Lest the recitation become meaningless, the phrase "upaiteḍa upaiteḍa" is employed to express the sense of the verbal root; or rather, a prohibition is made against the repetition of words that are identical, as in the case of the "aparācī" [verse].
Therefore, it is explained by another scriptural passage that the invitation (upahava) must be performed facing westward.

4. [The repetition] is by way of the subsequent [verse]. 3.5. Alternatively, the meaning is that our [position] is not prohibited. That is indeed another case where there is an equal repetition of words; this is the Saṅkarṣa-pakṣa. 20. Let it not be so—because of the lack of injunction—the state of being "parācī" (turned away) implies non-repetition. Or rather, because of the scriptural observation "nine are parācī," there is an instruction for repetition in the form "pratīcīm" (towards oneself) as its counterpart, specifically regarding the mantra "upahūteḍā."

Although in the Śruti text the first recitation belongs to the *parācī* (the subsequent one), nevertheless, according to the view that it is a *dvandva* compound—namely, "the prohibition of the repetition of words"—the term "prohibition of the repetition of words" (*padābhyāsa-pratiṣedha*) is placed first because it is more important as something to be performed by the *pratīcī* (the preceding one). Alternatively, when it is understood as a *ṣaṣṭhī* (genitive) compound, then the prohibition applies specifically to the *parācī*, namely, "the [recitation] of 'iḍopahūtā'."

Furthermore, even though a single [mantra] is being employed with both directness and repetition, because of the statement that "repetition of a word is prohibited," the quality of repetition is only figurative when two similar words are used; the prohibition "of that which follows" applies to the case where "iḍopahūta" is recited.

Therefore, [the phrase] "by the west" (pratīcyā) is understood through the subsequent passage beginning with "O Upahūta, come to us," and so forth; thus, it is taken as being for the purpose of an injunction regarding the necessity of performing the *upahava* (invocation) toward the west, according to another Vedic recension (*śruti*). This is one interpretation. Alternatively, "the meaning" (*atha vārtha*) refers to another interpretation. Our own position (*asmadīya-pakṣa*)—namely, that where in another branch (*śākhāntara*) the repetition of a single word is primarily recited, there is a prohibition of that—is the view of the *Sakarṣa* school.

In this view, the application follows the reading as follows: 3. Regarding "prohibition of invitation" (pratiṣiddhopahava): [The text] "asmatīyā na pratiṣiddhā" (our own [invitations] are not prohibited) is found in versions a, 2, and parācya-kha-ga-gha. 4. "Sāda" is in version kha. 5. "Itareṇeti" is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) according to version ṅa. 6. "ddhā" is in version ṅa; "anyaiva" is in version kha-ga; "mathaveti" is in version gha. 7. "asmatīyā" is in version gha. 8. "tata" is in version gha. 9. "miti" refers to another interpretation. 10. "asmatīyān pratiṣiddhā" is in version kha; "anyaiva pratiṣiddhā" is in version kha.

The repetition of words similar to those found elsewhere is the position of Śākara. (Sūtra 462). In the commentary adorned by Vartasvāmin and accompanied by the gloss of Śrī Rāmāgnicit: [Section 14, Sūtra 21] "From this point onward, the other rites belong to the Adhvaryu; the others are taught for the Hotṛ because of direct instruction. (21). (Bhāṣya) The duties of the Adhvaryu have been stated, and the duties of the Hotṛ in their entirety regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. "Direct instruction" refers to the Bahvṛca-Āmnāya (the Ṛgveda corpus).

Therefore, the modified (*vaikṛta*) rites are not distinct from what is handed down in scripture (*āgama*). Something is prescribed in the modification; in that case, because our *hautra* (the portion recited by the Hotṛ priest) is largely based on the Ṛgveda, something is prescribed [from it]. Alternatively, there is an option between what is prescribed in one's own tradition or in the Ṛgvedic collection. However, regarding the repetition of quarters (*pādābhyāsa*), the author of the Sūtra would certainly not have recited them incompletely.

—(vṛ) Regarding the *ādhvaryava* and *hautra*: since the remaining duties of the *hautra* not mentioned in this section, such as "he recites fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses," and so forth, are taught in the *ādhvaryava-kāṇḍa*, it follows that for us, the entire *hautra* of the New and Full Moon sacrifices has been taught [there]. This teaching of the *hautra* is because it is stated in the *paribhāṣā* that "the *hotṛ* performs his duty with the *Ṛgveda*"; or else, the term may be analyzed as a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "because it is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to the *Bahvṛca*."

Wherever there is an option (*vikalpa*), for us, however, because there is no instruction regarding the *sāman* as being like the original form (*prakṛti*), there is an option between our own [text] and that which is taught in the *Bahvṛca* concerning the modified form (*vikṛti*). But where the author of the Sūtras states, "But where there is the repetition of words," and so forth, and it is said, "The instruction of the modified property (*vaikṛta-dharma*) is prohibited for the sake of the modification (*vikṛti*)," in those cases there is an option with the *Bahvṛca*.

"The author of the Sūtras does not recite [the mantra] in its entirety"—because the author of the Sūtras is one who interrupts the ritual application (*prayoga*), and since the application is impossible if it is not recited in its entirety, there is an option (*vikalpa*) even regarding the instruction of the Sūtra-author. [Notes on variants: - *vaikṛtāni* (variant readings: *baḍhaca*, *ga*; *dikṛta*, *kha ga*). - *ukta hotra kātsnrena* (variant: *vikṛtāvasmadīyaṃ tatra*, *gha*). - *paṭhanti* (variant: *paṭhalīti*, *ga*). [Translation of the full passage: "The author of the Sūtras does not recite [the mantra] in its entirety," because the author of the Sūtras is one who interrupts the ritual application; since the application is impossible if it is not recited in its entirety, there is an option even regarding the instruction of the Sūtra-author. [The preliminary limb of the establishment and the manner of the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): One should purify oneself through austerity, burnt offerings, and recitations.

Having established friendship with all beings along with his wife, [he should proceed]. Regarding this, there is the traditional authority (*āgama*): "In whatever matter the sequence of mantras (*mantrāmnāya*)—such as the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses—is found in our own [Vedic school], in that case the application (*prayoga*) according to the *Bahvṛca* is fixed. Even though the complete instruction is given for the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the application according to the *Bahvṛca* is nonetheless optional.

Thus ends the *Hautrakalpa* (the section on the duties of the Hotṛ priest) in the commentary on the *Śrīmad-Āpastamba-Śrautasūtra* composed by Vartasvāmin, as prepared by Śrī Rāmāgnicid. Now begins the Fifth Book (*Praśna*), concerning the specific application and the authoritative evidence for the oblations and other rites as shown in the commentaries. [To be purified]—one should offer these [oblations] at the beginning of the rituals; for it is seen in the *Śruti*: "Being purified, he attains the worlds of the gods," and so forth. Furthermore, it is seen in the *Smṛti*: "Having first performed [this], one becomes pure," and so forth. Thus, this applies to all Vedic rites.

For the purpose of establishing the fitness for accomplishing the fires that serve as the means for performing ritual acts (*karma-sādhana*), the purification of both the wife and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*)—who are the qualified persons (*adhikārin*) for the *ādhāna*—must be performed. Now, indeed, who is purified? [The answer follows: "Only he who has previously performed the *iṣṭi*... Thus, having explained the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, [the author] now begins the *Āgnīdhreya* (the laying of the sacred fires), which is the very first to occur and serves as a benefit to the entire Śrauta section. The term *āgnīdhreya* is formed with the suffix *ya* in the sense of the action itself (*bhāve*), according to the rule of "diversity" (*bāhulakāt*).

The term *abhirādheya* is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "that action by which [the person] is to be propitiated. This is because even in the *Smṛtis*, it is listed among the necessary purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) for a person, just like initiation (*upanayana*) and others; because of the statement of Vasiṣṭha; because the Teacher [Āpastamba] also enumerates it as a duty of the twice-born (*varṇadharma*); and because Manu also mentions the state of not maintaining the sacred fires (*anāhitāgnitā*) among the minor offenses (*upapātaka*).

Because Bodhāyana has also taught that there is a specific fruit pertaining to this world. (BaudhŚS 2.464) In the commentary adorned by the *Dhūrtasvāmibhāṣya* together with the *Śrīrāmāgnicidvṛtti*, Fascicle 1, Sūtra 2: On whichever lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) he desires to establish the sacred fires, or on a full-moon day (*parvan*), one year prior to that, or twelve days before, he performs the formal resolve (*sakalpa*). "I shall establish the fires for the sake of all sacrifices—those by which I have been consecrated and those which I shall be able to perform."

"In the spring, under the Kṛttikās, on the full moon, or on such-and-such a festival" (Sūtra). [The fetching of the fire-drills; a difference of opinion regarding lightning and the sword. "The Aśvattha tree which has grown from the womb of the Śamī, having ascended together with you—that I fetch for you by means of the sacred word (*brahman*), along with the sacrificial signs. With this, he fetches the two fire-drills from an Aśvattha tree that has grown from the womb of a Śamī. (2) 886. (Vṛtti): Indeed, that which manifests in a pure womb...

Now, why indeed is the sacrificer [called] "Agni-purified" (agni-śuddha), or why is he said to be "born of Agni," since he is afflicted by evil? [The answer is: "Indeed, there is for him a fulfillment (*pūrti*) in his ritual acts; austerity (*tapas*) itself burns away his evil. This is because of the scriptural vision: "Therefore, he becomes pure and gentle (*saumya*). Alternatively, for the sake of completing the ritual without obstacle, a friendly disposition (*maitra*) must be maintained toward all beings by both the wife and the sacrificer.

"In which constellation"—that is, in whichever constellation one intends to establish the fires (*agnyādheya*), [one should do so] in that year, according to the times to be mentioned hereafter, such as "previously" and so forth. Regarding "the joints of the fire-sticks" (*agnīnām parvaṇīti*), this includes the ritual manual (*kalpa*). [The role belongs to] the Adhvaryu. Regarding "of the *śamī*-womb" (*śamīgarbhasya*), there is a genitive compound; since the measurement of the two kindling woods (*araṇi*) has not been explicitly stated, it is defined by its functional purpose. Baudhāyana says: "It should be four finger-breadths in height, twelve finger-breadths in width, and sixteen finger-breadths in length."

"Kātyāyana says it should be twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). One should have the two fire-drills (*araṇī*) made while reciting the *Gāyatrī* mantra; for one who recites it, the fire-drills come to be exactly the number of finger-breadths corresponding to the syllables of the mantra," so it is stated in the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa (Ru. 3). [Notes: *asivā*—kha, ga; "Again and again, his very austerity burned away his evil"—kha, ga; "Likewise, for the sake of completion without obstacle, O Pārtha, friendliness toward all beings must be practiced"—gha; because it is common to the *Homa* and other rites—465; *ayajña*—khaṃ.]

[1, sū 6. Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra, Fifth Book, First Patala. (Commentary: Then follows the procedure beginning with the fetching of the two kindling woods (*araṇi*) and ending with the placing of the fuel-sticks (*samidh*). [The mantra] "thou art lightning" (*vidyud asi*) is not used because of its nature. However, in the case of *iṣṭi* sacrifices, since they are modifications (*vikāra*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the mantras "thou art lightning" and "and rain" (*vṛṣṭiś ca*) are employed. According to the direct instruction (*upadeśa*), the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is "thou art lightning. Furthermore, in the *iṣṭis*, the fetching of the two kindling woods and so forth is accompanied by the mantras for lightning and rain.

[The agent, place, time, etc., of the fetching of the kindling woods: 3. The fetching of the two kindling woods (*araṇi*)—even if they have been previously cut—is performed by the Adhvaryu at the same time with a single mantra near the *aupāsana* fire in the morning. 2. The upper kindling wood (*uttarāraṇi*) is fetched in a quantity sufficient for as long as one lives. In the phrase "that which is the *aśvattha* tree," the whole is used figuratively for a part. And the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) is performed simultaneously. [Here ends the section characterized by the commentary text. (Ghṛ) Then, from the placing of the kindling woods until the end of the gift of the *brahmaudana*.

[The justification for the presence of *vidyut* in the context of the true state of being: Regarding the instruction on the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*)—"in all sacrifices"—the mention of "sacrifice" (*yajña*) is intended as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of oblations (*homa*) and so forth; therefore, the formula "thou art lightning" (*vidyud asi*) should be employed even in the *āghāra* libations, the *caturhotṛ* recitations, and the like. After the mental resolve, the lightning indeed comes into existence. [The cause for the difference in the application of the unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) of lightning: Regarding the two fire-drills (*araṇī*), the instruction is that there is a difference in application due to the difference in ritual performance (*prayoga*). The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that this is because [the fire-drills] are not auxiliary parts (*anaṅga*).

When the offerings are performed immediately after the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), then the *vidhu* and *dṛṣṭi* sacrifices are obligatory (*nitya*). However, when they are performed on the same day (*sadyas*), even though the offerings are auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the *ādhāna*, the effect produced by the *ādhāna* still occurs. [This is established through the examples of the taking up of two previously broken vessels and the designation of a tree. Because two vessels that have not been previously broken or dried out lack the capacity to produce fire, it is only with those previously broken that this applies in rites such as the *dvādaśāha*.

Even though the words of the mantra are in the singular number, because they refer to the pair of fire-drills (*araṇī-yugala*), the singular form is to be employed simultaneously as uttered once; there is no repetition. The term *yo aśvattha-paryāyaḥ* [means] that the word *aśvattha* refers to both [drills]. And the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) is simultaneous, even though it ends in the singular. [Note: *uttarāraṇyapi* (also the upper drill), *paryāptāyāvajjīvasya hriyate* (is carried for as long as one lives), *rekhā* (line/mark), *bhāvitatvāt* (because of being manifested/contemplated). [The analysis of the compound *śamīgarbha-pada*] (Bṛhadāraṇyaka-bhāṣya): According to the view that it is not *a-śamīgarbha*, the term *śamī* is used; thus, *śamyā garbhaḥ śamīgarbhaḥ* is a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound, and not [a bahuvrīhi] meaning "that of which the womb is a śamī tree. This is because the earth is praised as being "the śamī," and thus the *śamī* serves as the substratum. [Sūtra and Bhāṣya]—[The establishment of the distinction in number shown in the Bhāṣya, and the resulting difference in fruit]: "Of the many"—eight earthen and eight wooden [vessels] always; those ending with gold are the eight to be employed.

In the sevenfold option, there is the omission of the sugar-candies (*śarkarā*), because gold (*hiraṇya*) is necessarily present. And so says the author of the *Bhāṣya*: "In the fivefold option, he will state that copper fragments take the place of gold as the fifth. Some maintain that even in the fivefold option, eight larger earthen pieces are not obtained. [Note: Even in the case of a fire produced from a *śamī* tree, there is no cessation of the mantras, because the praise is directed toward the *aśvattha* tree alone when it is within a *śamī*, and because this is stated by Hiraṇyakeśin and Bodhāyana.

Alternatively, the construction is: "If one were to install [the fires] on the full moon day of Phalgunī, the Adhvaryu would place that sacrificer into the mouth of the year. This is because the use of the *parasmaipada* (active voice) is appropriate here. Therefore, the installation must indeed take place two days or one day prior to the full-moon festival (*parvan*). Furthermore, this deprecation of the Phalgunī full moon follows the logic of deprecating what has not been prescribed; it is intended as a praise for the subsequent injunction, not for the purpose of its total rejection, as that would result in the injunction being rendered meaningless.

Therefore, two options are prescribed; however, Bhāradvāja says that one should not establish the sacred fires on the full moon day that falls between the two former Phalgunīs (Kha. 3; *vā* is not seen in manuscript Kha).
