Here, the arrangement of the seasons is either by the solar year or by the lunar month; both ways are established in the scriptures. Some [cite]: "The Moon is the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ; he shall determine the seasons," according to the Śruti.

Some say that [the determination of seasons] follows the lunar month (*cāndramasī*); that is incorrect, because there is scriptural authority for another way as well: "O gods, we shall purchase Soma; prepare the seasons. However, in the *Kālatantra*, the calculation of seasons generally proceeds by following the solar month (*saura*). In that system, when the sun stands in Aries or Taurus, that is the solar spring (*vasanta*). As stated by the elders: "In the northern solstice (*udagayana*), beginning with Capricorn, the seasons such as winter and the rest [proceed] according to the sun. And: "The equinox (*viṣuva*) occurs between autumn and spring."

Thus it is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*. The lunar [year] consists of seasons formed by lunar months. When the sun has entered Aries and so forth, each new moon (*darśa*) that arrives marks the end of the respective lunar months beginning with Caitra. Among these, Caitra and Phālguna constitute the spring; for the Śruti declares: "Spring is indeed the face of the seasons," and "Phālgunī Pūrṇamāsa is indeed the face of the year."

The statement, "The full moon of Citrā is indeed the mouth of the year," intends to show that it is included within the [beginning of the] season, for it is impossible for it to be the mouth of both seasons. Nor can the opposite be maintained, because the full moon of Phālgunī cannot be included within the [specific] season. Furthermore, in the Vājasaneyaka, with reference to the Aśvamedha sacrifice, it is recorded: "Therefore, one should begin sacrificing in spring itself; the full moon occurs on the two Phālgunīs. Therefore, spring begins with Phālgunī.

Others say it begins with Caitra, as they have stated: "The six seasons are traditionally remembered as beginning with Māgha in pairs of months; however, the northern transit (*uttarāyaṇa*) should be known as beginning with Śiśira, consisting of three [months] each. Also, in the *Chāndogya-kalpa*: "One should sacrifice in the autumn month of Kārtika. Therefore, Vaiśākha is also considered the spring according to the lunar calendar. When possible, the conjunction of the aforementioned seasons, sacrificial festivals, and asterisms is the proper course, as stated by Āśvalāyana.

"Where the three—the season (*ṛtu*), the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), and the lunar phase (*parvan*)—concur, that [time] is successful; but in case of conflict, the season and the lunar mansion are stronger," so says Satyāṣāḍha. However, it is heard in the *Vājasaneyaka*: "Just as one might attempt to enter a city through a place other than the gate when the gate is closed, he would be like one entering the city crookedly; even so, he who establishes the sacred fires under an inauspicious lunar mansion—he therefore should not establish them under a lunar mansion. Furthermore, praise is shown for establishing the fires on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*).

Likewise, [it is said]: "On that new moon day of Vaiśākha which coincides with Rohiṇī, one should establish the sacred fires. This has been explained by Baudhāyana: "That new moon day which follows the full moon of Vaiśākha coincides with Rohiṇī several times in a year; on such a day, one should establish the fires. Having cited the scriptural passage, "One should establish the fires as soon as the sacrifice approaches him," he explains it as referring to one who is distressed and possessed of excessive faith.
And Bhāradvāja said: "Now, therefore, one who has faith does not ask about the season, nor about the lunar mansion" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.19).

Or he may set out on a one-day journey. [Third Khaṇḍikā: The Installation of the Sacred Fires in Spring for the Purpose of Both [Soma and Agnyādheya], and the Commentary-author’s Agreement. (Bṛhaddevatā commentary): The installation of the fires (*ādhāna*) does not, by its very nature, coincide with the spring season as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the Soma sacrifice; rather, the spring serves the purpose of both. Thus, according to the Commentary-author, even in the case of the "Soma-installation" (*somādhāna*), when one performs it on the New Moon day (*amāvāsyā*), where there is no water... [text fragment ends].

In the statement "they are filled," the attainment of the *ajasra* (perpetual) fires is mentioned by virtue of the installation on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). Since no disregard for the lunar festival days (*parvan*) has been stated even regarding the installation for the Soma sacrifice, for this very reason some maintain that the Soma-installation—under the view that there is only one initiation (*ekadīkṣā*) and so forth—must be performed only on a festival day and not on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) or other such dates, because the Soma-installation also necessitates all [the requirements of the ritual]. [Conclusion of the stated argument and Jaimini’s consensus: Therefore, if the time for the installation were merely set aside, the injunction "one should not shave" would be rendered meaningless in the case of a Brāhmaṇa.

Likewise, regarding the statement "Soma may belong to a Brāhmaṇa by virtue of his excellence" (*Jaimini Sūtra* 5.4.10), in the section concerning the womb (*garbhādhikaraṇa*), in the case of the injunction "one who intends to sacrifice with Soma," the time for Soma—which consists of the period following the New and Full Moon sacrifices—is set aside by the force of the connection between the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) and the Soma sacrifice occurring on the same day. By parity of reasoning, if the *ādhāna* is performed at another time, disregarding the spring season, then for the sake of connecting that very day with the Soma sacrifice, the Soma itself must necessarily be set aside from its [prescribed] time.

Therefore, the statement, "On whatever day faith approaches him," is intended to indicate that there is no restriction regarding the interval between the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) and the *Soma* sacrifice, because of the intention to perform the *Soma* sacrifice as soon as possible. [This is our own view. However, according to Bharadvāja’s statement, "But for us, 'on whatever day the sacrifice approaches' indicates a disregard for all specific times," it follows that for that *ādhāna*, there is likewise disregard for the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and other such factors. (Note: *sambandha* is the reading in manuscript *kha*).

[The meaning of the terms *śālīna* and *yāyāvara*: *Udavasānam* means departing for another place. [He departs] together with the *aupāsana* fire. A *śālīna* is one who dwells in a single place. A *yāyāvara* is one who is constantly traveling. Third Khaṇḍikā. *Āpastamba Śrautasūtra*, Fifth Praśna, First Paṭala, Sūtra 2. [The meaning of the terms *śālīna* and *yāyāvara*. (Commentary): *Udavasānam* is the departure to another region. Together with the *aupāsana* fire. A *śālīna* is a resident of one place. One who is constantly on the move is a *yāyāvara*. Third Khaṇḍikā.

"May the impurity being dug up destroy the evil of the sacrificer. May the four quarters be auspicious to us; may Mother Earth be propitious to our offspring. Having thus dug up the sacrificial ground for the gods, which slopes toward the east, and having sprinkled it with water while reciting, "May the divine waters be for our aid and for our drink; may they flow toward us for health and prosperity," he constructs a shelter there with its beams pointing northward.

[The time for the moving of the fires according to specific alternatives: (Bhāṣya) In the *asambhāra* alternative, the bringing of the two fire-sticks (*araṇi*) and the moving of the fires after the sacrifice (*udavasāna*) are indeed required. The bamboo-pole—namely, the rain from the north—is itself the middle one. (Sūtra) 4.5: "In front of that, the site of the *gārhapatya* fire is along the middle bamboo-pole. 2.24.920. [The obligatory nature of the moving of the fires: (Vṛtti) *sahau*—the dweller; for him, the moving of the fires (*udavasāna*) is obligatory.

[The place for the *ādheya* of the *yāyāvara*: The *yāyāvara* is one who is constantly traveling; his place for the *aupāsana* fire is precisely that very spot. His residence—there he does not construct a *gārhapatya* shed. Or rather, even the *yāyāvara* may reside wherever he halts during a journey of a single day. [The fire] should be kindled while it is still raining. [The fire] is oriented toward the north (*udīcīna-vaśa*, i.e., *udīcīna-pṛṣṭha-vaśa*). For the sake of the water-retreat (*udavāsāya*), he should establish the fires.

Having placed the oxen facing north, [the measurements are as follows]: facing north, facing north, facing north—31, 482 (Bhāṣya) (Sūtra), accompanied by the commentary of Śrī Rāmāgnicit and adorned with the Bhāṣya of Dhūrtasvāmin. To the east of that [central point] is the site for the Āhavanīya fire. To the east of that, at eight *prakramas*, is the site for the Brāhmaṇa’s Āhavanīya fire; at eleven [steps], that of the Rājanya; and at twelve, that of the Vaiśya. || 3 || 25 || 921 ||

(Śūtra): "In twenty-four [steps], or in an unlimited [distance], or as far as one judges with the eye; therefore, it should not be placed too far away. This is heard as applying without distinction to all [the fires]. [The commonality of the differences in the location and measurement for the establishment of the fire, and the divergence of opinion in certain cases. (Bhāṣya): "In twelve strides, the purpose is fulfilled for us all. [This is the explanation of the commentary beginning with *tasyāgreṇa*: Its measurement is explained by the sūtra: "The middle [line] is measured by its tip (*atreṇa*)."

The northern direction is the middle direction. The site for the *gārhapatya* fire is in front of that *śaraṇa* shed, at its middle point toward the east. [Regarding the measurement for all purposes: "In twelve"—meaning "in our twelve," because there is no specific mention in the scripture that one should place the fire in exactly twelve strides (*vikrama*). The site for the *gārhapatya* fire is in front of the lower part of the spine of that *śaraṇa* shed. When eight *prakramas* have been traversed from that, the site for the *āhavanīya* fire is reached.

A *prakrama* consists of two or three steps (*pada*). According to Bodhāyana, it is fifteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) long; according to Kātyāyana, it is twelve finger-breadths. The fire should be established at a distance of twenty-four *prakramas* or in a location of unlimited extent. It has already been stated previously that "unlimited" refers to a distance greater than the aforementioned measurement.

Regarding the phrase "as far as [measured] by the eye," and so forth, its meaning is as follows: one does not measure the dust by means of the eight-step distance (*prakrama*) and so on; rather, it refers to that extent of space which one determines with the eye according to the aforementioned *prakramas*, such that when it is seen, it is twenty-four [units]. Therefore, "not too far" means that the object to be placed should be at a proximity within a small interval of that limit. Thus says the Brāhmaṇa: "One should place [the fire] measured by the eye, as far as it can be seen. Satyāṣāḍha has also stated this.

Regarding these three injunctions, even in the view stated by Baudhāyana—"One should establish the fire for all castes within twelve strides"—the Hiraṇyakeśins have shown them to be for the sake of all [castes], since it is heard without qualification: "One should establish the fire within twelve strides. This is the explanation of the phrase "for the sake of all [castes]."

[Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra, Fifth Book, First Chapter, Sūtra 4. (Commentary): As much as one deems sufficient—whether eight strides or twelve—is the measure by sight (*cakṣurmāna*). And [distances] of twenty-four [strides] and so forth apply to all [cases], because it is heard in the scripture without distinction and without regard for a specific person. "Unmeasured" (*aparimita*) means uncounted. Since [the distance] would otherwise be obtained as either too short or too long, therefore [it is said]: "It should not be placed too far away."

Therefore, it is not too far from that which is prescribed—meaning, even in the absence of a specific measurement, it is "not too far. Even though there is no specific measurement, because of the prohibition against being too far, it is understood to be within [the prescribed distance]. According to some, it may also be obtained beyond that; for them, "too far" is what is commonly known in the world.

"One should maintain the eye-measure" (cakṣurmitaparigraha)—up to when one considers "ten"—the meaning of this is as follows: because it is intended to demonstrate that there are ten strides measured by the eye, the eye-measure is connected to all numbers. [The meaning of words such as "all"]: the eye-measure applies to all castes. Therefore, even in the absence of a prescribed measurement—meaning even when a specific distant measurement is lacking—one should proceed according to the twenty-four [strides] and so forth.

"From that which is prescribed as not too far"—because of the prohibition of "too far" and because twelve strides (*dvādaśavikrāma*) and so forth have been prescribed, there is a prohibition of even greater distance than those; thus, "unlimited" (*aparimitam*) refers to [a distance] prior to twenty-four [strides]. This is what is meant: the measure by sight (*cakṣurmāna*) is unlimited, and [the terms] are for the purpose of prescribing another location that excludes excessive distance among all possible numbers. Some maintain that it is obtained even beyond twenty-four [strides].

[The cause for obtaining supreme honor is established] because there is no indication of a limit that is very far from them. 1. "How many are these eight?"—there are eight *ga*s. 8. "Ati" is a prohibition—*gha*. 4. "Dhāt"—*sva*. *ga*. 6. "Thāt"—*kha*. 2. 923. [The Location of the Southern Fire] (Bhāṣya): The *dakṣiṇāgni* fires are situated slightly beyond the third part [of the distance] from the *gārhapatya*, either in the *āhavanīya* hall or in the *gārhapatya* hall. (Sūtra 2): The *āhavanīya* hall is one, and the *gārhapatya* hall is another. 6. 28. 924. In front of the *āhavanīya*, in the assembly hall (*sabhā*), is the *sabhyāgni*. 7. 29. 925. To its east, in the guest-house (*āvasatha*), is the *āvasathyāgni*. 8. 30. 926. A Brāhmaṇa may also have four such halls.

(Bhā) [The meaning of the Bhāṣya through the explanation of the third part]: (Vṛ) "Slightly removed from the southern corner"—having set aside a portion of the western third part in the space between the two corners, the site for the southern corner-fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*) is to the south. [Regarding the measurement when there are four huts]: "Four huts" means that for that [fire-altar] there are four huts: those for the *sabhya*, *āvasathya*, *gārhapatya*, and *āhavanīya* fires.

Because [the term] *brāhmaṇa* is also present [in the context], [the word *samīpa*] is used in the sense of proximity (*samīpa-saptamī*). [The phrase] "to the south and slightly east of the Gārhapatya" refers to that place which has departed from the third part of the space between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires; it is so described in order to refute the opinion that it is closer to the Gārhapatya.

According to Bodhāyana’s statement regarding the Middle Country, "to the south of the Viṣuvat [day], behind the Anvāhāryapacana fire"—meaning at a short distance behind the third part [of the sacrificial ground]—the house for the Āhavanīya fire must be constructed separately; the meaning is that the sacrificial shed for the Dakṣiṇāgni should be established in either of those two [locations].

4. *Sabhā* (the assembly hall): the meaning is that its sacrificial altar (*āyatana*) should be located there; [it is] the dwelling place for guests. 6. Regarding the *udīcīnavaṃśāśālā* (the hall with beams pointing north), only this much was stated by Hiraṇyakeśin in the section on the *Ādhāna* (fire-consecration); however, in the *Yājamāna* (section on the duties of the sacrificer), two types of houses are mentioned (second book). The altars for the *Sabhya* and *Āvasathya* fires are mentioned (third book). (In the context of commenting on Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.1.17, it is stated: "One should prepare the fire-altars. 5. *Āvasatha* (the guest-house).

In the commentary on the fourth *sūtra* of the first chapter of the fifth book of the *Āpastamba Śrautasūtra*, in the explanation of the fourth *sūtra* regarding the observation of the sacrificer’s attendance [at the fires] ending with the *pūrṇāhuti*, it is stated that the binding of the *anvāhāryapacana* and *sabhyā* fires is performed silently (*tūṣṇīm*). [Sūtra 9]: He shaves his hair and beard, trims his nails, and does not cut them [too short]. The wife does likewise, except for the hair. (9) [Commentary]: *Vapate* means he causes [his hair] to be shaved.

[The attire of the couple at the time of the fire-consecration (ādhāna): (Sūtra) The husband and wife, wearing linen garments, shall establish the sacred fires. [Etymology of the terms *sabhya* and *āvasathya*, and the section defining the measurement of the sacrificial site, etc. According to the statement, "that which exists in the assembly (*sabhā*) is *sabhya*; that which belongs to the dwelling (*āvasatha*) is *āvasathya*," there is a distinction between these two as well. The measurement of the area for these and their construction are stated precisely in the *Śulba-sūtra*.

In that regard, although the measurements for the space between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires have been stated, nevertheless, because of the technical rule (paribhāṣā) stating that it should end toward the east or toward the north, the intermediate space would be either to the east or to the north. Therefore, in some cases, one should establish the Āhavanīya at eight steps to the north of the Gārhapatya. Furthermore, there would be no fixed rule as to which end of the interval constitutes the site of the Gārhapatya and which the site of the Āhavanīya.

Although in that case all [details] could be restricted by other characteristics such as the Āhavanīya fire, the sacrificer's height, and the square shape of the altar, nevertheless, because they are part of the injunction for performance (*prayogavacana*), it is also appropriate to adopt the position of ending toward the east (*prāgapavarga*) for the sake of ease of execution, just as in the case of the injunction "having offered oblations from the hair down to the base of the pillar."

[The intention of the commentary here and the intention of the statement by Vaikhanasa: Therefore, for the purpose of removing all doubts regarding that, the middle point of the Gārhapatya hearth is established by means of its front edge. Consequently, this is stated again here in order to enjoin the meaning: "To the east of that, at eight steps, is the front edge of the Āhavanīya hearth. However, in the *Śulba-sūtra*, this measurement is intended only for the sacrificial altar (*vihāra*) and not for the daily fire ritual (*darśika*); thus, the details concerning the location and so forth as stated by Vaikhanasa should be consulted therein. (Note: *vāpayate* is the reading in the *Ga* manuscript.)

However, Bharadvāja says: "Some say they should be worn before the *brāhmaudanika* fire; others say before the pouring down of the *saṃbhāra* materials. 3. Regarding the *sabhya* fire... [text fragment] ...according to the *śruti* concerning the *agnyādheya*... [text fragment] ...Śrī Rāma... [text fragment] ...accompanied by the *icidvṛtti* commentary, adorned with the *bhāṣya* of Dhūrtasvāmin. [Section 4, Sūtra 13.]

1. Wearing two new, unwashed linen garments (*kṣauma*), the husband and wife should kindle the fires beginning with the *gārhapatya*. They themselves should perform the kindling; for it is not only the *adhvaryu* who performs the placement of the *brāhmaudana* fire. While all the fires beginning with the *gārhapatya* are being established, the husband and wife remain present, wearing their linen garments, as they possess the right to perform the ritual acts. Alternatively, they may both hold onto the *adhvaryu*. At the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), these two garments are given to the *adhvaryu*. 11 || 33 || (Sūtra) || 929 ||

In the afternoon, or when the sun is behind the trees, having taken fire from the *aupāsana* hearth, he establishes the *brāhmaudanika* fire to the west of the site of the *gārhapatya*. (Sūtra 3.12.34; 930). It may be either the *aupāsana* fire or the fire produced by friction (*nirmanthya*), or indeed the entire [set of fires]. (Sūtra 3.13.35; 931). [Regarding the acceptance of the *aupāsana* fire, the merits and defects of the views that it is either the whole or a part, and the view of direct instruction. (Bhāṣya): In the case of one who has not performed the complete establishment of the fires (*asarvādhāna*), there is no cessation of the rites belonging to the *aupāsana* fire.

[The justification for the husband and wife being agents by virtue of mere proximity: "Wearing two linen garments, they remain in close proximity"—this is the meaning. Because the phrase "wearing two linen garments" is intended as an injunction regarding the linen, because the term *jāyāpatī* (husband and wife) is a restatement (*anuvāda*), because the fire-installation (*ādhāna*) is prescribed in the section on the *Ami* sacrifice, and because it has the *adhvaryu* priest as its agent, the status of the husband and wife as agents in the performance of the rite arises merely through their proximity.

Alternatively—[the nature of the Adhvaryu’s indirect agency in the act of following]: "The two should follow the Adhvaryu"—this is for the purpose of establishing indirect agency, just as in the case of the subsequent oblations when one has already taken hold of the Gārhapatya and other ritual fires. [Regarding the non-cessation of the relationship]: in the absence of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), there is no cessation of the duties related to the *aupāsana* fire—namely, the *aupāsana* oblations and so forth. He alone performs them. (Manuscript *gha*).
